docs.title: ECEG-6201 — Analytical Optimization and Stochastic Processes
docs.text:
MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester I

Welcome to the course website. This site hosts the complete lecture notes, worked examples, computational implementations (Python / Java / C#), quizzes, and tutorial problems for the two halves of this course: optimization (Chapters 1–3) and stochastic processes (Chapters 4–7).

docs.title: Course at a glance
docs.text:
Course code ECEG-6201 Credit hours (ECTS) 3 (5) Semester Year 1, Semester I Status General Area Compulsory Course Pre-requisites None Instructor Dr. Tesfamichael Gebregziabher Contact (office, email, office hours)

Teaching & learning methods. Lectures supported by tutorials and assignments.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Formulate and solve optimization problems

    Recognize an optimization problem, characterize its minima, and choose a gradient / Newton / quasi-Newton / penalty method appropriate to its smoothness, dimension, and cost per evaluation.

  • Model and analyze random phenomena

    Work with random processes, correlations, spectra, and mean-square estimation. Apply stochastic-process tools to communication-engineering systems.

  • Analyze Markov chains and queues

    Classify a Markov chain, compute its stationary distribution, and derive the performance measures of elementary queuing systems.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• Optimization — Preliminaries

    Minima, gradients, Hessians, optimality conditions (KKT), line search, numerical vs. analytic gradients, adjoint variables.

    Chapter 1

  • Unconstrained Optimization

    Direct search (Nelder–Mead, pattern search), Newton, quasi-Newton (BFGS), Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt.

    Chapter 2

  • Constrained Optimization

    Penalty and barrier functions, augmented Lagrangian, quadratic programming (KKT system, active-set preview).

    Chapter 3

  • Stochastic Processes & Random Walks

    WSS vs. SSS, correlations, random walks, Poisson points, shot noise, cyclostationarity, sampling, matched filter, entropy.

    Chapter 4

  • Spectral Representation & Estimation

    Wiener–Khinchin, Karhunen–Loève, spectral factorization, ergodicity, periodogram/Welch, LMMSE, Wiener filter, Kalman filter.

    Chapter 5

  • Markov Chains

    DTMC, classification (recurrent/transient/periodic), stationary distribution, ergodicity, CTMC and generator matrix.

    Chapter 6

  • Introduction to Queuing Theory

    Kendall notation, Little's formula, M/M/1, M/M/s (Erlang-C), M/M/1/K, Pollaczek–Khinchine, Jackson networks, discrete-event simulation.

    Chapter 7

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Read in order

    Chapters are designed to be read in sequence — each builds on the previous. Chapter 1 lays the mathematical foundations for optimization; Chapter 4 introduces the probabilistic tools that Chapters 5–7 build on.

  • Check your understanding

    Every chapter has a three-part quiz (MCQ, fill-in, define/explain) with an inline answer key. The tutorial problems at the end of each chapter are extra exercises; solutions are in the Solutions page.

  • Run the code

    Every chapter has Python, Java, and C# implementations of its main algorithms. Copy the snippets, run them, and compare against the analytical answers worked out by hand.

  • See the schedule

    The Schedule page has the week-by-week plan: lecture topics, tutorial sessions, reading assignments, and assessment dates.

docs.title: Recommended preparation
docs.text:
No prior background in optimization or stochastic processes is assumed, but the following will make the course much easier:

  • Linear algebra — matrix algebra, eigenvalues, positive-definite matrices
  • Calculus — partial derivatives, gradients, Taylor expansion
  • Probability — random variables, expectation, variance, common distributions
  • Python — NumPy and SciPy are used throughout for the computational demos (Java and C# equivalents are also provided for students from those backgrounds)

If any of these feels shaky, review Boyd & Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Appendices A–C (free PDF online) or Papoulis & Pillai, Chapters 1–5 before the first lecture. Both are linked from the Resources page.

docs.text: How you are graded, how to submit, and what happens when things go wrong.

docs.title: Breakdown
docs.text:
Component Weight Timing Format Assignments (7, one per chapter) 20% Weeks 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 16 Take-home; theory + code Mid-semester examination 30% Week 8 2 h, closed book Final examination 50% Week 18 3 h, closed book Total 100%

Per-assignment weight: ~3% each (7 × 3% = 21%; the actual split is announced with each assignment to reflect the size of the task — the total is exactly 20%).

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
Each assignment covers one chapter and combines theory with computation:

  • ~60% theory. Analytical problems similar to the tutorial problems, but longer and requiring a full solution — derivation, justification, and interpretation of the result.
  • ~40% implementation. A Python / Java / C# program that implements an algorithm from the chapter, runs it on a specified problem, and reports the results. Code must be your own; libraries such as scipy.optimize are allowed only when the assignment explicitly permits them.

docs.title: Rubric (per assignment)
docs.text: Criterion Weight What earns full marks Correctness of final answers 40% All answers correct and complete, including units and interpretation Rigour of derivations 20% Each step justified; no hidden assumptions; notation consistent Computational implementation 20% Code runs, produces correct results, is readable and commented Interpretation and discussion 15% Results placed in context; limitations and edge cases discussed Presentation 5% Clear structure; plots labelled; references cited

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
• Format. A single .pdf report (typeset with LaTeX, Markdown → PDF, or Word) plus the source code in a .zip bundle. The PDF must also contain the code listings (or an appendix with the source).
  • Naming. A<n>-<lastname>-<student-id>.pdf and A<n>-<lastname>-<student-id>.zip.
  • Channel. Upload to the course Moodle/LMS assignment dropbox.
  • Deadline. 23:59 local time on the due date. Late submission loses 10% of the maximum mark per calendar day; after 3 days, the submission scores zero.

docs.title: Mid-semester examination (30%)
docs.text:
• Format. 2 h, closed book, no calculators beyond a basic scientific one.
  • Content. Covers Chapters 1–3 in full. Weighting is approximately 30% / 40% / 30% across the three chapters — reflecting the amount of material in each.
  • Structure. Typically 4–6 questions, mixed theory and computation: state a definition or theorem; derive a result; solve a small problem by hand; interpret a numerical result.
  • Sample papers. Past mid-semester papers are available on the LMS; the solutions are discussed in the tutorial in week 7.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Confusing necessary and sufficient conditions (FONC vs. SOSC).
  • Forgetting to check convexity before claiming a stationary point is a global minimum.
  • Sign errors in the KKT multipliers — the sign convention matters.
  • Wrong condition-number intuition — a small condition number is good.
  • Copying a formula without stating the assumptions — most formulas in Chapter 3 (penalty, barrier, augmented Lagrangian) require specific conditions (feasibility, strict feasibility, rank conditions).

docs.title: Final examination (50%)
docs.text:
• Format. 3 h, closed book, same calculator policy as the mid-semester.
  • Content. Covers the whole syllabus, with approximately 40% on Chapters 1–3 and 60% on Chapters 4–7 (matching the split of teaching hours).
  • Structure. Typically 6–8 questions. Theory and computation as in the mid-semester, with longer multi-part problems.
  • Emphasis. Chapters 4–7 are examined more heavily because they contain most of the applied material — random walks, shot noise, cyclostationarity, sampling, spectral factorization, LMMSE, Wiener, Kalman, Markov chains, M/M/1, M/M/s.

docs.title: What to bring
docs.text:
• Non-programmable calculator.
  • One hand-written A4 formula sheet, both sides. This must be your own handwriting — printed or photocopied sheets are not allowed.
  • Student ID card.

The formula-sheet rule is deliberate: writing it forces you to review every formula, and consulting it during the exam saves you the risk of a sign error.

docs.title: Grade boundaries
docs.text:

docs.title: Late policy
docs.text:
• Assignments: 10% of the maximum mark per calendar day (including weekends), capped at 3 days. After 3 days, the submission scores zero.
  • Examinations: no late sitting. Missing an examination without documented cause scores zero.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Extensions are granted only for documented medical, family, or other exceptional circumstances:

  1. Submit a request before the deadline, with documentation (medical certificate, family emergency record).
  2. The instructor will grant an extension of typically 3–7 days, proportional to the disruption.
  3. If the deadline is missed due to a sudden emergency, contact the instructor within 48 hours of the deadline with documentation.

Unsubstantiated requests are declined. Extensions are never granted retroactively except for a confirmed emergency.

docs.title: Make-up examinations
docs.text:
• Mid-semester: students with documented medical or family emergencies may sit a make-up examination in week 10. The content and format are the same as the original; the maximum mark is capped at the class median of the original exam (standard practice to remove the "second chance" advantage).
  • Final: governed by the university's rules for deferred examinations. Application is made to the Registrar's Office, with medical documentation, within 5 working days of the missed exam.

docs.title: Academic integrity
docs.text: All submitted work (assignments, exams) must be your own.

docs.title: What is allowed
docs.text:
• Discussing the concepts and methods with classmates — this is encouraged.
  • Consulting textbooks, lecture notes, and online references (cite them).
  • Using standard libraries (numpy, scipy, matplotlib) as permitted by the assignment brief.
  • Comparing your final answers with classmates after both have submitted — to check your reasoning.

docs.title: What is not allowed
docs.text:
• Copying code or text from another student, past submissions, or an online source.
  • Sharing your code or write-up with classmates before the deadline.
  • Using AI tools to generate code or text that you present as your own (see below).
  • Re-submitting work submitted in another course.

docs.title: On AI tools
docs.text:
Large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, etc.) are powerful learning tools but cannot be used to generate submitted work. Permitted uses:

  • Explaining a concept you don't understand.
  • Debugging your own code (show the code, ask "why is this wrong?").
  • Checking a derivation you have already done.

Not permitted: pasting an AI-generated answer or code as your submission. If in doubt, ask the instructor before submitting.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Confirmed plagiarism or unauthorised AI use results in:

  • First offence: zero on the assessment component, and a written warning on file.
  • Second offence: zero on the assessment component and a report to the Dean's office, which may lead to academic probation or expulsion.

All submissions are screened with plagiarism-detection tools. Code is additionally screened for AI-generated signatures.

docs.title: Feedback and grades
docs.text:
• Assignment feedback: returned within 2 weeks of the submission deadline. Feedback is delivered through the LMS, with comments on each rubric criterion and a numeric mark.
  • Examination grades: posted within 3 weeks of the exam date.
  • Grade queries: if you believe a mark is incorrect, email the instructor within 1 week of receiving the result, with a written justification (what you expected, what you received, and why). Regrade requests that result in a lower mark are not reversed.

docs.title: Exam Bank — ECEG-6201 Analytical Optimization and Stochastic Processes
docs.text:
40 questions spanning all seven chapters. Use for self-assessment and exam preparation. Answers and grading rubric at the end.

Instructions (for a mock exam):

  • Time: 3 hours
  • Closed book; one A4 handwritten formula sheet allowed
  • Non-programmable calculator permitted
  • Total marks: 100
  • Marks per question in brackets

docs.title: A1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which of the following is a necessary condition for a differentiable \(f\) to have a local minimum at an interior point \(x^\star\)?

(a) \(f(x^\star) = 0\) (b) \(\nabla f(x^\star) = 0\) (c) \(\nabla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\) (d) \(f\) is convex

docs.title: A2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In multi-objective optimization, a point \(x^\star\) is Pareto-optimal if:

(a) It minimizes a weighted sum of objectives (b) No feasible point improves some objective without worsening another (c) It is a local minimum of each individual objective (d) It satisfies the KKT conditions

docs.title: A3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Define the gradient and Hessian for a function \(f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R\). State the geometric interpretation of the Hessian's eigenvalues.

docs.title: A4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the first-order necessary condition (FONC) and the second-order sufficient condition (SOSC) for a strict local minimum. Give an example of a function that satisfies FONC but not SOSC at a point that is not a minimum.

docs.title: A5. Derivation [5]
docs.text: Starting from the line-search subproblem \(\min_{\alpha > 0} \phi(\alpha) = f(x_k + \alpha d_k)\), derive the golden-section search update rule. State the shrinkage factor per iteration and the number of iterations needed to reach tolerance \(\epsilon\) from initial bracket length \(L_0\).

docs.title: B1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Newton's method converges in how many iterations on a strictly convex quadratic?

(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) \(n\) (d) arbitrarily many

docs.title: B2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The secant condition for the BFGS Hessian approximation is:

(a) \(B_{k+1} y_k = s_k\) (b) \(B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\) (c) \(B_{k+1} = I\) (d) \(B_{k+1} = \nabla^2 f\)

docs.title: B3. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Describe the Nelder–Mead simplex algorithm. State its reflection, expansion, contraction, and shrink steps with their standard parameters.

docs.title: B4. Derivation [4]
docs.text: Derive the Newton step for unconstrained minimization from the second-order Taylor expansion. State the local convergence rate and one reason plain Newton can fail.

docs.title: B5. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the Gauss–Newton step for nonlinear least squares. Under what condition does it achieve quadratic convergence?

docs.title: C1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which method requires a strictly feasible starting point?

(a) Exterior penalty (b) Logarithmic barrier (c) Augmented Lagrangian (d) QP active-set

docs.title: C2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In the exterior penalty method, the penalty parameter \(\mu\) must tend to:

(a) \(0^+\) (b) \(1\) (c) \(+\infty\) (d) any value

docs.title: C3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the KKT conditions for \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x) \le 0\), \(h_j(x) = 0\). Include complementary slackness.

docs.title: C4. Derivation [5]
docs.text: For a quadratic program \(\min \tfrac12 x^\top Q x + c^\top x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), derive the KKT linear system. State the existence and uniqueness condition.

docs.title: C5. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Compare the augmented Lagrangian and the exterior penalty method. Why does the augmented Lagrangian avoid the ill-conditioning of pure penalties?

docs.title: Section D — Stochastic Processes & Random Walks (Ch 4) — 15 marks
D1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A WSS process has:

(a) Constant variance, arbitrary mean (b) Constant mean, autocorrelation depending only on lag (c) Gaussian distribution (d) Finite energy

docs.title: D2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The variance of a shot-noise process \(\sum_i h(t - t_i)\) (Poisson arrivals, rate \(\lambda\)) is:

(a) \(\lambda \int h(s)\, ds\) (b) \(\lambda \int h^2(s)\, ds\) (c) \(\lambda^2 (\int h)^2\) (d) \(0\)

docs.title: D3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State Campbell's theorem. Give two engineering applications of shot noise.

docs.title: D4. Derivation [4]
docs.text: For \(X(t) = \sum_k a_k\, p(t - kT)\) with i.i.d. zero-mean \(a_k\), derive \(R_X(t + \tau, t)\). Show that \(X\) is cyclostationary with period \(T\).

docs.title: D5. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Derive the matched filter for detecting a known signal \(s(t)\) in white Gaussian noise. State the maximum output SNR.

docs.title: Section E — Spectral Representation & Estimation (Ch 5) — 15 marks
E1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The Wiener–Khinchine theorem states that the PSD is:

(a) The variance of the autocorrelation (b) The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation (c) The reciprocal of the autocorrelation (d) The mean of the signal

docs.title: E2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The periodogram of white noise is:

(a) A flat line (b) Unbiased but has variance equal to its mean (c) Consistent (d) Zero at all frequencies

docs.title: E3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the Spectral Factorization Theorem. Why must the factor \(L(z)\) be causal, monic, and minimum-phase?

docs.title: E4. Derivation [4]
docs.text: For an observed process \(Y = S + N\) with \(S \perp N\), derive the non-causal Wiener filter \(H_{\text{opt}}(\omega)\) that minimizes the mean-square error.

docs.title: E5. Short answer [4]
docs.text: State the Kalman filter predict and update equations. Interpret the Kalman gain \(K_k\) in words.

docs.title: F1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A probability vector \(\pi\) is a stationary distribution of a DTMC with transition matrix \(P\) if:

(a) \(\pi P = \pi\) and \(\sum \pi_i = 1\) (b) \(P\pi = \pi\) and \(\sum P = 1\) (c) \(\pi = P^T\) (d) \(P = \pi \pi^\top\)

docs.title: F2. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Classify states as recurrent / transient and periodic / aperiodic. State the ergodic theorem for finite irreducible aperiodic chains.

docs.title: F3. Derivation [4]
docs.text: For a birth–death DTMC with birth probabilities \(p_k\) and death probabilities \(q_k\), use detailed balance to derive the stationary distribution \(\pi_k\). State the positive-recurrence condition.

docs.title: F4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Write the generator matrix \(Q\) for a CTMC. State the Kolmogorov forward equation and how the stationary distribution is obtained from \(Q\).

docs.title: G1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Little's formula \(L = \lambda W\) holds:

(a) Only for M/M/1 (b) Only for Poisson arrivals (c) For any stable queuing system (d) Never

docs.title: G2. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the stability condition for an M/M/1 queue. What happens to the stationary distribution when the condition is violated?

docs.title: G3. Derivation [4]
docs.text: For an M/M/1 queue with arrival rate \(\lambda\) and service rate \(\mu\), derive the stationary distribution \(\pi_n\) and the mean number in system \(L\). Assume \(\lambda < \mu\).

docs.title: G4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the Erlang-C formula. Give one practical application in call-centre staffing.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text: Click to reveal answers

docs.title: Section A
docs.text:
A1. (b) — \( abla f(x^\star) = 0\) is necessary; SOSC \(\succ 0\) is sufficient.

A2. (b) — Pareto-optimality: no feasible point Pareto-dominates it.

A3. Gradient: \( abla f = (\partial f/\partial x_1, \ldots, \partial f/\partial x_n)^ op\). Hessian: \( abla^2 f = [\partial^2 f/\partial x_i \partial x_j]_{i,j}\). Geometric: eigenvalues of the Hessian are the principal curvatures of \(f\) at that point; eigenvectors are the directions of maximum and minimum curvature. Positive eigenvalues ⇒ bowl up (convex); negative ⇒ bowl down; mixed ⇒ saddle.

A4. FONC: \( abla f(x^\star) = 0\) if \(x^\star\) is a local min and \(f\) is differentiable. SOSC: \( abla f(x^\star) = 0\) and \( abla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\) ⇒ \(x^\star\) is a strict local min. Counterexample: \(f(x) = x^3\) at \(x = 0\) has \(f'(0) = 0\) but \(f''(0) = 0\) — the point is an inflection, not a minimum.

A5. Golden-section places two interior points \(c = b - au(b-a)\) and \(d = a + au(b-a)\) with \( au = (\sqrt 5 - 1)/2 \approx 0.618\). Evaluate \(\phi(c), \phi(d)\); keep the subinterval that contains the smaller value. Each iteration reduces the bracket by \( au\) with one new evaluation. Number of iterations to reach tolerance \(\epsilon\) from initial bracket \(L_0\): \(k = \lceil \log(\epsilon / L_0)/\log au ceil\).

docs.title: Section B
docs.text:
B1. (a) — one step for a strictly convex quadratic.

B2. (b) — \(B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\) with \(s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k\), \(y_k = abla f(x_{k+1}) - abla f(x_k)\).

B3. Nelder–Mead: maintain a simplex of \(n+1\) points. Sort by \(f\) value. Compute centroid \( ar v\) of all but worst. Reflection \(\alpha = 1\): \(r = ar v + ( ar v - v_{ ext{worst}})\). Expansion \(\gamma = 2\): \(e = ar v + 2(r - ar v)\) if reflection is better than the best. Contraction \( ho = frac12\): \(c = ar v + frac12(v_{ ext{worst}} - ar v)\) if reflection is worse than second-worst. Shrink \(\sigma = frac12\): \(v_i \leftarrow v_{ ext{best}} + frac12(v_i - v_{ ext{best}})\) if contraction also fails.

B4. Taylor: \(f(x_k + d) \approx f(x_k) + abla f(x_k)^ op d + frac12 d^ op abla^2 f(x_k)\, d\). Set gradient in \(d\) to zero: \( abla f(x_k) + abla^2 f(x_k)\, d = 0\), giving \(d_k = -( abla^2 f(x_k))^{-1} abla f(x_k)\). Convergence: local quadratic if Hessian at the solution is positive-definite. Fails: when the Hessian is singular (no unique step) or indefinite (not a descent direction); a line search or regularization \(H + \mu I\) fixes this.

B5. For least squares \(\min frac12 \|r( heta)\|^2\), the Gauss–Newton step solves \((J^ op J)\Delta = -J^ op r\), where \(J = \partial r/\partial heta\). Quadratic convergence iff the residuals at the solution are zero (dropped term \(\sum r_i abla^2 r_i = 0\)); otherwise only linear.

docs.title: Section C
docs.text:
C1. (b) — logarithmic barrier requires strictly feasible interior point.

C2. (c) — \(\mu o \infty\).

C3. KKT for \(\min f\) s.t. \(g_i \le 0\), \(h_j = 0\): (i) \( abla f + \sum_i \mu_i abla g_i + \sum_j \lambda_j abla h_j = 0\); (ii) \(g_i(x) \le 0\), \(h_j(x) = 0\) (feasibility); (iii) \(\mu_i \ge 0\) (dual feasibility); (iv) \(\mu_i g_i(x) = 0\) for each \(i\) (complementary slackness).

C4. Lagrangian \(\mathcal L = frac12 x^ op Q x + c^ op x + \lambda^ op(Ax - b)\). Gradient in \(x\): \(Qx + c + A^ op\lambda = 0\). Gradient in \(\lambda\): \(Ax - b = 0\). Combine: \( egin{bmatrix}Q & A^ op \ A & 0\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}x \ \lambda\end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix}-c \ b\end{bmatrix}\). Existence & uniqueness: \(Q \succ 0\) and \(A\) full row rank.

C5. Exterior penalty drives \(\mu o \infty\), which makes the Hessian eigenvalues grow like \(\mu\) in constraint-normal directions — condition number grows like \(\mu\); simple solvers fail. Augmented Lagrangian \(\mathcal L_ ho = f + \lambda^ op h + frac{ ho}{2}\|h\|^2\) uses a multiplier update \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + ho h(x)\). When \(\lambda\) converges to the true KKT multiplier \(\lambda^\star\), the constrained optimum is the exact minimizer of \(\mathcal L_ ho\) for any fixed \( ho > 0\). No need to drive \( ho o \infty\) ⇒ no ill-conditioning.

docs.title: Section D
docs.text:
D1. (b).

D2. (b) — \(\lambda\int h^2(s)\,ds\).

D3. Campbell's theorem: for Poisson arrivals rate \(\lambda\) and response \(h\), \(\mathbb E[X(t)] = \lambda\int h\), \(\operatorname{Var}[X(t)] = \lambda\int h^2\), \(R_X(\tau) = \lambda\int h(s) h(s+\tau)\,ds + \lambda^2 (\int h)^2\). Applications: photodetector current (photon arrivals), neural spike trains (synaptic filtering), interference modeling in wireless.

D4. \(R_X(t+\tau,t) = \sum_{k,m}\mathbb E[a_k a_m] p(t+\tau-kT)p(t-mT) = \sigma_a^2\sum_k p(t+\tau-kT)p(t-kT)\). The right side is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T\) — so \(X\) is cyclostationary. The time-averaged autocorrelation \(\bar R_X(\tau) = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\int p(s+\tau)p(s)\,ds\) is the WSS-equivalent.

D5. Output SNR at time \(T\): \(\text{SNR} = |\int s(\tau) h(T-\tau)\,d\tau|^2 / \left[(N_0/2)\int h^2(u)\,du\right]\). By Cauchy–Schwarz, \(\text{SNR} \le 2E_s/N_0\) with equality iff \(h(t) \propto s(T-t)\). Matched filter: \(h(t) = s(T-t)\), maximum output SNR \(= 2 E_s / N_0\).

docs.title: Section E
docs.text:
E1. (b).

E2. (b).

E3. Any rational PSD with no zeros on the unit circle and \(\int\log S > -\infty\) can be factored uniquely as \(S_X(z) = \sigma_e^2 L(z)L(z^{-1})\) with \(L\) causal, monic, minimum-phase. Why: (i) causality makes \(1/L\) causal (whitening realizable); (ii) monic fixes the scale so \(\sigma_e^2\) is uniquely the innovations variance; (iii) minimum-phase ensures smallest \(\sigma_e^2\) — any non-minimum-phase factor would have larger innovation energy.

E4. \(H_{\text{opt}}(\omega) = S_{SY}(\omega)/S_{YY}(\omega) = S_{SS}/(S_{SS} + S_{NN})\). High SNR → \(H \approx 1\) (pass); low SNR → \(H \approx 0\) (reject); equal → \(H = 0.5\). The filter shapes the passband by the local SNR.

E5. Predict: \(\hat x_{k|k-1} = A\hat x_{k-1|k-1}\), \(P_{k|k-1} = AP_{k-1|k-1}A^\top + Q\). Gain: \(K_k = P_{k|k-1}H^\top(HP_{k|k-1}H^\top + R)^{-1}\). Update: \(\hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1} + K_k(z_k - H\hat x_{k|k-1})\), \(P_{k|k} = (I - K_kH)P_{k|k-1}\). \(K_k\) is the weight on the new information — large when measurements are reliable (small \(R\)) or prediction is uncertain (large \(P\)), small in the opposite case.

docs.title: Section F
docs.text:
F1. (a).

F2. Recurrent: return probability \(f_i = 1\). Transient: \(f_i < 1\). Periodic: period \(d(i) = \gcd\{n \ge 1 : P^n_{ii} > 0\} > 1\); aperiodic if period 1. Ergodic theorem: for a finite irreducible aperiodic DTMC with stationary \(\pi\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty} P^n = \mathbf 1\pi\) and \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N f(X_n) \to \sum_j \pi_j f(j)\) a.s.

F3. Detailed balance for birth–death chain: \(\pi_k p_k = \pi_{k+1} q_{k+1}\), so \(\pi_k = \pi_0\prod_{j=0}^{k-1} p_j/q_{j+1}\). Normalize: \(\pi_0 = 1/(1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} p_j/q_{j+1})\). Positive recurrence: the infinite sum converges.

F4. Generator \(Q\): \(Q_{ij} \ge 0\) for \(i \ne j\) (transition rate \(i \to j\)), \(Q_{ii} = -\sum_{j \ne i} Q_{ij}\) (so each row sums to 0). Kolmogorov forward: \(\dot P(t) = P(t) Q\), solution \(P(t) = e^{Qt}\). Stationary distribution solves \(\pi Q = 0\) with \(\sum \pi_i = 1\).

docs.title: Section G
docs.text:
G1. (c).

G2. \(\rho = \lambda/\mu < 1\). If \(\rho \ge 1\), the queue is not positive recurrent — no stationary distribution; queue length grows unboundedly.

G3. Detailed balance: \(\pi_n \lambda = \pi_{n+1}\mu\), so \(\pi_n = \pi_0 \rho^n\) with \(\rho = \lambda/\mu\). Normalize: \(\pi_0 = 1 - \rho\). Mean: \(L = \sum n\pi_n = \rho/(1-\rho)\).

G4. \(C(s, a) = \Pr\{N \ge s\}\) for an \(s\)-server queue with offered load \(a = \lambda/\mu\): \(C(s,a) = \pi_0 a^s / (s!(1 - \rho))\) with \(\rho = a/s\). Application: given target wait probability (say 20%), find the minimum \(s\) such that \(C(s,a) \le 0.20\) — the standard staffing formula used in call centres.

docs.title: Grading rubric (for instructors)
docs.text:
Band Marks Criteria A 90–100 All correct or with trivial slips; rigorous derivations; clear interpretation B 75–89 Most correct; occasional gaps; derivations mostly sound C 60–74 Basic understanding; some errors in derivations or interpretation F < 60 Major conceptual gaps; significant derivations missing

Point allocation. MCQ all-or-nothing. Short answers partial credit per correct step. Derivations partial credit per correct line.

Common error checks (and deductions):

  • Wrong sign in KKT or Lagrange multiplier: −1 to −2.
  • FONC/SOSC confusion (claiming FONC ⇒ minimum): −2.
  • Golden-section factor wrong (0.5 instead of 0.618): −1.
  • Confusing WSS and stationarity conditions: −1.
  • Wiener–Khinchine sign convention (using \(+j\omega\) instead of \(-j\omega\)): −1.
  • Uniqueness condition wrong for QP (missing full row rank): −1.
  • Little's formula misapplied to unstable queue: −2.
  • Stationary distribution of M/M/1 wrong (\(\pi_n = \rho^n\) instead of \((1-\rho)\rho^n\)): −2.

docs.title: Feedback and Corrections
docs.text: This site is a living document. If you spot an error, a typo, a broken link, or an explanation that isn't clear, please report it — the course improves when students tell me what doesn't work.

docs.title: What to report
docs.text: Category Examples Typo Misspelled word, wrong punctuation, inconsistent symbol (\(\lambda\) vs. \(\Lambda\)) Mathematical error Wrong sign, missing factor, incorrect formula, incorrect numeric answer Broken link A chapter link that returns 404, a reference to a textbook chapter that doesn't exist Rendering problem Equation not displaying, table misaligned, code block unreadable on mobile Clarity issue A worked example whose steps don't follow; a definition that is ambiguous; a solution step that skips justification Tutorial problem A problem that is under-specified, has no solution, or contradicts the chapter Attribution A borrowed figure or example that isn't credited Accessibility Missing alt text, poor colour contrast, keyboard-inaccessible interaction

docs.text:

docs.title: Acknowledged contributions
docs.text:
Contributors who report errors that lead to a substantive fix are acknowledged by name on the affected page (with permission). This is a small way of recognising the effort of the students and colleagues who help improve the course.

If you would rather stay anonymous, just say so when you report — the acknowledgment is entirely opt-in.

docs.title: How this page is maintained
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs + Material theme, deployed via GitHub Pages. All content lives in the docs/ directory of the repository. Corrections are made by editing the corresponding .md file and pushing to main — the GitHub Actions workflow rebuilds and redeploys in under a minute.

The # file name: header at the top of each chat exchange is not part of the published site; it's an artefact of how the course materials are drafted and reviewed.

docs.title: Thank you
docs.text: A course is never finished. Every correction you send makes the next cohort's experience a little better. Thank you for taking the time to write one.

docs.title: Optimization (Chapters 1–3)
docs.text: Book Chapters used Notes Boyd & Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Cambridge University Press, 2004 1–5, 9–11 🆓 PDF at web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook. Clearest treatment of optimality conditions and interior-point methods. Nocedal & Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2nd ed., Springer, 2006 1–3, 6, 10, 16–17 The standard reference for the algorithms in Chapters 1–3. Luenberger & Ye, Linear and Nonlinear Programming, 4th ed., Springer, 2016 1–4 Classical engineering treatment, lighter on convex analysis. Bertsekas, Nonlinear Programming, 3rd ed., Athena Scientific, 2016 1, 3, 4 The definitive reference on constrained optimization and duality. docs.title: Stochastic processes (Chapters 4–6)
docs.text: Book Chapters used Notes Papoulis & Pillai, Probability, Random Variables, and Stochastic Processes, 4th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2002 8–11 The standard stochastic-processes reference. Chapter 9 (spectra) is the source for Chapter 5. Leon-Garcia, Probability, Statistics, and Random Processes for Electrical Engineering, 3rd ed., Pearson, 2008 5–9 Gentle, engineering-oriented, with good examples. Karlin & Taylor, A First Course in Stochastic Processes, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 1975 1–4, 12–14 The classical reference for random walks, Poisson, and Markov chains (Chapters 4 and 6). Ross, Introduction to Probability Models, 11th ed., Academic Press, 2014 2–6 Excellent balance of theory and application; also the source for many queuing exercises. Norris, Markov Chains, Cambridge University Press, 1997 All The definitive modern reference for Markov chains (Chapter 6). Levin, Peres & Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, AMS, 2009 1–4, 12 Modern treatment with applications to MCMC. Kemeny & Snell, Finite Markov Chains, Springer, 1976 All Matrix-theoretic treatment of finite chains. Kay, Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing: Estimation Theory, Prentice-Hall, 1993 2–5, 12 Rigorous treatment of LMMSE, Wiener, and Kalman. Hayes, Statistical Digital Signal Processing and Modeling, Wiley, 1996 8, 10 The definitive textbook for spectrum estimation (periodogram, Welch, AR, MUSIC). Stoica & Moses, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Prentice-Hall, 2005 2–4 Modern spectral analysis with rigorous treatment. Kailath, Sayed & Hassibi, Linear Estimation, Prentice-Hall, 2000 All Unifies LMMSE, Wiener, and Kalman in one orthogonality framework. Anderson & Moore, Optimal Filtering, Dover, 2005 All The classical Kalman and Wiener reference. Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 2–3, 8–10 Rigorous treatment of Shannon entropy, differential entropy, and the Gaussian channel.

docs.title: Queuing theory (Chapter 7)
docs.text: Book Chapters used Notes Gross, Shortle, Thompson & Harris, Fundamentals of Queueing Theory, 5th ed., Wiley, 2018 1–5 The standard textbook. Medhi, Stochastic Models in Queueing Theory, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2003 1–4 Comprehensive single-volume reference.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text:
This course introduces the mathematical foundations and practical algorithms of two complementary areas that underpin modern communication engineering:

  • Optimization — how to formulate engineering design problems as mathematical programs and how to solve them numerically: unconstrained and constrained methods, gradient-based and derivative-free algorithms, penalty/barrier and augmented-Lagrangian approaches, quadratic programming.
  • Stochastic processes — how to model random signals, noise, arrivals, and Markovian systems: stationarity and correlation, spectral representation, Karhunen–Loève expansion, innovations and factorization, Wiener and Kalman filtering, Markov chains, and queuing theory.

The two halves connect where they always do in practice: estimation (Chapter 5) is optimization of a mean-square-error criterion under a stochastic model, and queuing (Chapter 7) is a birth–death Markov chain whose stationary distribution drives every performance measure.

docs.title: Course objectives and competences
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  1. Familiarize themselves with engineering optimization methods and know which to apply for a given problem.
  2. Formulate and solve engineering design problems as optimization programs, choosing appropriate algorithms and justifying the choice.
  3. Understand the principles of the modelling and analysis of random phenomena, distinguishing wide-sense from strict-sense stationarity and using correlation and spectral tools.
  4. Apply the essential mathematical tools needed to analyze systems affected by random processes — including matched filtering, Wiener filtering, and Kalman filtering.
  5. Use the algorithms required for the representation and estimation of random signals — Karhunen–Loève, spectral factorization, innovations representation, mean-square estimation.
  6. Analyze Markov chains and elementary queuing systems, computing stationary distributions and performance measures.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
On successful completion, students will be able to:

# Outcome Assessed by LO1 Characterize a minimum (local, global, Pareto), compute gradients and Hessians, apply first- and second-order optimality conditions A1, Mid-sem LO2 Select and apply appropriate unconstrained algorithms (direct search, Newton, BFGS, Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt) A2, Mid-sem LO3 Formulate constrained problems and solve them via penalty, barrier, augmented-Lagrangian, and QP methods A3, Mid-sem LO4 Analyse random processes: WSS/SSS, correlations, spectra, sampling, matched filter, entropy A4, Final LO5 Apply spectral representation and estimation: KL, factorization, periodogram, LMMSE, Wiener, Kalman A5, Final LO6 Classify and analyse Markov chains; compute stationary distributions; model as CTMC A6, Final LO7 Analyse queuing systems: Little's formula, M/M/1, M/M/s, M/M/1/K, PK formula, Jackson networks A7, Final

docs.title: Teaching and learning methods
docs.text:
• Lectures (2 h/week). Motivate and derive each topic; work through at least one example per method; demonstrate the computational implementations on the laptop (Python is the primary language; Java and C# alternatives are provided in the notes).
  • Tutorials (3 h/week). Small-group problem-solving sessions. The tutorial problems at the end of each chapter are worked on in class; solutions are posted to the Solutions page after the tutorial.
  • Assignments (7, one per chapter). Longer problems combining theory and computation; graded with detailed feedback.
  • Independent study (5 h/week). Reading, tutorial problems, assignment work, and running the computational examples.

docs.title: Course content
docs.text: The syllabus comprises seven chapters, grouped into two halves.

docs.title: Part I — Optimization (Chapters 1–3)
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — Optimization: Preliminaries

  • Characterization of a minimum; local vs. global minima; Pareto-optimality in multi-objective optimization
  • Gradient and Hessian; slope and curvature
  • Properties of linear and quadratic functions
  • Optimality conditions: unconstrained; linearly constrained (equality, inequality); nonlinearly constrained (KKT)
  • Line-search subproblem: bracketing, sectioning, golden-section
  • Numerically derived gradients, analytically derived gradients, adjoint-variable approach

Chapter 2 — Unconstrained Optimization

  • Non-derivative methods: polytope algorithm, Nelder–Mead simplex, pattern search (Hooke–Jeeves), AD-HOC methods
  • Second-derivative methods: Newton, damped Newton
  • First-derivative methods: quasi-Newton (BFGS), L-BFGS
  • Sums of squares and nonlinear equations: Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt

Chapter 3 — Constrained Optimization

  • Penalty functions, barrier functions
  • Augmented Lagrangian (method of multipliers)
  • Quadratic programming with equality constraints (KKT system)
  • QP with inequalities (active-set preview)

docs.title: Part II — Stochastic processes (Chapters 4–7)
docs.text:
Chapter 4 — Stochastic Processes, Random Walks, and Applications

  • General concepts, definitions, correlations
  • Random walks, Brownian-motion limit
  • Poisson point processes; shot noise; Campbell's theorem
  • Modulation and cyclostationary processes
  • Band-limited processes and sampling theory
  • Deterministic signal in noise; matched filter
  • Shannon entropy and differential entropy

Chapter 5 — Spectral Representation and Estimation

  • Power spectral density and Wiener–Khinchin
  • Karhunen–Loève expansion
  • Spectral factorization; innovations representation
  • Ergodicity; periodogram; Welch's method
  • Mean-square estimation and the orthogonality principle
  • Wiener filter (non-causal and causal)
  • Kalman filter; Riccati equation

Chapter 6 — Markov Chains

  • Markov property; DTMC; transition matrix; Chapman–Kolmogorov
  • Classification: recurrent/transient, periodic/aperiodic, communicating classes
  • Stationary distribution; detailed balance; ergodic theorem
  • Continuous-time Markov chains; generator matrix; Kolmogorov equations
  • Birth–death chains

Chapter 7 — Introduction to Queuing Theory

  • Kendall notation; elements of a queuing system
  • Little's formula
  • Birth–death process (CTMC)
  • M/M/1: stationary distribution, performance measures, waiting-time distribution
  • M/M/s: Erlang-C, performance measures
  • M/M/1/K; Pollaczek–Khinchine (M/G/1); Jackson networks
  • Simulation and data analysis of queuing systems
