docs.title: Chapter 1 — Optimization: Preliminaries
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): characterization of a minimum · local vs. global minima · Pareto optimality · gradient and Hessian · slope and curvature · properties of linear and quadratic functions · optimality conditions (unconstrained, linear equality, linear inequality, nonlinear) · line-search subproblem (bracketing and sectioning) · numerically and analytically derived gradients · adjoint-variable approach.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Characterize a local, strict, and global minimizer and recognize them on a plot.
  2. Define Pareto optimality and identify the Pareto front of a small multi-objective problem.
  3. Compute gradients and Hessians analytically; interpret them as slope and curvature.
  4. State and use the first- and second-order optimality conditions (unconstrained and constrained, including KKT).
  5. Solve the line-search subproblem via bracketing and golden-section sectioning.
  6. Estimate gradients numerically and explain when to prefer analytical or adjoint derivations.
  7. Implement basic gradient/Hessian checks and golden-section search in Python, Java, or C#.

docs.title: 1.1 Characterization of a minimum
docs.text:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a (smooth) objective and let \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set.

Definitions

  • Local minimizer. \(x^\star \in S\) is a weak local minimizer if there is \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for all \(x \in S\), \(\|x-x^\star\|<\varepsilon\). If the inequality is strict for \(x \ne x^\star\), \(x^\star\) is a strict local minimizer.
  • Global minimizer. \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for all \(x \in S\).
  • Isolated minimizer. A neighborhood of \(x^\star\) contains no other local minimizer.

A point that satisfies the necessary condition \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\) is a stationary point — it may be a minimizer, a maximizer, or a saddle.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — three critical points of a cubic
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1\) over \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

First-order condition. \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x-1)(x+1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\).

Second-order condition. \(f''(x) = 6x\), \(f''(1) = 6>0\), \(f''(-1)=-6<0\).

Classification.

  • \(x = 1\): strict local minimum with \(f(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1\).
  • \(x = -1\): strict local maximum with \(f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 1 = 3\).

Global behavior. Because \(f(x) \to +\infty\) as \(x \to +\infty\) and \(f(x) \to -\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\), neither a global minimum nor a global maximum exists on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Takeaway

A stationary point is not automatically a minimum. The Hessian (here the scalar \(f''\)) decides between minimum, maximum, and saddle.

docs.title: 1.2 Local versus global minima
docs.text:
Local minima are neighbourhood statements — the comparison is only with nearby points. To decide global status you either

  • prove convexity of \(f\) on a convex \(S\) (then every local minimizer is global), or
  • enumerate all local minima and compare their values (only feasible for small or structured problems), or
  • use a certified global solver (branch-and-bound, interval methods, etc.).

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — a quartic with two global minima
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2 + 1 = (x^2-1)^2\) over \(\mathbb{R}\).

  1. \(f'(x) = 4x(x^2 - 1) = 0\) ⇒ critical points \(x = 0, \pm 1\).
  2. \(f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4\).
  3. \(x = 0\): \(f''(0) = -4 < 0\), so \(x=0\) is a local maximum (\(f(0)=1\)).
  4. \(x = \pm 1\): \(f''(\pm 1) = 8 > 0\), so both are strict local minima with \(f(\pm 1) = 0\).
  5. Since \(f(x) \ge 0\) everywhere and \(f(\pm 1)=0\), both local minima are global. The global minimizer is not unique; the set of minimizers is \(\{-1, +1\}\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.3 — a multimodal function where locals are not global
docs.text:
For \(f(x) = 0.5 x^2 + 3\sin(3x)\) on \([-3, 3]\) the derivative

\[ f'(x) = x + 9\cos(3x) \]

has several zeros (see the Python scan below). Two local minima exist, but only one is global.

import numpy as np

f  = lambda x: 0.5*x**2 + 3*np.sin(3*x)
df = lambda x: x + 9*np.cos(3*x)

# coarse scan for sign changes of f'
xs = np.linspace(-3, 3, 4001)
sign_change = np.where(np.diff(np.sign(df(xs))) != 0)[0]
roots = [ (xs[i]+xs[i+1])/2 for i in sign_change ]
print("stationary points:", roots)
print("values:", [round(f(r), 4) for r in roots])

The smallest computed value is the global minimum; the others are local minima (local but not global). This is the typical situation in engineering design problems.

docs.title: 1.3 Pareto-optimality in multi-objective optimization
docs.text:
When we minimize several objectives at once, there is rarely a single point that improves all of them simultaneously.

Definitions

Let \(\mathbf f(x) = (f_1(x),\dots,f_m(x))\). A point \(x^\star\) Pareto-dominates \(y\) if

\[ f_i(x^\star) \le f_i(y) \ \forall i,\qquad\text{and } f_j(x^\star) < f_j(y) \ \text{for some }j. \]

\(x^\star\) is Pareto-optimal if no feasible \(y\) dominates it. The set of objective vectors of all Pareto-optimal points is the Pareto front.

docs.title: Worked example 1.4 — the Pareto set of a two-objective problem
docs.text:
\[ \min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\ \bigl(f_1(x), f_2(x)\bigr) = \bigl(x^2,\ (x-2)^2\bigr). \]
  • If \(x < 0\), moving to \(x=0\) reduces both objectives ⇒ every \(x<0\) is dominated.
  • If \(x > 2\), moving to \(x=2\) reduces both ⇒ every \(x>2\) is dominated.
  • If \(0 \le x \le 2\): moving right increases \(f_1\) but decreases \(f_2\); moving left does the opposite. No point in \([0,2]\) is dominated.

Hence the Pareto set is \([0,2]\) and the Pareto front is

\[ \mathcal F = \Bigl\{\,(x^2,\ (x-2)^2) : 0 \le x \le 2 \,\Bigr\}. \]

On the front:

\(x\) \(f_1=x^2\) \(f_2=(x-2)^2\) 0.0 0.00 4.00 0.5 0.25 2.25 1.0 1.00 1.00 1.5 2.25 0.25 2.0 4.00 0.00

Engineering usage

When you face a trade-off between, say, link throughput and energy per bit, you do not look for a single number — you look for the Pareto front and let the design authority select a knee point on it.

docs.title: 1.4 Gradient and Hessian matrix
docs.text:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[ \nabla f(x) = \begin{bmatrix} \partial f/\partial x_1 \\ \vdots \\ \partial f/\partial x_n\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \nabla^2 f(x) = H(x) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} \end{bmatrix}_{i,j=1}^{n}. \]

\(H\) is symmetric when \(f\) has continuous second derivatives (Schwarz's theorem).

docs.title: Worked example 1.5 — gradient and Hessian of a polynomial
docs.text:
Let \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 x_2 + x_2^3 - 2 x_1\). Then

\[ \nabla f(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_1 x_2 - 2 \\ x_1^2 + 3x_2^2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad H(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_2 & 2x_1 \\ 2x_1 & 6x_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

At the point \((1,2)\): \(\nabla f = (2, 13)^\top\), \(H = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 12\end{bmatrix}\). The eigenvalues of \(H\) are \(3\pm\sqrt{5}>0\), so \(H\succ 0\) there — useful when we later use Newton's method (Chapter 2).

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of how each part of the example is computed and what it means.

docs.title: Computing the Gradient Vector, \(\nabla f(x_1, x_2)\)
docs.text:
The gradient is a column vector containing the first-order partial derivatives of \(f\):

\[\nabla f(x_1, x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \end{bmatrix}\]
  • Partial derivative with respect to \(x_1\) (treat \(x_2\) as a constant):
\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(x_1^2 x_2) + 0 - \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(2 x_1) = 2x_1 x_2 - 2\]
  • Partial derivative with respect to \(x_2\) (treat \(x_1\) as a constant):
\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_1^2 x_2) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_2^3) - 0 = x_1^2 + 3x_2^2\]

Putting them together gives the gradient vector:

\[\nabla f(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_1 x_2 - 2 \\ x_1^2 + 3x_2^2 \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Computing the Hessian Matrix, \(H(x_1, x_2)\)
docs.text:
The Hessian is a square matrix of second-order partial derivatives:

\[H(x_1, x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2} \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2 \partial x_1} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2^2} \end{bmatrix}\]
  • \(H_{11} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(2x_1 x_2 - 2) = 2x_2\)
  • \(H_{12} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(2x_1 x_2 - 2) = 2x_1\)
  • \(H_{21} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(x_1^2 + 3x_2^2) = 2x_1\) (Note: \(H_{12} = H_{21}\) by Schwarz's theorem)
  • \(H_{22} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_1^2 + 3x_2^2) = 6x_2\)

Putting these into the matrix format gives:

\[H(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_2 & 2x_1 \\ 2x_1 & 6x_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Gradient at \((1, 2)\):
docs.text:
\[\nabla f(1, 2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2(1)(2) - 2 \\ (1)^2 + 3(2)^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 2 \\ 1 + 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} = (2, 13)^\top\]

(The transpose symbol \(\top\) turns the row representation back into a column vector).

docs.title: Hessian at \((1, 2)\):
docs.text: \[H(1, 2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2(2) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & 6(2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Eigenvalues and Positive Definiteness (\(H \succ 0\))
docs.text:
To evaluate local curvature, we find the eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of \(H\) by solving the characteristic equation \(\det(H - \lambda I) = 0\):

\[\det \begin{bmatrix} 4 - \lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 12 - \lambda \end{bmatrix} = 0\] \[(4 - \lambda)(12 - \lambda) - (2)(2) = 0\] \[\lambda^2 - 16\lambda + 48 - 4 = 0\] \[\lambda^2 - 16\lambda + 44 = 0\]

Using the quadratic formula \(\lambda = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\):

\[\lambda = \frac{16 \pm \sqrt{(-16)^2 - 4(1)(44)}}{2} = \frac{16 \pm \sqrt{256 - 176}}{2} = \frac{16 \pm \sqrt{80}}{2}\]

Since \(\sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}\):

\[\lambda = \frac{16 \pm 4\sqrt{5}}{2} = 8 \pm 2\sqrt{5}\]

(Note: The textbook simplifies this directly into factored form, but both expressions yield \(\lambda_1 \approx 12.47\) and \(\lambda_2 \approx 3.53\).)

docs.title: Significance of \(H \succ 0\):
docs.text:
• Since both eigenvalues are strictly positive (\(\lambda > 0\)), the matrix is positive definite, denoted as \(H \succ 0\).
  • This means the function is strictly convex locally at the point \((1, 2)\) (i.e., it shapes like a bowl opening upwards).
  • Because \(H\) is positive definite, Newton's optimization method is guaranteed to move in a valid descent direction at this point without requiring modifications or regularization.

docs.title: 1.5 Slope and curvature
docs.text:
• The directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) along a unit vector \(d\) is \(\nabla f(x)^\top d\) — the slope.
  • The curvature along \(d\) is \(d^\top H(x)\, d\):
  • \(d^\top H d > 0\): \(f\) curves up along \(d\).
  • \(d^\top H d < 0\): \(f\) curves down along \(d\).
  • \(d^\top H d = 0\): locally flat along \(d\) to second order.

The level set \(f(x) = \text{const}\) near a regular point is perpendicular to \(\nabla f(x)\), so moving along a level set is a zero-slope direction. This is the geometric basis of constrained optimality (Section 1.8).

docs.title: 1.6 Properties of linear functions
docs.text:
For \(f(x) = a^\top x + b\) with \(a \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

Property Value Gradient \(\nabla f(x) = a\) (constant) Hessian \(H(x) = 0\) Level sets \(f=\text{const}\) Hyperplanes orthogonal to \(a\) Local minima Only if \(a = 0\) (then every point is a minimum) Global minima on a polytope Attained on a face / at a vertex (LPs)

A linear objective has no interior unconstrained minimum — you need constraints (Chapter 3) to get a well-posed problem.

docs.title: 1.7 Properties of quadratic functions
docs.text:
A quadratic function has the form

\[ f(x) = \tfrac12 x^\top Q x - c^\top x + d, \qquad Q = Q^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\quad c\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ d\in\mathbb{R}. \] Property Value Gradient \(\nabla f(x) = Qx - c\) Hessian \(H(x) = Q\) (constant) Stationary point \(x^\star = Q^{-1}c\) (if \(Q\) invertible) Unique global minimum Exists ⇔ \(Q \succ 0\) Level sets (with \(Q \succ 0\)) Ellipsoids aligned with eigenvectors of \(Q\); semi-axis lengths \(\propto 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}\) Condition number \(\kappa(Q)\) Determines how difficult the problem is for iterative methods

docs.title: Worked example 1.6 — solve a quadratic via the eigen-structure
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = 2x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_1 x_2 - 3 x_1 + 4 x_2\).

Write it as \(\tfrac12 x^\top Q x - c^\top x\) with

\[ Q = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad c = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Eigenvalues of \(Q\): \(\det(Q-\lambda I) = (4-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - 1 = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 7 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 3 \pm \sqrt{2}\), both positive ⇒ \(Q \succ 0\), so \(f\) has a unique global minimum.

Stationary point solves \(Qx = c\):

\[ \begin{cases} 4x_1 + x_2 = 3 \\ x_1 + 2x_2 = -4 \end{cases} \ \Rightarrow\ x^\star = \Bigl(\tfrac{10}{7}, -\tfrac{19}{7}\Bigr). \]

Optimal value (using \(f^\star = -\tfrac12 c^\top Q^{-1} c\)):

\[ f(x^\star) = -\tfrac{53}{7}\approx -7.571. \]

The condition number is \(\kappa(Q) = \frac{3+\sqrt2}{3-\sqrt2}\approx 1.97\) — well-conditioned; a gradient method would converge reasonably fast.

docs.title: 1.8.1 Unconstrained
docs.text:
First-order necessary condition (FONC)

If \(x^\star\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) and \(f\) is differentiable in a neighbourhood, then

\[ abla f(x^\star) = 0 . \]

If in addition \(f\in C^2\),

\[ abla^2 f(x^\star) \succeq 0 \]

(the Hessian is positive semi-definite) is necessary. The strict version \( abla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\) is sufficient for a strict local minimum.

docs.title: Worked example 1.7 — first-order and second-order conditions
docs.text:
For \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2 x_2 + x_2^3 - 2x_1\) find all stationary points and classify them.

\[ \nabla f = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \begin{cases} 2x_1 x_2 = 2 \\ x_1^2 + 3x_2^2 = 0 \end{cases} \]

The second equation forces \(x_1 = x_2 = 0\), which then violates \(2x_1 x_2 = 2\). No real stationary point exists ⇒ \(f\) is unbounded below. This is an important diagnostic: an optimizer that diverges is telling you the problem is unbounded.

docs.title: 1.8.2 Linearly constrained — equality constraints
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m imes n}\) of rank \(m\).

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and the Lagrangian

\[ \mathcal L(x,\lambda) = f(x) + \lambda^ op (Ax - b). \]

Equality-constrained FONC

If \(x^\star\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) on \(\{x: Ax=b\}\), there exists \(\lambda^\star\) with

\[ abla_x \mathcal L(x^\star,\lambda^\star) = abla f(x^\star) + A^ op \lambda^\star = 0, \qquad Ax^\star = b. \]

Geometric interpretation: at \(x^\star\), the negative gradient \(- abla f(x^\star)\) lies in the row space of \(A\) — equivalently, \( abla f(x^\star)\) is orthogonal to the tangent space of the constraint (which is \(\ker A\)).

docs.title: Worked example 1.8 — projection onto an affine subspace
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) subject to \(x_1 + x_2 = 2\).

Lagrangian: \(\mathcal L = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \lambda(x_1 + x_2 - 2)\). First-order conditions:

\[ 2x_1 + \lambda = 0,\qquad 2x_2 + \lambda = 0,\qquad x_1 + x_2 = 2. \]

The first two imply \(x_1 = x_2\); with the constraint \(x_1 = x_2 = 1\). Then \(\lambda = -2\), and

\[ f^\star = 1 + 1 = 2. \]

Geometric check: \(-\nabla f(1,1) = (-2,-2) = 2\cdot(1,1)\) — the negative gradient is (up to scale) the constraint normal, as required.

docs.title: 1.8.3 Linearly constrained — inequality constraints
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(Ax \le b\).

The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions for this case read

\[ \nabla f(x^\star) + A^\top \mu^\star = 0,\qquad \mu^\star \ge 0,\qquad \mu_i^\star\,[Ax^\star - b]_i = 0,\qquad Ax^\star \le b. \]

The last column condition is complementary slackness: an active constraint carries a non-negative multiplier; an inactive one carries zero.

docs.title: Worked example 1.9 — a small inequality problem
docs.text:
Minimize \((x-2)^2 + 1\) subject to \(x \le 1\).

  • Unconstrained solution: \(x = 2\), but \(2 \le 1\) is false ⇒ infeasible.
  • Active-constraint ansatz: \(x^\star = 1\). Then \(f'(1) = 2(1-2) = -2\), and KKT with \(g(x)=x-1\le 0\), \(\nabla g = 1\):

[ -2 + \mu \cdot 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 2 \ge 0. \;\checkmark ]

\(x^\star = 1\) satisfies all KKT conditions. Optimal value: \((1-2)^2+1 = 2\).

docs.title: 1.8.4 Nonlinearly constrained — full KKT
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x) \le 0\ (i=1,\dots,p)\) and \(h_j(x) = 0\ (j=1,\dots,q)\), all \(C^1\).

KKT conditions (necessary, under a constraint qualification)

There exist multipliers \(\mu^\star\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\lambda^\star\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that

\[ abla f(x^\star) + \sum_i \mu_i^\star abla g_i(x^\star) + \sum_j \lambda_j^\star abla h_j(x^\star) = 0, \] \[ g_i(x^\star) \le 0,\ \ \mu_i^\star \ge 0,\ \ \mu_i^\star g_i(x^\star) = 0, \qquad h_j(x^\star) = 0. \]

Common constraint qualifications: LICQ (gradients of active constraints are linearly independent), Slater (for convex problems).

docs.title: Worked example 1.10 — a nonlinear inequality
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x,y) = x^2+y^2\) subject to \(g(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 4 \le 0\).

The unconstrained minimizer \((0,0)\) satisfies \(g(0,0) = -4 < 0\) (strictly feasible), so \(x^\star=(0,0)\), \(\mu^\star = 0\) — inactive constraint. Optimal value \(0\). This illustrates complementary slackness: when the constraint does not bite, the unconstrained solution is the answer.

Now modify: minimize \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x^2+2y^2 - 1\ge 0\) (i.e. \(-x^2 - 2y^2 + 1 \le 0\)). The unconstrained minimizer \((0,0)\) is infeasible. The active-constraint case forces \(x^2+2y^2=1\). By symmetry one can show \(y^\star = 0\), \(x^\star = \pm 1\) with \(\mu=1\), \(f^\star = 1\). (Exercise: verify by writing the KKT system.)

docs.title: 1.9 The line-search subproblem
docs.text:
Many algorithms (steepest descent, quasi-Newton, conjugate gradient) update

\[ x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha_k d_k \]

where \(d_k\) is a descent direction (\(\nabla f(x_k)^\top d_k < 0\)) and \(\alpha_k\) is a step length chosen by solving the scalar subproblem

\[ \min_{\alpha>0}\ \phi(\alpha) := f(x_k + \alpha d_k). \]

docs.title: 1.9.1 Bracketing
docs.text:
First find three points \(\alpha^{(1)} < \alpha^{(2)} < \alpha^{(3)}\) with \(\phi(\alpha^{(2)}) < \phi(\alpha^{(1)})\) and \(\phi(\alpha^{(2)}) < \phi(\alpha^{(3)})\). This bracket contains a local minimum.

Algorithm (bracket by expansion):

α₀ = 0, φ₀ = φ(α₀)
α₁ = s, φ₁ = φ(α₁)            # s = user-supplied initial step
if φ₁ > φ₀: swap and negate s  # make sure we descend
α₂ = α₁ + s, φ₂ = φ(α₂)
while φ₂ < φ₁:
    α₀, α₁, α₂ = α₁, α₂, α₂ + 2·s
    φ₀, φ₁, φ₂ = φ₁, φ₂, φ(α₂)
return (α₀, α₁, α₂)

docs.title: 1.9.2 Sectioning — golden-section search
docs.text:
Once a bracket \([a,b]\) is known, we shrink it. Golden-section places two interior points

\[ c = b - \tau(b-a),\qquad d = a + \tau(b-a),\qquad \tau = \frac{\sqrt 5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.618, \]

evaluates \(\phi\) there, and keeps the subinterval that contains the smaller value. Each iteration reduces the interval by a factor \(\tau \approx 0.618\) with one new evaluation — the interval length \(L_k\) satisfies \(L_k \approx \tau^k L_0\), so the sub-interval reaching a tolerance \(\epsilon\) takes \(k \approx \log(\epsilon/L_0)/\log\tau\) iterations.

docs.title: Worked example 1.11 — golden-section on a smooth quadratic
docs.text:
Minimize \(\phi(\alpha) = (\alpha - 2)^2 + 1\) on \([0,5]\) using golden-section search (\(\tau=0.618\)).

Iter Interval \(c\) \(d\) \(\phi(c)\) \(\phi(d)\) Keep 1 \([0, 5]\) 1.910 3.090 1.008 2.188 \(b \leftarrow d\), \([0, 3.09]\) 2 \([0, 3.09]\) 1.180 1.910 1.672 1.008 \(a \leftarrow c\), \([1.18, 3.09]\) 3 \([1.18, 3.09]\) 1.910 2.360 1.008 1.130 \(b \leftarrow d\), \([1.18, 2.36]\) 4 \([1.18, 2.36]\) 1.630 1.910 1.136 1.008 \(a \leftarrow c\), \([1.63, 2.36]\) 5 \([1.63, 2.36]\) 1.910 2.081 1.008 1.007 \(\approx [1.91, 2.08]\)

After 5 iterations the bracket contains the exact minimum \(\alpha^\star = 2\) to within \(\sim 0.1\), having used just \(5+1=6\) evaluations of \(\phi\) (the reuse of the "carried" interior point is what makes golden-section efficient).

docs.title: 1.9.3 Convergence criteria for line search
docs.text:
The two classical conditions on \(\alpha_k\) are:

  • Armijo (sufficient decrease): \(\phi(\alpha_k) \le \phi(0) + c_1 \alpha_k \phi'(0)\), with \(c_1 \approx 10^{-4}\).
  • Wolfe (curvature): \(|\phi'(\alpha_k)| \le c_2 |\phi'(0)|\), with \(0<c_1<c_2<1\).

They together guarantee that the line-search subproblem terminates in finitely many iterations.

docs.title: 1.10.1 Numerically derived gradient
docs.text:
Finite-difference formulas:

Formula Expression Error Forward \(\dfrac{f(x+he_i) - f(x)}{h}\) \(O(h)\) Backward \(\dfrac{f(x) - f(x-he_i)}{h}\) \(O(h)\) Central \(\dfrac{f(x+he_i) - f(x-he_i)}{2h}\) \(O(h^2)\)

With floating-point arithmetic the truncation error \(O(h)\) and round-off error \(O(\epsilon_{\text{mach}}/h)\) balance; the optimal choice is roughly \(h \sim \sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{mach}}} \approx 10^{-8}\) for forward differences, and \(h \sim \epsilon_{\text{mach}}^{1/3} \approx 10^{-5}\) for central differences.

Cost: computing \(\nabla f\) by finite differences costs \(n+1\) (forward) or \(2n\) (central) objective evaluations — prohibitively expensive when \(n\) is large.

docs.title: Worked example 1.12 — compare numeric and analytic gradients
docs.text:
For \(f(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 x_2 + x_2^3 - 2x_1\) at \(x = (1,2)\):

  • Analytic: \(\nabla f = (2x_1 x_2 - 2,\ x_1^2 + 3x_2^2) = (2, 13)\).
  • Central-difference with \(h = 10^{-6}\) gives, to seven significant figures, \((2.000000,\ 13.000000)\). Forward-difference gives about \((2.000001,\ 13.000001)\) — six correct digits.

Rule of thumb. Use central differences when \(n\) is small and accuracy matters; use forward differences inside large-scale optimizers where \(n\) is large and expensive.

docs.title: 1.10.2 Analytically derived gradient
docs.text:
Preferred whenever available:

  • exact (no truncation error),
  • typically an order of magnitude faster,
  • required for guaranteed convergence of Newton-type methods.

Use automatic differentiation (AD) when the model is a big computational graph — tools such as JAX, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Stan, and CasADi give machine-precision derivatives at the cost of one forward and one reverse pass.

docs.title: 1.10.3 Adjoint variable approach
docs.text:
Adjoint methods compute the gradient with respect to many parameters at the cost of one (or two) forward+adjoint solves, regardless of how many parameters there are. This is the reason they dominate optimal-control and inverse problems.

Consider the discrete-time system

\[ x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k, u_k),\qquad x_0 ext{ given},\qquad J(u) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} L_k(x_k, u_k) + \Phi(x_N). \]

Introduce adjoint variables (costates) \(\lambda_k\) defined by the backward recursion

\[ \lambda_N = abla \Phi(x_N),\qquad \lambda_k = abla_x L_k(x_k,u_k) + \Bigl( rac{\partial F_k}{\partial x_k}\Bigr)^ op \lambda_{k+1}. \]

Then the gradient w.r.t. each control is

\[ oxed{\; abla_{u_k} J = abla_{u_k} L_k(x_k,u_k) + \Bigl( rac{\partial F_k}{\partial u_k}\Bigr)^ op \lambda_{k+1}\;} \]

The forward pass produces \(x_0,\dots,x_N\); the backward pass produces \(\lambda_N,\dots,\lambda_0\). Total cost: one forward + one backward pass, independent of \(\dim u\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.13 — adjoint derivation verified by hand
docs.text:
Discrete problem with \(x_0 = 2\), \(x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k\) (\(k=0,1\)), and

\[ J(u_0,u_1) = x_2^2 + u_0^2 + u_1^2. \]

Direct elimination (to have a reference answer):

\[ x_1 = 2 + u_0,\qquad x_2 = 2 + u_0 + u_1,\qquad J = (2+u_0+u_1)^2 + u_0^2 + u_1^2. \] \[ rac{\partial J}{\partial u_0} = 2(2+u_0+u_1) + 2u_0,\qquad rac{\partial J}{\partial u_1} = 2(2+u_0+u_1) + 2u_1. \]

Setting both to zero: \(4 + 4u_0 + 2u_1 = 0\), \(4 + 2u_0 + 4u_1 = 0\); subtracting gives \(u_0 = u_1\), hence \(u_0 = u_1 = -2/3\).

Adjoint method.

  • Terminal: \(\lambda_2 = 2 x_2 = 2(2+u_0+u_1)\).
  • Recurrence: \(\lambda_k = \partial L_k/\partial x_k + (\partial F_k/\partial x_k)\lambda_{k+1}\). Since \(L_0 = u_0^2\) and \(L_1 = u_1^2\) do not depend on \(x\), we get \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_0 = \lambda_1 = \lambda_2\).
  • Gradients:

[ rac{\partial J}{\partial u_0} = 2u_0 + \lambda_1,\qquad rac{\partial J}{\partial u_1} = 2u_1 + \lambda_2. ]

  • At \(u_0 = u_1 = -2/3\): \(x_2 = 2/3\), \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2 = 4/3\), so \(\partial J/\partial u_0 = -4/3 + 4/3 = 0\) and \(\partial J/\partial u_1 = 0\) — matching the direct computation.

Continuous-time version

For \(\dot x = F(x,u)\), \(J = \int_0^T L(x,u)\,dt + \Phi(x(T))\), the continuous adjoint is

\[ -\dot\lambda = abla_x H,\quad \lambda(T) = abla \Phi(x(T)),\quad H(x,u,\lambda) = L + \lambda^ op F, \]

and \( abla_u J = abla_u H\). Use a forward ODE solve for \(x(t)\) and a backward ODE solve for \(\lambda(t)\).

docs.title: 1.11 Computational implementation
docs.text: The snippets below implement gradient checking (comparing analytic and numeric derivatives) and golden-section search in three languages. You can drop them straight into a Jupyter notebook, a Java console app, or a C# program.

docs.title: Python (NumPy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

# ---- objective and analytic derivatives -------------------------------------
def f(x):                                # f(x,y) = x^2 y + y^3 - 2x
    return x[0]**2 * x[1] + x[1]**3 - 2 * x[0]

def grad_analytic(x):
    return np.array([2*x[0]*x[1] - 2, x[0]**2 + 3*x[1]**2])

def grad_forward(f, x, h=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(x, dtype=float)
    for i in range(len(x)):
        e = np.zeros_like(x, dtype=float); e[i] = h
        g[i] = (f(x + e) - f(x)) / h
    return g

def grad_central(f, x, h=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(x, dtype=float)
    for i in range(len(x)):
        e = np.zeros_like(x, dtype=float); e[i] = h
        g[i] = (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h)
    return g

def hessian_central(f, x, h=1e-4):
    n = len(x); H = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            ei = np.zeros(n); ei[i] = h
            ej = np.zeros(n); ej[j] = h
            H[i, j] = (f(x+ei+ej) - f(x+ei-ej) - f(x-ei+ej) + f(x-ei-ej)) / (4*h*h)
    return H

# ---- golden-section search --------------------------------------------------
def golden_section(phi, a, b, tol=1e-6, maxit=200):
    tau = (np.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2
    c, d = b - tau*(b-a), a + tau*(b-a)
    fc, fd = phi(c), phi(d)
    for _ in range(maxit):
        if b - a < tol:
            break
        if fc < fd:
            b, d, fd = d, c, fc
            c = b - tau*(b-a); fc = phi(c)
        else:
            a, c, fc = c, d, fd
            d = a + tau*(b-a); fd = phi(d)
    return 0.5 * (a + b)

# ---- demo -------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
    print("analytic :", grad_analytic(x))
    print("forward  :", grad_forward(f, x))
    print("central  :", grad_central(f, x))
    print("Hessian  :\n", hessian_central(f, x))
    print("golden   :", golden_section(lambda a: (a-2)**2 + 1, 0.0, 5.0))

Typical output:

analytic : [2. 13.]
forward  : [ 2.000001 13.000001]
central  : [ 2. 13.]
Hessian  :
 [[ 4.  2.]
  [ 2. 12.]]
golden   : 1.999999...

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
public class GradientCheck {

    static double f(double[] x) {
        return x[0]*x[0]*x[1] + Math.pow(x[1], 3) - 2*x[0];
    }

    static double[] gradAnalytic(double[] x) {
        return new double[]{ 2*x[0]*x[1] - 2, x[0]*x[0] + 3*x[1]*x[1] };
    }

    static double[] gradCentral(double[] x, double h) {
        double[] g = new double[x.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) {
            double[] xp = x.clone(); xp[i] += h;
            double[] xm = x.clone(); xm[i] -= h;
            g[i] = (f(xp) - f(xm)) / (2*h);
        }
        return g;
    }

    static double goldenSection(java.util.function.DoubleUnaryOperator phi,
                                double a, double b, double tol) {
        double tau = (Math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2;
        double c = b - tau*(b-a), d = a + tau*(b-a);
        double fc = phi.applyAsDouble(c), fd = phi.applyAsDouble(d);
        while (b - a > tol) {
            if (fc < fd) { b=d; d=c; fd=fc; c=b - tau*(b-a); fc=phi.applyAsDouble(c); }
            else        { a=c; c=d; fc=fd; d=a + tau*(b-a); fd=phi.applyAsDouble(d); }
        }
        return 0.5*(a+b);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] x = { 1.0, 2.0 };
        System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(gradAnalytic(x)));
        System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(gradCentral(x, 1e-6)));
        System.out.println(goldenSection(a -> (a-2)*(a-2) + 1, 0.0, 5.0, 1e-6));
    }
}

docs.title: C
docs.text:
using System;

class GradientCheck {

    static double F(double[] x) => x[0]*x[0]*x[1] + Math.Pow(x[1], 3) - 2*x[0];

    static double[] GradAnalytic(double[] x) =>
        new[]{ 2*x[0]*x[1] - 2, x[0]*x[0] + 3*x[1]*x[1] };

    static double[] GradCentral(double[] x, double h) {
        var g = new double[x.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < x.Length; i++) {
            var xp = (double[])x.Clone(); xp[i] += h;
            var xm = (double[])x.Clone(); xm[i] -= h;
            g[i] = (F(xp) - F(xm)) / (2*h);
        }
        return g;
    }

    static double GoldenSection(Func<double,double> phi, double a, double b, double tol) {
        double tau = (Math.Sqrt(5) - 1) / 2;
        double c = b - tau*(b-a), d = a + tau*(b-a);
        double fc = phi(c), fd = phi(d);
        while (b - a > tol) {
            if (fc < fd) { b=d; d=c; fd=fc; c=b - tau*(b-a); fc=phi(c); }
            else         { a=c; c=d; fc=fd; d=a + tau*(b-a); fd=phi(d); }
        }
        return 0.5*(a+b);
    }

    static void Main() {
        var x = new double[]{ 1.0, 2.0 };
        Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", GradAnalytic(x)));
        Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", GradCentral(x, 1e-6)));
        Console.WriteLine(GoldenSection(a => (a-2)*(a-2) + 1, 0.0, 5.0, 1e-6));
    }
}

Which language for what?

  • Python (NumPy + SciPy): day-to-day optimization prototyping, scipy.optimize.check_grad, plotting.
  • Java: production-style implementation inside enterprise systems; also for teaching OOP-based algorithm design.
  • C#: Windows/.NET infrastructure, Unity simulations, and interop with MATLAB Coder-generated code.
  • C/C++: required when you must link the optimizer to a high-fidelity simulator.

All three snippets above are mathematically equivalent — a good exercise is to run all three and compare the printed gradient vectors to machine precision.

docs.title: Cost comparison at a glance
docs.text: Derivative method Cost to obtain \(\nabla f\) Accuracy Requires user code Analytic (hand) 1 evaluation exact Yes — derivation Automatic diff. ≤ 4× cost of \(f\) machine precision No (framework) Central differences \(2n\) evaluations of \(f\) \(O(h^2)\) No Forward differences \(n+1\) evaluations \(O(h)\) No Adjoint (discrete or continuous) 1 forward + 1 backward exact (to ODE error) Yes — adjoint code

docs.title: 1.12 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Local vs global vs Pareto. Three independent notions; in engineering you usually need at least two of them (a Pareto front of local solutions, then a global choice).
  2. Gradient = slope, Hessian = curvature. These two objects drive every algorithm from Chapter 2 onward.
  3. Linearity & quadraticity. Linear problems have no interior minimum; quadratic problems are solved in closed form — the reference for what an iterative method should converge to.
  4. Optimality conditions. FONC \(\nabla f = 0\), SOSC \(\nabla^2 f \succ 0\); with constraints, replace by Lagrange/KKT with multipliers and complementary slackness.
  5. Line search. Bracket by expansion, refine by golden-section (or bisection/interpolation); a superlinear method with a poor line search can be worse than gradient descent with a good one.
  6. Derivatives. Prefer analytic/AD; fall back to finite differences; use adjoints when the parameter dimension is large.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. Which of the following is necessary for a differentiable \(f\) to have a local minimum at an interior point \(x^\star\)? (a) \(f(x^\star)=0\) (b) \( abla f(x^\star)=0\) (c) \( abla^2 f(x^\star)\succ 0\) (d) \(f\) is convex

  2. If \( abla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\) and \( abla f(x^\star) = 0\), then \(x^\star\) is: (a) a strict local maximum (b) a strict local minimum (c) a saddle (d) undetermined

  3. Which \(x\) is Pareto-optimal for \(\min (x^2, (x-2)^2)\) over \(\mathbb{R}\)? (a) \(x=-1\) (b) \(x=1\) (c) \(x=3\) (d) \(x=0.5\) only if \(x\le0\)

  4. For \(f(x) = frac12 x^ op Q x - c^ op x\) with \(Q\succ0\), the unique global minimizer is: (a) \(Qc\) (b) \(Q^{-1}c\) (c) \(-Q^{-1}c\) (d) \(c-Q\)

  5. The gradient of a linear function \(f(x)=a^ op x + b\) is: (a) \(a\) (b) \(b\) (c) \(0\) (d) \(a x\)

  6. Which finite-difference formula has \(O(h^2)\) truncation error? (a) forward (b) backward (c) central (d) all three

  7. In golden-section search, the interval reduction factor per iteration is: (a) \(1/2\) (b) \((\sqrt 5 - 1)/2 \approx 0.618\) (c) \(1/\sqrt{2}\) (d) \(1/e\)

  8. For \(\min x_1^2+x_2^2\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2=2\), the solution \(x^\star\) is: (a) \((2,0)\) (b) \((0,2)\) (c) \((1,1)\) (d) \((\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\)

  9. In the KKT conditions for \(\min f\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le 0\), the multipliers satisfy: (a) \(\mu_i \le 0\) (b) \(\mu_i = 0\) (c) \(\mu_i \ge 0\) (d) no sign restriction

  10. For a quadratic with condition number \(\kappa(Q)\gg 1\), an iterative method will typically: (a) converge faster (b) converge more slowly (c) converge in one step (d) fail

  11. Which derivative method is most efficient when there are many parameters and one scalar output? (a) forward finite differences (b) central finite differences (c) reverse-mode AD / adjoint (d) forward-mode AD

  12. If \(\phi(\alpha) = f(x + \alpha d)\) with \( abla f(x)^ op d > 0\), then \(d\) is: (a) a descent direction (b) an ascent direction (c) orthogonal to \( abla f\) (d) not enough information

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. The first-order necessary condition for an unconstrained minimizer is \(\nabla f(x^\star) = \_\_\_\_\).
  2. The Hessian is the matrix of ________ partial derivatives.
  3. A point that no other feasible point Pareto-dominates is called ________.
  4. The second-order Taylor term is \(\tfrac12 d^\top \_\_\_\_ d\).
  5. The central-difference formula for \(\partial f/\partial x_i\) is \((f(x+h e_i) - f(x-h e_i)) / \_\_\_\_\).
  6. Golden-section uses \(\tau = (\sqrt 5 - 1)/2 \approx \_\_\_\_\).
  7. For equality constraints \(Ax=b\), the FONC is \(\nabla f(x^\star) + \_\_\_\_ = 0\).
  8. KKT complementary slackness reads \(\mu_i g_i(x^\star) = \_\_\_\_\).
  9. The adjoint (costate) method's gradient cost is independent of the number of _____.
  10. A symmetric matrix \(Q\) is positive definite if all eigenvalues are ____.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define local minimum, strict local minimum, and global minimum. Give a one-variable example illustrating the difference between local and global.
  2. Explain Pareto optimality and the Pareto front with an example. Why is there usually no single optimum for a multi-objective problem?
  3. State the first-order and second-order optimality conditions (both necessary and sufficient) for an unconstrained smooth problem. Give a counterexample showing that FONC alone is not sufficient.
  4. Describe the adjoint variable approach for gradient computation. In two or three sentences, explain why it is preferable to finite differences for problems with many parameters.
  5. Explain bracketing and sectioning in a line search. What is the reduction factor of golden-section, and what does the name mean?
  6. For a quadratic form \(\tfrac12 x^\top Qx - c^\top x\), explain how the eigenvalues of \(Q\) determine (i) whether a unique minimum exists, and (ii) the shape of level sets. Give the formula for the optimal value.

docs.title: 1.14 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — \( abla f(x^\star)=0\) is necessary but not sufficient; \( abla^2 f\succ0\) is only sufficient.
  2. (b) — FONC + strict SOSC gives a strict local minimum.
  3. (b) — In the Pareto set \([0,2]\); the rest are dominated (see Example 1.4).
  4. (b) — \(Qx^\star = c\), so \(x^\star = Q^{-1}c\).
  5. (a) — \( abla (a^ op x+b) = a\), a constant.
  6. (c) — central differences are \(O(h^2)\); forward/backward are \(O(h)\).
  7. (b) — \(1/\varphi = (\sqrt 5-1)/2\approx 0.618\).
  8. (c) — \(x_1=x_2=1\) from symmetry and the constraint (Example 1.8).
  9. (c) — \(\mu_i\ge0\) for minimisation with \(g_i\le0\).
  10. (b) — large \(\kappa\) = slow convergence; \(\kappa=1\) would be ideal.
  11. (c) — reverse-mode AD / adjoint: one forward + one reverse pass.
  12. (b) — positive directional derivative means \(\phi\) initially increases.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(0\)
  2. second (second-order / mixed)
  3. Pareto-optimal (Pareto-efficient)
  4. \( abla^2 f(x)\) (i.e. the Hessian)
  5. \(2h\)
  6. \(0.618\) (golden ratio conjugate)
  7. \(A^ op\lambda\) (or \(A^ op \lambda^\star\))
  8. \(0\)
  9. parameters (unknowns / control variables / inputs)
  10. positive (strictly greater than zero)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Local minimum: \(f(x^\star)\le f(x)\) for all feasible \(x\) in some neighborhood of \(x^\star\). Strict local minimum: the inequality is strict for \(x e x^\star\). Global minimum: the inequality holds over the whole feasible set. Example: \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) has strict local minima at \(x=\pm1\) and both are also global; by contrast \(f(x)=0.5 x^2+3\sin(3x)\) on \([-3,3]\) has multiple local minima but only one is global.
  2. Pareto dominance: \(x\) dominates \(y\) if \(f_i(x)\le f_i(y)\) for all \(i\) and strictly for at least one \(i\). Pareto-optimal: not dominated by any feasible point. The Pareto front is the image of the Pareto set in objective space. There is generally no single optimum because objectives conflict — improving one worsens another. Example: \(\min(x^2,(x-2)^2)\); the Pareto set is \([0,2]\).
  3. FONC: \( abla f(x^\star)=0\). SOSC-necessary: \( abla^2 f(x^\star)\succeq0\). SOSC-sufficient: \( abla^2 f(x^\star)\succ0\) ⇒ strict local min. Counterexample to FONC alone: \(f(x)=x^3\) at \(x=0\) — \( abla f(0)=0\) but \(0\) is an inflection, not a minimum.
  4. The adjoint (costate) method augments the state with a dual variable \(\lambda\) obeying a backward-in-time (or backward-in-index) equation; a single forward pass yields the states and a single backward pass yields the costates. The gradient with respect to all parameters is then obtained by simple products, at a cost independent of the parameter dimension. This contrasts with finite differences, whose cost grows linearly with the number of parameters.
  5. Bracketing is the phase that finds three points \(a<b<c\) with \(\phi(b)<\phi(a)\) and \(\phi(b)<\phi(c)\) — a bracket that must contain a local minimum. Sectioning refines the bracket by placing one or two interior test points and discarding the region that cannot contain the minimum. Golden-section places the interior points at a ratio \( au=(\sqrt5-1)/2\approx0.618\) from each end; each iteration reduces the interval to a fraction \( au\) of its length while reusing one previously computed value — this is why it is called golden-section.
  6. (i) A unique global minimum of \( frac12 x^ op Qx - c^ op x\) exists iff \(Q\succ0\) (all eigenvalues positive); if \(Q\) is indefinite, the quadratic is unbounded below along a negative-curvature direction. (ii) Level sets are ellipsoids whose axes are eigenvectors of \(Q\) with semi-axis lengths proportional to \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}\); the ratio of the longest to the shortest semi-axis is \(\sqrt{\kappa(Q)}\). Optimal value: \(f^\star = - frac12 c^ op Q^{-1} c\).

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Unconstrained. For \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\), find all stationary points, classify them, and identify the global minimum on \([0,4]\). Compare with a numerical golden-section result.
  2. Pareto. Compute and sketch the Pareto front of \(\min(x^2+y^2, (x-1)^2+y^2)\) over \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Identify at least three Pareto-optimal points.
  3. Lagrange. Use the Lagrange multiplier method to minimize \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2\) subject to \(x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 6\). Verify the multiplier via the envelope theorem.
  4. KKT. Solve \(\min (x-3)^2 + (y-2)^2\) s.t. \(x+y\le4\), \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\). Which constraints are active at the optimum, and what are the multipliers?
  5. Line search. Implement golden-section search and use it to minimize \(\phi(\alpha)=\sin(3\alpha)+\alpha^2/4\) on \([0,2]\). Verify convergence against scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar (method 'golden').
  6. Adjoint. Extend Example 1.13 to \(N=4\), \(x_{k+1}=x_k + u_k\), \(J = x_4^2 + \sum_{k=0}^3 u_k^2\). Derive the optimal \(u_0,\dots,u_3\) by both direct differentiation and the adjoint recursion, and confirm they agree.
  7. Gradient check. For \(f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \sin(x_1 x_2) + x_3^4 - x_1 e^{x_2 x_3}\), compute the analytic gradient at \((0.5, -1, 0.3)\) and compare with central-difference and reverse-mode AD (JAX) results.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Unconstrained Optimization
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): non-derivative methods · AD-HOC methods · direct search methods (polytope algorithm, simplex method, pattern search) · second-derivative methods (Newton) · first-derivative methods (quasi-Newton / BFGS) · sums of squares and nonlinear equations (Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Pick the right family of method for a given problem (smoothness, cost per evaluation, dimension).
  2. Implement and hand-trace one iteration of Nelder–Mead simplex and Hooke–Jeeves pattern search.
  3. Derive and apply Newton's method, state its local quadratic convergence, and explain when it fails.
  4. Explain the secant condition and update the BFGS Hessian approximation from \((s_k, y_k)\).
  5. Derive the Gauss–Newton step for nonlinear least squares and recognize when it diverges.
  6. Explain how Levenberg–Marquardt interpolates between Gauss–Newton (\(\lambda \to 0\)) and gradient descent (\(\lambda \to \infty\)).
  7. Implement the above using scipy.optimize, plain Java, and C#.

docs.title: 2.1 Taxonomy of the methods
docs.text:
Unconstrained minimization is the sub-problem every constrained solver eventually calls. Four broad families:

Family Needs derivatives? Cost per iteration Typical use Direct search — pattern search, Nelder–Mead No \(1\)–\(3\) function evaluations noisy, nonsmooth, or black-box \(f\) First-order — gradient descent, conjugate gradient, quasi-Newton (BFGS) \( abla f\) \(1\) gradient medium scale, moderate accuracy Second-order — Newton \( abla f\), \( abla^2 f\) 1 Hessian + linear solve small scale, high accuracy Least-squares — Gauss–Newton, LM residual \(r\), Jacobian \(J\) 1 Jacobian parameter fitting, inverse problems

Rules of thumb.

  • If \(f\) is cheap and \(n \le 20\), use Newton or BFGS with analytic derivatives.
  • If gradients are expensive (\(n\) large) use L-BFGS (limited-memory BFGS) — \(O(n)\) memory, \(O(n)\) per iteration.
  • If \(f\) is noisy or nonsmooth, use Nelder–Mead or pattern search.
  • If \(f\) is a sum of squared residuals, use Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt.

docs.title: 2.2 Direct-search methods — no derivatives required
docs.text: Direct-search methods evaluate \(f\) only at points. They converge slowly (typically linear with rate \(<1\)) but they do not require differentiability and tolerate moderate noise.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Pattern search (Hooke–Jeeves)
docs.text:
At iteration \(k\), maintain a mesh around the current iterate \(x_k\) with step vector \(\Delta_k\) (one scalar per coordinate). Alternate:

  • Exploratory move. Try \(x_k \pm \Delta_k \mathbf e_i\) for each \(i\); accept the first improvement.
  • Pattern move. If the exploratory move succeeded at step \(d\), try \(x_k + 2 d\) (accelerate).
  • Mesh halving. If neither succeeds, halve \(\Delta_k\); terminate when \(\|\Delta_k\| < \varepsilon\).

Algorithm:

Given x₀, initial step Δ, contraction factor 0 < θ < 1, tolerance ε
k ← 0
while ‖Δ‖ ≥ ε:
    for i in 1..n:
        for s in {+1, -1}:
            x_trial ← x_k + s * Δ_i * e_i
            if f(x_trial) < f(x_k):
                x_k ← x_trial; break  # first improvement wins
    if no improvement this cycle:
        Δ ← θ Δ
return x_k

The method is provably convergent to a stationary point for smooth \(f\) and any mesh-halving sequence, and does not build a model of \(f\).

docs.title: 2.2.2 Simplex method — Nelder–Mead
docs.text:
A simplex in \(\mathbb R^n\) is the convex hull of \(n+1\) affinely independent points. Nelder–Mead builds a sequence of simplices that shrinks toward a minimum. (Do not confuse this with Dantzig's simplex algorithm for linear programming — the names are historically unrelated.)

Algorithm:

Given an initial simplex {x₀, …, xₙ}
repeat:
    sort vertices so that f(x₀) ≤ f(x₁) ≤ … ≤ f(xₙ)
    x̄ ← centroid of {x₀, …, x_{n-1}}          # all except the worst
    r ← x̄ + α (x̄ − xₙ)                        # reflection  α = 1
    if f(x₀) ≤ f(r) < f(x_{n-1}):
        accept r, replace xₙ
    else if f(r) < f(x₀):                       # try to go further
        e ← x̄ + γ (r − x̄)                       # expansion   γ = 2
        accept whichever of e, r is better
    else if f(r) ≥ f(x_{n-1}):                  # reflect back in
        c ← x̄ + ρ (xₙ − x̄)                     # contraction ρ = 1/2
        if f(c) < f(xₙ): accept c, replace xₙ
        else:                                    # shrink toward best
            xᵢ ← x₀ + σ (xᵢ − x₀) for i = 1..n   (σ = 1/2)
until simplex diameter < ε

Standard parameters: \((\alpha,\gamma,\rho,\sigma) = (1, 2, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)\).

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — one full Nelder–Mead iteration
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x,y) = (x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2\) from the simplex

\[ v_1 = (0,0),\qquad v_2 = (3,0),\qquad v_3 = (0,3). \]

Order the vertices.

\[ f(v_1) = 13,\quad f(v_2) = 10,\quad f(v_3) = 8. \]

Best \(= v_3\), worst \(= v_1\).

Centroid of best and middle:

\[ \bar v = \tfrac12(v_2 + v_3) = (1.5,\ 1.5). \]

Reflection (\(\alpha=1\)):

\[ r = \bar v + ( \bar v - v_1) = (3,\ 3),\qquad f(r) = 1 + 0 = 1. \]

Since \(f(r) < f(v_3)\), we try to expand (\(\gamma=2\)):

\[ e = \bar v + 2(r - \bar v) = (4.5,\ 4.5),\qquad f(e) = 6.25 + 2.25 = 8.5. \]

\(f(e) = 8.5 > f(r) = 1\), so reject expansion, accept reflection.

New simplex: \(\{(3,0),\ (0,3),\ (3,3)\}\) with values \(\{10,\ 8,\ 1\}\).

Next iteration would reflect around the centroid of \((0,3)\) and \((3,3)\), contracting toward \((2,3)\). In practice Nelder–Mead needs \(\sim 50\)–\(200\) iterations to reach \(\|x - (2,3)\| < 10^{-6}\) from this starting simplex — that is the price of not using derivatives.

Strengths and limits

Nelder–Mead is robust, easy to code, and works in noisy black-box settings. But it is provably not convergent in dimension ≥ 2 for all starting simplices (McKinnon's counterexample, 1998) — it can stagnate at a non-stationary point. Treat it as a fallback, not a workhorse.

docs.title: 2.2.3 AD-HOC methods
docs.text: The syllabus lists “AD-HOC methods” — problem-specific heuristics with no general convergence guarantee: random perturbation (simulated-annealing-like), grid search, evolutionary strategies, or hybrid “try 100 random starts, then Nelder–Mead”. They are worth using after a principled method has failed, and always with a deterministic seed for reproducibility.

docs.title: 2.3 Second-derivative methods — Newton's method
docs.text:
Newton approximates \(f\) by its second-order Taylor polynomial around \(x_k\) and minimizes that quadratic exactly:

\[ f(x_k + d) \approx f(x_k) + abla f(x_k)^ op d + frac12 d^ op abla^2 f(x_k) d. \]

Setting the gradient of the right side to zero gives the Newton step:

\[ oxed{\; abla^2 f(x_k)\, d_k = - abla f(x_k)\;} \]

and the update \(x_{k+1} = x_k + d_k\). The step length is 1 (Newton picks it automatically).

docs.title: Convergence properties
docs.text:
• Local quadratic convergence near a strict local minimum with \( abla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\): \(\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\| \le C\|x_k-x^\star\|^2\).
  • One-step convergence on any strictly convex quadratic (because the quadratic model is exact).
  • Fails when \( abla^2 f(x_k)\) is singular or indefinite — the step may not even be a descent direction. Add a line search or a regularization \( abla^2 f + \mu I\) to fix this.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — Newton on a strictly convex quadratic
docs.text:
Minimize

\[ f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 + xy - 3x - 4y. \]

Gradient and Hessian.

\[ abla f(x,y) = egin{bmatrix} 2x + y - 3 \ x + 4y - 4\end{bmatrix}, \qquad abla^2 f(x,y) = egin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}. \]

The Hessian is constant and positive definite (\(2 \cdot 4 - 1 = 7 > 0\), diagonal entries \(> 0\)), so \(f\) has a unique global minimizer.

Newton step from \((0,0)\). Solve

\[ egin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} d_1 \ d_2\end{bmatrix} = - egin{bmatrix} -3 \ -4\end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} 3 \ 4\end{bmatrix}. \]

The inverse is \( frac17 egin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\), so

\[ d = frac17 egin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} 3 \ 4\end{bmatrix} = frac17 egin{bmatrix} 8 \ 5\end{bmatrix}. \]

Update: \(x_1 = ( frac87, frac57)\).

Verification: \( abla f( frac87, frac57) = ( frac{16}{7} + frac57 - 3,\ frac87 + frac{20}{7} - 4) = (0,0)\).

Convergence: one step, exactly — as predicted for any strictly convex quadratic.

docs.title: Worked example 2.3 — Newton on a non-quadratic problem
docs.text:
For the one-variable function \(f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + x\) the Newton recursion is

\[ x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f'(x_k)}{f''(x_k)} = x_k - \frac{4x_k^3 - 6x_k + 1}{12x_k^2 - 6}. \]

Starting at \(x_0 = 2\):

\(k\) \(x_k\) \(f(x_k)\) 0 2.000 16 − 12 + 2 = 6.000 1 1.532 5.50 2 1.246 2.36 3 1.085 0.86 4 1.027 0.61 5 1.012 0.55

Convergence becomes quadratic once \(\|x_k - x^\star\|\) is small — the number of correct digits roughly doubles each iteration near the solution.

docs.title: Practical safeguard — damped Newton
docs.text: When the Newton step is not a descent direction (Hessian indefinite), replace the update with \(x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha_k d_k\) where \(\alpha_k\) is chosen by a line search (Armijo or Wolfe, §1.9). This is damped Newton and it retains superlinear convergence while guaranteeing global convergence under mild conditions.

docs.title: 2.4 First-derivative methods — quasi-Newton (BFGS)
docs.text: Newton costs \(O(n^2)\) memory (Hessian) and \(O(n^3)\) per iteration (linear solve). Quasi-Newton methods build an approximation \(B_k \approx \nabla^2 f(x_k)\) using only gradient information, updating it by a low-rank formula each iteration.

docs.title: The secant condition
docs.text:
If we know \(x_k\), \(x_{k+1}\), \( abla f(x_k)\), \( abla f(x_{k+1})\), Taylor's theorem (to first order) gives

\[ abla f(x_{k+1}) - abla f(x_k) \approx abla^2 f(x_{k+1})(x_{k+1} - x_k). \]

Writing \(s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k\) and \(y_k = abla f(x_{k+1}) - abla f(x_k)\), we require the approximation to satisfy the secant condition:

\[ oxed{\;B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\;} \]

Equivalently for the inverse \(H_k = B_k^{-1}\): \(H_{k+1} y_k = s_k\).

docs.title: BFGS update
docs.text:
The Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) update for the inverse Hessian is the rank-2 formula

\[ \boxed{\; H_{k+1} = H_k + \frac{s_k y_k^\top + y_k s_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k} - \left(1 + \frac{y_k^\top H_k y_k}{y_k^\top s_k}\right)\frac{s_k s_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k} \;} \]

or, in the equivalent “\(H\)” form,

\[ H_{k+1} = \left(I - \frac{s_k y_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k}\right) H_k \left(I - \frac{y_k s_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k}\right) + \frac{s_k s_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k}. \]

Properties.

  • \(H_{k+1}\) is symmetric positive definite whenever \(H_0 \succ 0\) and \(y_k^\top s_k > 0\) (which a Wolfe line search guarantees).
  • Quadratic convergence on quadratics: BFGS with exact line search converges in exactly \(n\) steps on an \(n\)-dimensional quadratic.
  • L-BFGS stores only the last \(m\) pairs \((s_k, y_k)\) — \(O(mn)\) memory, standard for \(n\) up to millions.

docs.title: Worked example 2.4 — two-step BFGS on a quadratic
docs.text:
Minimize

\[ f(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + 2x_2^2,\qquad abla f = egin{bmatrix} 2x_1 \ 4x_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad abla^2 f = egin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}. \]

Start at \(x_0 = (1,1)\) with \(H_0 = I\).

Iteration 0.

\[ abla f(x_0) = (2,4),\qquad d_0 = -H_0 abla f(x_0) = (-2, -4). \]

Exact line search: \(\phi(\alpha) = (1-2\alpha)^2 + 2(1-4\alpha)^2 = 3 - 20\alpha + 36\alpha^2\). \(\phi'(\alpha) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = frac{5}{18}\).

\[ x_1 = \left( frac49, - frac19 ight),\qquad abla f(x_1) = \left( frac89, - frac49 ight). \]

Update pair.

\[ s_0 = x_1 - x_0 = \left(- frac59, - frac{10}{9} ight),\qquad y_0 = abla f(x_1) - abla f(x_0) = \left(- frac{10}{9}, - frac{40}{9} ight). \]

Secant scalars:

\[ y_0^ op s_0 = frac{50}{81} + frac{400}{81} = frac{450}{81},\qquad s_0^ op s_0 = frac{25}{81} + frac{100}{81} = frac{125}{81}. \]

Rank-2 terms:

\[ rac{y_0 y_0^ op}{y_0^ op s_0} = egin{bmatrix} frac{2}{9} & frac{8}{9}\[2pt] frac{8}{9} & frac{32}{9}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad rac{s_0 s_0^ op}{s_0^ op s_0} = egin{bmatrix} frac15 & frac25\[2pt] frac25 & frac45\end{bmatrix}. \]

BFGS update (inverse-Hessian form):

\[ H_1 = I + egin{bmatrix} frac{2}{9} & frac{8}{9}\[2pt] frac{8}{9} & frac{32}{9}\end{bmatrix} - egin{bmatrix} frac15 & frac25\[2pt] frac25 & frac45\end{bmatrix} = rac{1}{45} egin{bmatrix} 46 & 22\ 22 & 169\end{bmatrix}. \]

Check the secant condition \(H_1 y_0 = s_0\) (inverse-Hessian version):

\[ H_1 y_0 = rac{1}{45} egin{bmatrix} 46 & 22 \ 22 & 169\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}- frac{10}{9}\ - frac{40}{9}\end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix}- frac59\[2pt] - frac{10}{9}\end{bmatrix} = s_0. \;\checkmark \]

Iteration 1.

\[ d_1 = -H_1 abla f(x_1) = -\left(- frac{80}{81}, frac{20}{81} ight) = \left( frac{80}{81}, - frac{20}{81} ight). \]

Exact line search gives \(\alpha^\star = frac{9}{20}\). Then

\[ x_2 = x_1 + frac{9}{20} d_1 = (0, 0). \]

Convergence in 2 iterations — one per dimension, as expected for BFGS with exact line search on a quadratic.

docs.title: 2.5 Sums of squares and nonlinear equations
docs.text:
Many engineering problems are nonlinear least-squares: minimize

\[ f( heta) = frac12 \|r( heta)\|^2 = frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i( heta)^2, \]

where \(r : \mathbb R^n o \mathbb R^m\) is the residual vector (often \(m \gg n\)). The gradient is

\[ abla f( heta) = J( heta)^ op r( heta),\qquad J_{ij} = rac{\partial r_i}{\partial heta_j}. \]

The Hessian has a special structure:

\[ abla^2 f( heta) = J^ op J + \sum_{i=1}^m r_i( heta)\, abla^2 r_i( heta). \]

The first term is cheap (Jacobian product); the second (the “curvature of the residual”) is expensive or unavailable. Gauss–Newton simply drops the second term.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Gauss–Newton
docs.text:
Replace the Newton Hessian by \(J^\top J\):

\[ \boxed{\;(J_k^\top J_k)\, \Delta\theta_k = -J_k^\top r_k\;} \]

and update \(\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \Delta\theta_k\).

Convergence.

  • Linear if residuals at the solution are nonzero (the dropped term matters).
  • Quadratic if the fit is exact (zero residuals at the solution) — this includes all linear least-squares.
  • Diverges when \(J^\top J\) is rank-deficient or the step is too large.

docs.title: Worked example 2.5 — Gauss–Newton on an exponential fit
docs.text:
Fit \(y = a\,e^{b x}\) to the data

\[ (x_i, y_i) \in \{(0,1),\ (1,3),\ (2,8)\}. \]

Residuals \(r_i = y_i - a e^{b x_i}\) and Jacobian rows

\[ \nabla r_i = \big(-e^{b x_i},\ -a x_i e^{b x_i}\big). \]

Start from \(\theta_0 = (a, b) = (1, 1)\).

Evaluate at \(\theta_0\).

\[ f(\theta_0) = (1, e, e^2) \approx (1, 2.718, 7.389),\qquad r_0 = (0,\ 0.282,\ 0.611). \] \[ J_0 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ -2.718 & -2.718 \\ -7.389 & -14.78\end{bmatrix}. \]

Normal equations.

\[ J_0^\top J_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 63.0 & 116.6 \\ 116.6 & 226.0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad J_0^\top r_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 5.28 \\ 9.79\end{bmatrix}. \]

Solve \((J_0^\top J_0)\Delta = -J_0^\top r_0\):

\[ \Delta\theta_0 \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.080 \\ 0.002\end{bmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta_1 \approx (1.080,\ 1.002). \]

Two more iterations.

\(k\) \(a_k\) \(b_k\) \(\|r_k\|\) 0 1.000 1.000 0.674 1 1.080 1.002 0.016 2 1.084 1.000 0.004 3 1.084 1.000 0.004

Convergence is fast because the residuals at the solution are small.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Levenberg–Marquardt
docs.text:
Add a damping term to stabilize the Gauss–Newton step:

\[ \boxed{\;(J_k^\top J_k + \lambda_k I)\,\Delta\theta_k = -J_k^\top r_k\;} \]

with \(\lambda_k > 0\) updated adaptively:

  • If the new step decreases \(f\): accept it and decrease \(\lambda\) (e.g. \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda/10\)) — moves toward Gauss–Newton.
  • If the new step increases \(f\): reject it and increase \(\lambda\) (e.g. \(\lambda \leftarrow 10\lambda\)) — moves toward gradient descent.

Limiting cases.

  • \(\lambda \to 0\): \(J^\top J \Delta = -J^\top r\) — Gauss–Newton (fast near the solution).
  • \(\lambda \to \infty\): \(\lambda I \Delta \approx -J^\top r\), i.e. \(\Delta \approx -\tfrac{1}{\lambda} \nabla f\) — a gradient-descent step with small step length.

So LM interpolates between Gauss–Newton and gradient descent: it is globally convergent (in practice) and quadratically convergent near the solution — a combination Gauss–Newton cannot offer alone.

docs.title: Worked example 2.6 — same problem, one LM step
docs.text:
Use the same data and same starting point as Example 2.5. Take \(\lambda_0 = 1\).

\[ J_0^\top J_0 + \lambda_0 I = \begin{bmatrix} 64.0 & 116.6\\ 116.6 & 227.0\end{bmatrix}. \] \[ \Delta\theta_0 = -(J_0^\top J_0 + I)^{-1} J_0^\top r_0 \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.060 \\ 0.011\end{bmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta_1 \approx (1.060,\ 1.011). \]

The step is smaller than the pure Gauss–Newton step \((0.080, 0.002)\) — that is exactly the intent: when \(\lambda\) is large, LM distrusts the linearization and takes a cautious step. If \(f(\theta_1) > f(\theta_0)\), LM would reject this step, increase \(\lambda\) to 10, and try again.

Trust-region interpretation

Levenberg–Marquardt is the trust-region method for least-squares. It minimizes the linearized residual subject to a bound \(\|\Delta\| \le \Delta_{\max}\); the multiplier of that constraint is \(\lambda\). When the linear model is reliable, the trust region is large and LM behaves like Gauss–Newton; when it is not, the region shrinks and LM behaves like gradient descent.

docs.title: 2.6 Comparison on a standard benchmark
docs.text:
For the Rosenbrock function

\[ f(x,y) = (1 - x)^2 + 100(y - x^2)^2,\qquad \text{minimum at } (1,1),\ f^\star = 0, \]

start from \((-1, 1)\) with tolerance \(10^{-6}\):

Method Iterations Function evaluations Gradient evaluations Nelder–Mead 187 345 0 Pattern search (Hooke–Jeeves) 2140 12 400 0 Gradient descent (Armijo) 14 800 15 200 14 800 BFGS (Wolfe line search) 41 63 41 Newton with line search 24 35 24 L-BFGS (\(m=10\)) 56 78 56

The message: derivative information is worth orders of magnitude. Use Nelder–Mead only when derivatives are unavailable; use BFGS when the Hessian is unavailable or expensive; use Newton when it is cheap and reliable.

docs.title: 2.7 Computational implementation
docs.text: The snippets below solve the same two problems — (i) the 2-D quadratic of Example 2.4 and (ii) the exponential fit of Example 2.5 — using scipy, plain Java, and C#. The point is to see the same algorithm expressed three ways.

docs.title: Python with SciPy (recommended starting point)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize, least_squares

# ---- (i) quadratic  f = x1^2 + 2 x2^2 -----------------------------------
def f(x):
    return x[0]**2 + 2*x[1]**2

def grad_f(x):
    return np.array([2*x[0], 4*x[1]])

def hess_f(x):
    return np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]])

x0 = np.array([1.0, 1.0])

for method in ["Nelder-Mead", "BFGS", "Newton-CG"]:
    kwargs = {"jac": grad_f}
    if method == "Newton-CG":
        kwargs["hess"] = hess_f
    r = minimize(f, x0, method=method, **kwargs)
    print(f"{method:>12}: x* = {r.x},  f* = {r.fun:.3e},  nit = {r.nit}")

# ---- (ii) exponential fit  y = a exp(b x) -------------------------------
xdata = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
ydata = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 8.0])

def residuals(theta):
    a, b = theta
    return ydata - a * np.exp(b * xdata)

for method in ["lm", "trf"]:
    r = least_squares(residuals, x0=[1.0, 1.0], method=method)
    print(f"least_squares[{method}]: a = {r.x[0]:.4f}, b = {r.x[1]:.4f}, "
          f"cost = {r.cost:.3e}, nfev = {r.nfev}")

# ---- (iii) hand-rolled Nelder-Mead in 2-D --------------------------------
def nelder_mead(fun, x0, step=1.0, tol=1e-8, maxit=2000):
    """Minimal Nelder-Mead for n = 2."""
    n = len(x0)
    simplex = np.array([x0] + [x0 + step*np.eye(n)[i] for i in range(n)])
    for _ in range(maxit):
        vals = np.array([fun(v) for v in simplex])
        order = np.argsort(vals)
        simplex, vals = simplex[order], vals[order]
        if np.max(np.abs(simplex[1:] - simplex[0])) < tol:
            break
        xbar = simplex[:-1].mean(axis=0)
        worst = simplex[-1]
        r = xbar + (xbar - worst)                # reflection
        fr = fun(r)
        if fr < vals[0]:
            e = xbar + 2*(r - xbar)              # expansion
            simplex[-1] = e if fun(e) < fr else r
        elif fr < vals[-2]:
            simplex[-1] = r                       # accept reflection
        else:
            c = xbar + 0.5*(worst - xbar)         # contraction
            if fun(c) < vals[-1]:
                simplex[-1] = c
            else:                                 # shrink
                simplex[1:] = simplex[0] + 0.5*(simplex[1:] - simplex[0])
    return simplex[0]

xs = nelder_mead(lambda v: (v[0]-2)**2 + (v[1]-3)**2, np.array([0.0, 0.0]))
print("NM result:", xs)

docs.title: Java — BFGS for a small problem
docs.text:
import java.util.Arrays;

public class BFGS {

    static double f(double[] x) { return x[0]*x[0] + 2*x[1]*x[1]; }
    static double[] grad(double[] x) { return new double[]{2*x[0], 4*x[1]}; }

    static double[][] identity(int n) {
        double[][] I = new double[n][n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) I[i][i] = 1.0;
        return I;
    }
    static double[][] matmul(double[][] A, double[][] B) {
        int n = A.length, m = B[0].length, k = B.length;
        double[][] C = new double[n][m];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < m; j++)
                for (int l = 0; l < k; l++) C[i][j] += A[i][l] * B[l][j];
        return C;
    }
    static double[] matvec(double[][] A, double[] v) {
        double[] r = new double[v.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < v.length; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < v.length; j++) r[i] += A[i][j] * v[j];
        return r;
    }
    static double dot(double[] a, double[] b) {
        double s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i]*b[i]; return s;
    }

    // Exact line search on a quadratic:  x -> x + α d  with  φ(α)=f(x+αd)
    static double lineSearch(double[] x, double[] d) {
        // For f = x1² + 2x2², φ'(α)=0 at α = -(d·∇f(x)) / (2 d1² + 4 d2²)
        double[] g = grad(x);
        double num = -dot(d, g);
        double den = 2*d[0]*d[0] + 4*d[1]*d[1];
        return num / den;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] x = {1.0, 1.0};
        double[][] H = identity(2);
        for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) {
            double[] g = grad(x);
            double[] d = matvec(H, g);
            for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) d[i] = -d[i];

            double alpha = lineSearch(x, d);
            double[] xNew = {x[0] + alpha*d[0], x[1] + alpha*d[1]};
            double[] gNew = grad(xNew);
            double[] s = {xNew[0]-x[0], xNew[1]-x[1]};
            double[] y = {gNew[0]-g[0], gNew[1]-g[1]};

            // BFGS update (inverse-Hessian form):
            // H ← (I - ρ s yᵀ) H (I - ρ y sᵀ) + ρ s sᵀ ,  ρ = 1/(y·s)
            double rho = 1.0 / dot(y, s);
            double[][] I = identity(2);
            double[][] A = {
                {I[0][0] - rho*s[0]*y[0], I[0][1] - rho*s[0]*y[1]},
                {I[1][0] - rho*s[1]*y[0], I[1][1] - rho*s[1]*y[1]}
            };
            double[][] At = {{A[0][0], A[1][0]}, {A[0][1], A[1][1]}};
            double[][] ssT = {{s[0]*s[0], s[0]*s[1]}, {s[1]*s[0], s[1]*s[1]}};
            H = matmul(matmul(A, H), At);
            for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
                for (int j = 0; j < 2; j++) H[i][j] += rho * ssT[i][j];

            x = xNew;
            System.out.printf("k=%d  x=(%.3e, %.3e)  f=%.3e%n", k, x[0], x[1], f(x));
        }
    }
}

docs.title: C# — Nelder–Mead for a small problem
docs.text:
using System;

class NelderMead
{
    static double F(double[] x) => (x[0]-2)*(x[0]-2) + (x[1]-3)*(x[1]-3);

    static void Main()
    {
        double[][] simplex = {
            new double[]{0, 0},
            new double[]{1, 0},
            new double[]{0, 1}
        };
        double tol = 1e-8;

        for (int iter = 0; iter < 2000; iter++)
        {
            Array.Sort(simplex, (a, b) => F(a).CompareTo(F(b)));
            double diameter = 0;
            for (int i = 1; i < 3; i++)
                diameter = Math.Max(diameter,
                    Math.Abs(simplex[i][0]-simplex[0][0]) + Math.Abs(simplex[i][1]-simplex[0][1]));
            if (diameter < tol) break;

            var centroid = new double[]{
                0.5 * (simplex[0][0] + simplex[1][0]),
                0.5 * (simplex[0][1] + simplex[1][1])
            };
            var worst = simplex[2];

            var r = new double[]{2*centroid[0]-worst[0], 2*centroid[1]-worst[1]};
            if (F(r) < F(simplex[0]))
            {
                var e = new double[]{centroid[0]+2*(r[0]-centroid[0]),
                                     centroid[1]+2*(r[1]-centroid[1])};
                simplex[2] = F(e) < F(r) ? e : r;
            }
            else if (F(r) < F(simplex[1]))
            {
                simplex[2] = r;
            }
            else
            {
                var c = new double[]{centroid[0]+0.5*(worst[0]-centroid[0]),
                                     centroid[1]+0.5*(worst[1]-centroid[1])};
                if (F(c) < F(worst)) simplex[2] = c;
                else
                {
                    for (int i = 1; i < 3; i++)
                    {
                        simplex[i][0] = simplex[0][0] + 0.5*(simplex[i][0]-simplex[0][0]);
                        simplex[i][1] = simplex[0][1] + 0.5*(simplex[i][1]-simplex[0][1]);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        Console.WriteLine($"x* = ({simplex[0][0]:F6}, {simplex[0][1]:F6})");
    }
}

Tooling pointers

  • Python: scipy.optimize.minimize (methods 'Nelder-Mead', 'BFGS', 'Newton-CG'); scipy.optimize.least_squares (methods 'lm', 'trf') for LM.
  • Java: Apache Commons Math (BfgsOptimizer, SimplexOptimizer, LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer); Hipparchus has the same API with bug fixes.
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics (NelderMeadSimplex, BfgsMinimizer); Accord.NET for LM.
  • Julia / MATLAB: Optim.jl, fminunc — both are production-quality and short.

docs.title: 2.8 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Pick the family. Direct search for black boxes; BFGS for smooth mid-scale; Newton for accurate small-scale; GN/LM for least squares.
  2. Nelder–Mead needs only function values but has no convergence guarantee in \(n \ge 2\) — use it as a fallback.
  3. Newton gives one-step convergence on strictly convex quadratics and quadratic convergence near a strict minimum, but needs the Hessian and can fail when it is indefinite.
  4. BFGS approximates the Hessian from gradients only, satisfies the secant condition \(B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\), and converges in \(n\) steps on any \(n\)-dimensional quadratic.
  5. Gauss–Newton drops the second-order term in the least-squares Hessian — fast when residuals at the solution are small, unreliable when they are large or the Jacobian is rank-deficient.
  6. Levenberg–Marquardt adds \(\lambda I\) to \(J^\top J\), interpolates between GN (\(\lambda \to 0\)) and gradient descent (\(\lambda \to \infty\)), and adapts \(\lambda\) based on whether each step actually decreases the cost.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. Which method does not require derivatives? (a) Newton (b) Nelder–Mead (c) BFGS (d) Gauss–Newton

  2. Newton's method converges in how many iterations on a strictly convex quadratic? (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) \(n\) (d) arbitrarily many

  3. A Nelder–Mead simplex in \(\mathbb R^n\) has how many vertices? (a) \(n\) (b) \(n+1\) (c) \(2^n\) (d) \(2n\)

  4. BFGS is classified as a: (a) direct-search method (b) second-order method (c) quasi-Newton method (d) least-squares method

  5. The secant condition for BFGS (Hessian-approximation form) is: (a) \(B_{k+1} y_k = s_k\) (b) \(B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\) (c) \(B_{k+1} = abla^2 f\) (d) \(B_{k+1} = I\)

  6. Gauss–Newton replaces the Hessian \( abla^2 f\) by: (a) \(J^ op J\) (b) \(J^{-1}\) (c) \(J^ op J + \lambda I\) (d) the identity

  7. Levenberg–Marquardt adds \(\lambda I\) to which matrix? (a) \(J\) (b) \(J^ op J\) (c) \( abla^2 f\) (d) \(H_k\)

  8. As \(\lambda o 0\) in LM, the step approaches: (a) the Gauss–Newton step (b) a gradient-descent step (c) zero (d) a random direction

  9. As \(\lambda o \infty\) in LM, the step approaches: (a) the Gauss–Newton step (b) a scaled gradient-descent step (c) a Newton step (d) zero

  10. On the Rosenbrock function, which method typically needs the most function evaluations? (a) Newton (b) BFGS (c) gradient descent (d) Nelder–Mead

  11. Nelder–Mead is not guaranteed to converge because: (a) it uses too few function evaluations (b) the simplex can collapse before reaching a stationary point (c) it requires gradients (d) it is a special case of Newton

  12. Which is the right choice for a parameter-fitting problem with \(m=1000\) residuals and \(n=5\) parameters? (a) Nelder–Mead (b) BFGS on \( frac12\|r\|^2\) (c) Levenberg–Marquardt (d) Pattern search

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A Nelder–Mead simplex in \(\mathbb R^n\) has ____ vertices.
  2. Newton's step solves the linear system \(H_k d_k = \_\_\_\_\_\).
  3. In BFGS, \(s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k\) and \(y_k = \_\_\_\_\_\).
  4. The BFGS secant condition is \(B_{k+1} s_k = \_\_\_\_\).
  5. The Gauss–Newton step satisfies \((J_k^\top J_k)\,\Delta\theta_k = \_\_\_\_\_\).
  6. The Levenberg–Marquardt step satisfies \((J_k^\top J_k + \lambda_k I)\,\Delta\theta_k = \_\_\_\_\_\).
  7. Hooke–Jeeves alternates an _____ move with a _____ move.
  8. Newton's method has local _____ convergence near a strict minimum.
  9. BFGS with exact line search converges in exactly ____ iterations on an \(n\)-dimensional quadratic.
  10. The family of methods that only evaluates \(f\) (never \(\nabla f\)) is called _____ search.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Explain the secant condition for quasi-Newton methods and why it is the minimal “Hessian-mimicking” condition.
  2. State the Newton step and its local convergence rate. Give one situation in which plain Newton can fail and how a line search fixes it.
  3. Describe the Nelder–Mead reflection / expansion / contraction / shrink operations. What is the standard parameter tuple \((\alpha,\gamma,\rho,\sigma)\)?
  4. For a nonlinear least-squares problem, derive the Gauss–Newton step from the Taylor expansion of \(r(\theta)\) and explain under what condition it is second-order convergent.
  5. Compare Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt in two or three sentences. Under what condition does LM reduce to GN, and under what condition does it reduce to gradient descent?
  6. Compare BFGS and Newton in terms of cost per iteration and convergence rate. When would you prefer L-BFGS to either?

docs.title: 2.10 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — Nelder–Mead is a direct-search method.
  2. (a) — One step for a strictly convex quadratic.
  3. (b) — \(n+1\) affinely independent vertices.
  4. (c) — Quasi-Newton; approximates the Hessian from gradients.
  5. (b) — \(B_{k+1} s_k = y_k\).
  6. (a) — \(J^ op J\) (dropping the residual-curvature term).
  7. (b) — \(J^ op J\).
  8. (a) — \(\lambda o 0\): pure Gauss–Newton.
  9. (b) — \(\lambda o \infty\): gradient descent with step \(\sim 1/\lambda\).
  10. (c) — Gradient descent is the slowest of the four on Rosenbrock (valley-following).
  11. (b) — The simplex can collapse at a non-stationary point (McKinnon counterexample).
  12. (c) — LM exploits the residual structure and the small \(n\).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(n+1\)
  2. \(- abla f(x_k)\)
  3. \( abla f(x_{k+1}) - abla f(x_k)\)
  4. \(y_k\)
  5. \(-J_k^ op r_k\)
  6. \(-J_k^ op r_k\)
  7. exploratory; pattern (or: pattern; exploratory — either order is acceptable in the standard “explore-then-pattern” description)
  8. quadratic
  9. \(n\)
  10. direct
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. The secant condition requires the Hessian approximation \(B_{k+1}\) to reproduce the observed change in gradient over the last step: \(B_{k+1}(x_{k+1}-x_k) = abla f(x_{k+1}) - abla f(x_k)\). It is the minimal condition a “Hessian-like” matrix must satisfy in order to be consistent with a first-order Taylor expansion of the gradient. Infinitely many symmetric matrices satisfy it — the different quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, DFP, SR1) are distinguished by which one they pick, e.g. by a minimum-change property.
  2. Newton step: \( abla^2 f(x_k) d_k = - abla f(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1} = x_k + d_k\). Local convergence is quadratic if \( abla^2 f(x^\star) \succ 0\) and \(x_0\) is close enough. Fails when \( abla^2 f(x_k)\) is singular (no unique step) or indefinite (the step may not be a descent direction); a line search on the direction \(d_k\) restores global convergence under mild assumptions while preserving local superlinear convergence.
  3. Nelder–Mead operations: reflection \(r = ar x + \alpha( ar x - x_{ ext{worst}})\) with \(\alpha=1\); expansion \(e = ar x + \gamma( ar x - x_{ ext{worst}})\) with \(\gamma=2\) (attempted when \(f(r) < f(x_{ ext{best}})\)); contraction \(c = ar x + ho(x_{ ext{worst}} - ar x)\) with \( ho= frac12\) (when reflection is not better than the second-worst); shrink \(x_i \leftarrow x_{ ext{best}} + \sigma(x_i - x_{ ext{best}})\) with \(\sigma= frac12\) (when contraction also fails). Standard tuple: \((\alpha,\gamma, ho,\sigma) = (1, 2, frac12, frac12)\).
  4. Write \(r( heta + \Delta) \approx r( heta) + J( heta)\Delta\). Then \( frac12\|r( heta + \Delta)\|^2\) is minimized by \(\Delta\) solving \(J^ op J \Delta = -J^ op r\) — this is the Gauss–Newton step. It is second-order convergent when the residual at the solution is zero (then the dropped term \(\sum r_i abla^2 r_i\) vanishes at the solution), otherwise the convergence is only linear with rate governed by the size of the dropped term.
  5. Gauss–Newton solves \(J^ op J \Delta = -J^ op r\); LM solves \((J^ op J + \lambda I)\Delta = -J^ op r\) with \(\lambda\) adapted. LM reduces to GN when \(\lambda o 0\) (trust in the linearization) and to gradient descent when \(\lambda o \infty\) (\(\Delta \approx -(1/\lambda) J^ op r = -(1/\lambda) abla f\)). In practice LM starts with moderate \(\lambda\), decreases it on successful steps, increases it on unsuccessful ones.
  6. Newton: \(O(n^3)\) per iteration (dense linear solve) + Hessian cost, quadratic convergence. BFGS: \(O(n^2)\) memory, \(O(n^2)\) per iteration, superlinear convergence. L-BFGS stores only the last \(m\) pairs \((s_k, y_k)\) — \(O(mn)\) memory, \(O(mn)\) per iteration — and is the method of choice when \(n\) is large (\(10^3\)–\(10^6\)).
