docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Nelder–Mead by hand. Starting from the simplex \(\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}\) on \(f(x,y)=(x-2)^2+(y-3)^2\), trace two full iterations (sort → reflect → expand / contract / shrink). Verify your result against scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead').
  2. Newton with a line search. Implement damped Newton on the Rosenbrock function from \((-1,1)\). Compare iteration counts with plain Newton and with plain gradient descent. Plot \(\|x_k - (1,1)\|\) on a log axis vs \(k\).
  3. BFGS update. For \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+2x_2^2\) starting from \((1,1)\), verify by hand that the BFGS update of Example 2.4 satisfies \(H_1 s_0 = y_0\) and \(H_1 \succ 0\).
  4. Quasi-Newton failure. Show that the BFGS update breaks down when \(y_k^\top s_k \le 0\). Construct a one-dimensional counterexample where this occurs with an arbitrary step (no line search).
  5. Gauss–Newton at work. Fit \(y = a e^{b x}\) to \(x = (0,1,2,3)\), \(y = (1, 3, 7, 15)\). Use both GN and LM (with \(\lambda_0=1\), adaptive). Report the number of iterations each takes.
  6. Rank-deficient Jacobian. Construct a nonlinear least-squares problem with \(m > n\) where \(J\) is rank-deficient at the starting point. Show that Gauss–Newton fails and LM still converges.
  7. Global optimization benchmark. Compare Nelder–Mead, BFGS, and Newton on Rastrigin's function \(f(x) = 10n + \sum[x_i^2 - 10\cos(2\pi x_i)]\) in \(n=2\) from three different starts. Comment on which methods find the global minimum and why.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Constrained Optimization
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): penalty functions · barrier functions · augmented Lagrangian · quadratic programming — focus on QP with equality constraints, with an active-set preview for inequalities.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Formulate the constraint set \(g_i(x) \le 0\), \(h_j(x) = 0\) and identify feasible, strictly feasible, and boundary points.
  2. Build exterior penalty functions, prove that the solution of the penalized problem converges to the constrained optimum as the penalty parameter grows, and quantify the error \(O(1/\mu)\).
  3. Build logarithmic barrier functions, explain why the barrier requires a strictly feasible starting point, and show that the error is \(O(\mu)\) as \(\mu \to 0^+\).
  4. Derive and iterate the augmented Lagrangian (method of multipliers), and explain why it avoids the ill-conditioning of pure penalties.
  5. Solve a quadratic program with equality constraints by forming and solving the KKT linear system; state existence and uniqueness conditions.
  6. Describe the active-set method for QP with inequality constraints.
  7. Implement each of the above in Python, Java, or C#.

docs.title: 3.1 Problem statement
docs.text:
Minimize \(f : \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) subject to

\[ egin{aligned} & ext{minimize} && f(x) \ & ext{subject to} && g_i(x) \le 0, \quad i = 1,\dots,p, \ & && h_j(x) = 0, \quad j = 1,\dots,q. \end{aligned} \]

The feasible set is \(\Omega = \{ x : g_i(x) \le 0,\; h_j(x) = 0 \}\).

Concept Definition Feasible point \(x \in \Omega\) Strictly feasible point \(g_i(x) < 0\) for all \(i\), \(h_j(x) = 0\) for all \(j\) Active inequality \(g_i(x) = 0\) at a feasible point Inactive inequality \(g_i(x) < 0\) Local minimum \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for all feasible \(x\) near \(x^\star\)

In Chapter 1 you saw the KKT conditions:

\[ abla f(x^\star) + \sum_i \mu_i^\star abla g_i(x^\star) + \sum_j \lambda_j^\star abla h_j(x^\star) = 0, \] \[ \mu_i^\star \ge 0,\qquad \mu_i^\star\, g_i(x^\star) = 0,\qquad g_i(x^\star) \le 0,\qquad h_j(x^\star) = 0. \]

The methods in this chapter all converge to a KKT point — the difference is how they enforce feasibility.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Add a penalty for violating the constraints and minimize the penalized function without constraints:

\[ \boxed{\;P(x, \mu) = f(x) + \frac{\mu}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{p} \bigl[\max(0,\ g_i(x))\bigr]^2 + \frac{\mu}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{q} h_j(x)^2\;} \]

with penalty parameter \(\mu > 0\). Iterate \(\mu \to \infty\): the penalised minimiser \(x_\mu\) converges to the constrained optimum \(x^\star\).

Why “exterior”. Because the iterates stay outside the feasible set (or on its boundary); the penalty pulls them back in as \(\mu\) increases.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — exterior penalty on an inequality
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = (x-2)^2\) subject to \(x \le 1\).

The unconstrained minimiser is \(x = 2\), which is infeasible (\(2 \le 1\) is false). So the constraint is active at the solution.

Penalized problem. With \(g(x) = x-1 \le 0\):

\[ P(x, \mu) = (x-2)^2 + \frac{\mu}{2}\bigl[\max(0, x-1)\bigr]^2. \]

For \(x \le 1\): \(P = (x-2)^2\), decreasing in \(x\) ⇒ best is \(x = 1\). For \(x > 1\):

\[ P = (x-2)^2 + \tfrac{\mu}{2}(x-1)^2. \]

First-order condition on \(x > 1\):

\[ \frac{dP}{dx} = 2(x-2) + \mu(x-1) = 0. \]

Solving:

\[ 2x - 4 + \mu x - \mu = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_\mu = \frac{4+\mu}{2+\mu}. \]

Check convergence: \(x_\mu \to 1\) as \(\mu \to \infty\). ✓ The constrained optimum is \(x^\star = 1\) with \(f^\star = 1\).

\(\mu\) \(x_\mu\) \(\|x_\mu - x^\star\|\) 1 1.6667 6.67·10⁻¹ 10 1.1667 1.67·10⁻¹ 10² 1.0196 1.96·10⁻² 10³ 1.0020 2.00·10⁻³ 10⁴ 1.0002 2.00·10⁻⁴

The error is \(O(1/\mu)\) — to halve the error, double \(\mu\) — which is why exterior penalties are slow near the solution and get numerically fragile at \(\mu \sim 10^{10}\).

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — exterior penalty on an equality
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) subject to \(x + 2y = 4\).

KKT (reference answer).

\[ \mathcal L = x^2 + y^2 + \lambda(x + 2y - 4),\qquad 2x = -\lambda,\qquad 2y = -2\lambda,\qquad x + 2y = 4. \]

The first two equations give \(y = 2x\); substituting into the constraint, \(x + 4x = 4\), so \(x^\star = 0.8\), \(y^\star = 1.6\), \(\lambda^\star = -1.6\), \(f^\star = 0.64 + 2.56 = 3.2\).

Penalized problem.

\[ P(x, y, \mu) = x^2 + y^2 + \frac{\mu}{2}(x + 2y - 4)^2. \]

First-order conditions.

\[ \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} = 2x + \mu(x + 2y - 4) = 0,\qquad \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2y + 2\mu(x + 2y - 4) = 0. \]

From the first equation, \(\mu(x + 2y - 4) = -2x\). Substituting into the second:

\[ 2y = -2\bigl(-2x\bigr) = 4x \;\Longrightarrow\; y = 2x. \]

With \(y = 2x\) in the first equation:

\[ 2x + \mu(5x - 4) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_\mu = \frac{4\mu}{5\mu + 2}. \]

As \(\mu \to \infty\): \(x_\mu \to 4/5 = 0.8\), \(y_\mu \to 1.6\) — recovering the KKT solution. ✓

\(\mu\) \(x_\mu\) \(y_\mu\) \(\|(x_\mu, y_\mu) - (0.8, 1.6)\|\) 1 0.571 1.143 5.11·10⁻¹ 10 0.769 1.538 7.02·10⁻² 10² 0.797 1.594 7.34·10⁻³ 10³ 0.800 1.599 7.38·10⁻⁴

Again \(O(1/\mu)\) convergence.

docs.title: Properties and pitfalls
docs.text:
Ill-conditioning

The Hessian of \(P\) at the penalised minimiser has eigenvalues that scale like \(\mu\) in directions normal to the active constraints — so as \(\mu \to \infty\), the condition number grows like \(\mu\). Simple unconstrained solvers (Newton, BFGS) will struggle to solve the inner problem accurately at large \(\mu\).

When the constraint is inactive

If the unconstrained minimiser of \(f\) already satisfies \(g_i(x) \le 0\), then for any \(\mu\) the penalised minimiser equals it. Complementary slackness automatically — no penalty is paid.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Instead of penalising violations from outside, add a term that goes to \(+\infty\) as the boundary is approached, keeping iterates strictly inside the feasible set:

\[ \boxed{\;B(x, \mu) = f(x) - \mu \sum_{i=1}^{p} \log\bigl(-g_i(x)\bigr)\;} \]

with barrier parameter \(\mu > 0\), and \(\mu \to 0^+\) as the method converges. This is the logarithmic barrier, the basis of modern interior-point methods.

Why “interior”. Because the barrier is defined only when every \(g_i(x) < 0\) strictly. The iterates stay inside the feasible set — the opposite of the penalty method.

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — logarithmic barrier on a simple inequality
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = x\) subject to \(x \ge 1\) (equivalently \(g(x) = 1 - x \le 0\)).

Unconstrained minimum would be \(x \to -\infty\); the constraint forces \(x^\star = 1\) with \(f^\star = 1\).

Barrier problem.

\[ B(x, \mu) = x - \mu \log(x - 1), \qquad x > 1. \]

First-order condition.

\[ B'(x) = 1 - \frac{\mu}{x-1} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_\mu = 1 + \mu. \]

Convergence. \(x_\mu \to 1\) as \(\mu \to 0^+\); the gap is exactly \(\mu\). ✓

Optimal barrier value.

\[ B(x_\mu, \mu) = (1 + \mu) - \mu \log \mu \;\xrightarrow{\mu \to 0^+}\; 1. \] \(\mu\) \(x_\mu\) \(\|x_\mu - x^\star\|\) 1 2.00 1.00 0.5 1.50 0.50 0.1 1.10 0.10 0.01 1.01 0.01

The duality gap between the barrier value and the true optimum is \(O(\mu)\) — so to reach tolerance \(\varepsilon\), use \(\mu \sim \varepsilon\). Contrast with the exterior penalty, which needs \(\mu \sim 1/\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Starting point and Slater's condition
docs.text:
Requirement

The barrier is well-defined only at points where \(g_i(x) < 0\) for all \(i\) — a strictly feasible point. If none exists, the barrier method cannot start.

Slater's condition

There exists a point \(x_0\) with \(g_i(x_0) < 0\) for all \(i\) and \(h_j(x_0) = 0\) for all \(j\). Slater's condition guarantees strong duality (the KKT multipliers exist and the duality gap vanishes in the limit); it is the standard assumption for interior-point methods on convex problems.

docs.title: Convergence proof sketch
docs.text:
Differentiate \(B\) at the barrier minimiser \(x_\mu\):

\[ 0 = abla B(x_\mu, \mu) = abla f(x_\mu) - \mu \sum_{i=1}^{p} rac{1}{-g_i(x_\mu)} abla g_i(x_\mu). \]

Compare with the KKT stationarity condition, \( abla f + \sum \mu_i abla g_i = 0\). This suggests identifying

\[ \mu_i(\mu) := rac{\mu}{-g_i(x_\mu)} > 0. \]

The complementary-slackness gap at the barrier minimiser is then

\[ \sum_i \mu_i(\mu)\, g_i(x_\mu) = \sum_i rac{\mu\, g_i(x_\mu)}{-g_i(x_\mu)} = -\mu\, p, \]

i.e. the total duality gap is \(p\,\mu\) — hence \(O(\mu)\). That is the mathematical content behind “take \(\mu o 0\) to reach the constrained optimum.”

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Exterior penalty methods are ill-conditioned as \(\mu \to \infty\); barrier methods need a strictly feasible start. The augmented Lagrangian (also called the method of multipliers) fixes both problems by adding a Lagrange multiplier term alongside the quadratic penalty:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathcal L_\rho(x, \lambda) = f(x) + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \lambda_j h_j(x) + \frac{\rho}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{q} h_j(x)^2\;} \]

with penalty parameter \(\rho > 0\) and multiplier estimate \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Algorithm (equality-constrained case)
docs.text:
Choose x₀, λ₀, ρ > 0, tolerance ε
repeat:
    x_{k+1} ← argmin_x  L_ρ(x, λ_k)      (unconstrained, or box)
    λ_{k+1} ← λ_k + ρ · h(x_{k+1})       (multiplier update)
until ‖h(x_{k+1})‖ < ε

docs.title: Why it works — and why it is better than pure penalty
docs.text:
Consider the augmented Lagrangian and differentiate with respect to \(x\):

\[ abla_x \mathcal L_ ho = abla f(x) + \sum_j igl[\lambda_j + ho\, h_j(x) igr] abla h_j(x). \]

Compare with the KKT condition \( abla f(x^\star) + \sum \lambda_j^\star abla h_j(x^\star) = 0\). If we set the effective multiplier to be

\[ \lambda_j^{ ext{eff}} := \lambda_j + ho\, h_j(x), \]

then stationarity of the augmented Lagrangian is exactly the KKT stationarity condition — provided \(\lambda_j^{ ext{eff}} = \lambda_j^\star\). The multiplier update \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + ho\, h(x)\) is a fixed-point iteration that drives \(\lambda o \lambda^\star\) and, simultaneously, \(h(x) o 0\).

The key advantage

Once \(\lambda = \lambda^\star\) is reached, the constrained minimiser is the exact unconstrained minimiser of \(\mathcal L_ ho\) for any fixed \( ho > 0\) — no need to drive \( ho o \infty\). This is why the augmented Lagrangian avoids the ill-conditioning of pure penalties.

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — augmented Lagrangian on a one-dimensional problem
docs.text:
Minimize \(f(x) = x^2\) subject to \(x = 3\).

Constrained optimum. \(x^\star = 3\), \(\lambda^\star = -2x^\star = -6\), \(f^\star = 9\).

Augmented Lagrangian.

\[ \mathcal L_\rho(x, \lambda) = x^2 + \lambda(x - 3) + \frac{\rho}{2}(x - 3)^2. \]

Inner minimisation. For fixed \(\lambda\):

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal L_\rho}{\partial x} = 2x + \lambda + \rho(x - 3) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = \frac{3\rho - \lambda}{2 + \rho}. \]

Multiplier update. \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rho(x - 3)\).

Iterations (\(\rho = 1\), \(\lambda_0 = 0\)):

\(k\) \(x_k\) \(\lambda_k\) \(\|x_k - 3\|\) 0 1.0000 0.0000 2.000 1 1.6667 −2.0000 1.333 2 2.1111 −3.3333 0.889 3 2.4074 −4.2222 0.593 4 2.6049 −4.8148 0.395 5 2.7366 −5.2100 0.263

Convergence analysis. With the closed form \(x_k = (3\rho - \lambda_k)/(2 + \rho)\), one verifies by algebra:

\[ \lambda_{k+1} - \lambda^\star = \frac{2}{2+\rho}\,(\lambda_k - \lambda^\star). \]

So the multiplier converges geometrically with rate \(2/(2+\rho)\) — for \(\rho = 1\), rate \(= 2/3\). With a larger \(\rho\), faster convergence but a more ill-conditioned inner problem; with a smaller \(\rho\), slower convergence but a well-conditioned inner problem. The trick is to choose \(\rho\) (or adapt it) to balance these.

docs.title: Combined equality + inequality
docs.text:
For inequalities \(g_i(x) \le 0\), add a barrier-like penalty on the positive part of the multiplier-adjusted slack:

\[ \mathcal L_\rho(x, \lambda, \mu) = f(x) + \sum_j \lambda_j h_j(x) + \frac{\rho}{2}\sum_j h_j(x)^2 + \frac{1}{2\rho} \sum_i \Bigl[\max\bigl(0,\ \mu_i + \rho\, g_i(x)\bigr)^2 - \mu_i^2\Bigr], \]

with updates

\[ \lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rho\, h(x), \qquad \mu_i \leftarrow \max\bigl(0,\ \mu_i + \rho\, g_i(x)\bigr). \]

This is the ALGENCAN / LANCELOT formulation and is what practical solvers such as Ipopt, Algencan, and MINOS build on.

docs.title: Standard form
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} & \text{minimize} && \tfrac{1}{2} x^\top Q x + c^\top x \\ & \text{subject to} && A x = b, \\ & && G x \le h. \end{aligned} \]

with \(Q = Q^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(G \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}\).

Key fact. If \(Q \succ 0\) and the feasible set is non-empty, QP is a convex problem — any KKT point is a global minimum, and solvers converge reliably.

docs.title: 3.5.1 QP with equality constraints only
docs.text:
Minimize \(\tfrac12 x^\top Q x + c^\top x\) subject to \(A x = b\).

Lagrangian.

\[ \mathcal L(x, \lambda) = \tfrac12 x^\top Q x + c^\top x + \lambda^\top(Ax - b). \]

KKT conditions (linear in \((x, \lambda)\)).

\[ Q x + c + A^\top \lambda = 0, \qquad A x = b. \]

Stack into a single linear system — the KKT matrix:

\[ \boxed{\; \begin{bmatrix} Q & A^\top \\ A & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -c \\ b \end{bmatrix} \;} \]

Existence and uniqueness.

Case Solution set \(Q \succ 0\), \(A\) full row rank Unique \((x^\star, \lambda^\star)\) \(Q \succ 0\), \(A\) rank-deficient Unique \(x^\star\); \(\lambda\) not unique \(Q\) indefinite, \(A\) full row rank Unique stationary point; not necessarily a minimum \(Q\) indefinite, problem unbounded No solution

Practical solvers

For small problems, just solve the KKT matrix directly (numpy.linalg.solve). For larger problems, exploit structure: solve the Schur complement \(A Q^{-1} A^\top \lambda = A Q^{-1} c - b\) first, then recover \(x = Q^{-1}(-c - A^\top \lambda)\). This reduces the dense system from \((n+m)\times(n+m)\) to \(m\times m\).

docs.title: Worked example 3.5 — QP with an equality constraint, solved by KKT
docs.text:
Minimize

\[ f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 + xy - 2x + y \quad \text{subject to} \quad x + y = 3. \]

Standard form. Write as \(\tfrac12 z^\top Q z + c^\top z\) with \(z = (x, y)\):

\[ Q = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix},\qquad c = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},\qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\qquad b = 3. \]

Since \(Q \succ 0\) (eigenvalues \(1, 3\)) and \(A\) has rank \(1\), the solution is unique.

KKT system.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Row reduction. Row 1 − Row 2 gives \(x - y = 3\). With Row 3 (\(x + y = 3\)), we get \(x = 3\), \(y = 0\). Then Row 1 gives \(\lambda = 2 - 2 \cdot 3 - 0 = -4\).

Verification. \(x^\star = (3, 0)\), \(\lambda^\star = -4\), \(f^\star = 9 + 0 + 0 - 6 + 0 = 3\).

Direct check by eliminating the constraint: with \(y = 3 - x\),

\[ f(x) = x^2 + (3-x)^2 + x(3-x) - 2x + (3-x) = x^2 - 6x + 12. \]

\(df/dx = 2x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 3\), \(y = 0\), \(f = 3\). ✓

docs.title: 3.5.2 QP with inequality constraints — active-set preview
docs.text:
The QP with both equalities and inequalities is handled by identifying the active set \(\mathcal W\) (indices of constraints satisfied as equalities at the solution) and solving the equality-constrained KKT system on \(\mathcal W\).

Active-set algorithm (conceptual).

Choose a feasible starting point x₀ and an initial working set W
repeat:
    solve the equality-constrained QP with Ax = b, G_W x = h_W
        -> candidate step d
    if d = 0 (current point is optimal for W):
        compute multipliers μ for constraints in W
        if all μ_i ≥ 0:  STOP (KKT satisfied)
        else:  remove the most negative μ_i from W
    else:
        take a step in direction d, stopping at the first
        constraint that becomes active; add that constraint to W
until convergence

This is the classical Wolfe / Goldfarb–Idnani algorithm used in production QP solvers (quadprog, OSQP uses a different interior-point approach).

docs.title: Worked example 3.6 — QP with an inequality, solved by inspection
docs.text:
Minimize

\[ f(x,y) = (x-2)^2 + (y-2)^2 \quad ext{subject to} \quad x + y \le 3,\ x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0. \]

Step 1 — guess the active set. The unconstrained minimiser is \((2, 2)\), but \(2 + 2 = 4 > 3\) ⇒ the inequality \(x + y \le 3\) is violated ⇒ it is active. Both non-negativity constraints hold at the solution (to be verified).

So \(\mathcal W = \{x + y \le 3\}\).

Step 2 — solve the equality-constrained QP on \(x + y = 3\). Substitute \(y = 3 - x\):

\[ f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + (1 - x)^2,\qquad rac{df}{dx} = 2(x-2) - 2(1-x) = 4x - 6 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = frac{3}{2}. \]

So \(x = 1.5\), \(y = 1.5\), \(f = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5\).

Step 3 — verify KKT multipliers.

\[ abla f(1.5, 1.5) = (2(1.5-2),\ 2(1.5-2)) = (-1, -1). \]

For the constraint \(x + y - 3 \le 0\), \( abla g = (1, 1)\). Stationarity:

\[ abla f + \mu abla g = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (-1,-1) + \mu(1,1) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \mu = 1 \ge 0. \;\checkmark \]

For \(x \ge 0\): at \(x = 1.5 > 0\) the constraint is inactive, so its multiplier is \(0\) (complementary slackness). Similarly for \(y \ge 0\). All KKT conditions hold.

Answer. \(x^\star = (1.5, 1.5)\), \(f^\star = 0.5\), \(\mu^\star_{x+y} = 1\), all other multipliers zero.

docs.title: 3.6 Computational implementation
docs.text: The examples below solve the same three problems — (i) Example 3.4's augmented Lagrangian, (ii) Example 3.5's QP with equality constraint, and (iii) Example 3.6's inequality-constrained QP — using SciPy, Java, and C#. The point is to show the same algorithm expressed three ways.

docs.title: Python with SciPy
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize, minimize_scalar

# ---- (i) augmented Lagrangian for min x^2 s.t. x = 3 --------------------
def aug_lag_demo(rho=1.0, maxiter=30, tol=1e-8):
    x, lam = 1.0, 0.0
    for k in range(maxiter):
        # inner: unconstrained in x, fixed lam and rho
        f_inner = lambda x: x**2 + lam*(x - 3) + 0.5*rho*(x - 3)**2
        x = minimize_scalar(f_inner, bounds=(-50, 50), method='bounded').x
        gap = abs(x - 3)
        print(f"k={k:2d}  x={x:.6f}  λ={lam:+.6f}  |x-3|={gap:.2e}")
        if gap < tol:
            break
        lam += rho * (x - 3)

print("=== augmented Lagrangian ===")
aug_lag_demo()

# ---- (ii) QP with equality, KKT linear system --------------------------
Q = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 2.]])
c = np.array([-2., 1.])
A = np.array([[1., 1.]])
b = np.array([3.])

n, m = Q.shape[0], A.shape[0]
KKT = np.block([[Q, A.T], [A, np.zeros((m, m))]])
rhs = np.concatenate([-c, b])
sol = np.linalg.solve(KKT, rhs)
xstar, lamstar = sol[:n], sol[n:]
print("\n=== QP with equality (KKT) ===")
print("x* =", xstar, "  λ* =", lamstar,
      "  f* =", 0.5*xstar@Q@xstar + c@xstar)

# ---- (iii) QP with inequality — scipy SLSQP -----------------------------
def f_qp(z):
    return (z[0]-2)**2 + (z[1]-2)**2
def df_qp(z):
    return np.array([2*(z[0]-2), 2*(z[1]-2)])

cons = [
    {'type': 'ineq', 'fun': lambda z: 3 - z[0] - z[1],
                     'jac': lambda z: np.array([-1., -1.])},
    {'type': 'ineq', 'fun': lambda z: z[0], 'jac': lambda z: np.array([1., 0.])},
    {'type': 'ineq', 'fun': lambda z: z[1], 'jac': lambda z: np.array([0., 1.])},
]
r = minimize(f_qp, x0=np.array([0.1, 0.1]), jac=df_qp,
             constraints=cons, method='SLSQP', options={'ftol': 1e-12})
print("\n=== QP with inequality (SLSQP) ===")
print("x* =", r.x, "  f* =", r.fun)

# ---- (iv) exterior penalty, educational --------------------------------
print("\n=== exterior penalty on min (x-2)^2 s.t. x <= 1 ===")
for mu in [1., 10., 100., 1000.]:
    P = lambda x: (x-2)**2 + 0.5*mu*max(0, x-1)**2
    x = minimize_scalar(P, bounds=(-5, 5), method='bounded').x
    print(f"μ={mu:6.0f}  x*={x:.6f}  exact={(4+mu)/(2+mu):.6f}")

Expected output (abridged).

=== augmented Lagrangian ===
k= 0  x=1.000000  λ=+0.000000  |x-3|=2.00e+00
k= 1  x=1.666667  λ=-2.000000  |x-3|=1.33e+00
...
k=12  x=2.999323  λ=-5.998645  |x-3|=6.77e-04
=== QP with equality (KKT) ===
x* = [3. 0.]   λ* = [-4.]   f* = 3.0
=== QP with inequality (SLSQP) ===
x* = [1.5 1.5]   f* = 0.5

docs.title: Java — augmented Lagrangian
docs.text:
public class AugmentedLagrangian {

    // min  f(x) = x^2  s.t.  h(x) = x - 3 = 0
    static double innerMin(double lambda, double rho) {
        // d/dx [ x² + λ(x-3) + (ρ/2)(x-3)² ] = 0
        //  2x + λ + ρ(x-3) = 0  =>  x = (3ρ - λ)/(2+ρ)
        return (3*rho - lambda) / (2 + rho);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double rho = 1.0, lam = 0.0, tol = 1e-8;
        for (int k = 0; k < 50; k++) {
            double x = innerMin(lam, rho);
            double gap = Math.abs(x - 3);
            System.out.printf("k=%2d  x=%.8f  λ=%+.6f  |x-3|=%.2e%n",
                              k, x, lam, gap);
            if (gap < tol) break;
            lam += rho * (x - 3);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: C# — exterior penalty + QP by KKT
docs.text:
using System;

class ConstrainedOptimization
{
    // ---- (i) exterior penalty for min (x-2)^2 s.t. x <= 1 --------
    static double PenaltyMin(double mu) {
        // P(x) = (x-2)² + (μ/2) max(0, x-1)²
        // For x > 1: x = (4+μ)/(2+μ); for x ≤ 1: x = 1.
        double x = (4 + mu) / (2 + mu);
        return x > 1 ? x : 1.0;
    }

    // ---- (ii) QP with equality: solve KKT by Gaussian elimination ----
    static (double[] x, double[] lam) SolveQP(double[,] Q, double[] c,
                                              double[,] A, double[] b)
    {
        int n = Q.GetLength(0), m = A.GetLength(0);
        int N = n + m;
        var M = new double[N, N + 1];

        // top-left Q, top-right Aᵀ
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) M[i, j] = Q[i, j];
            for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) M[i, n + j] = A[j, i];
            M[i, N] = -c[i];
        }
        // bottom-left A, bottom-right 0
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) M[n + i, j] = A[i, j];
            for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) M[n + i, n + j] = 0.0;
            M[n + i, N] = b[i];
        }

        // Gauss-Jordan elimination
        for (int col = 0; col < N; col++) {
            int piv = col;
            for (int r = col + 1; r < N; r++)
                if (Math.Abs(M[r, col]) > Math.Abs(M[piv, col])) piv = r;
            for (int j = col; j <= N; j++)
                (M[col, j], M[piv, j]) = (M[piv, j], M[col, j]);

            double d = M[col, col];
            for (int j = col; j <= N; j++) M[col, j] /= d;
            for (int r = 0; r < N; r++) {
                if (r == col) continue;
                double factor = M[r, col];
                for (int j = col; j <= N; j++) M[r, j] -= factor * M[col, j];
            }
        }

        var sol = new double[N];
        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sol[i] = M[i, N];
        var x = new double[n]; var lam = new double[m];
        Array.Copy(sol, 0, x, 0, n);
        Array.Copy(sol, n, lam, 0, m);
        return (x, lam);
    }

    static void Main() {
        Console.WriteLine("=== exterior penalty ===");
        foreach (double mu in new[]{1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0})
            Console.WriteLine($"μ={mu,6:F0}  x*={PenaltyMin(mu):F6}  " +
                              $"exact={(4+mu)/(2+mu):F6}");

        Console.WriteLine("\n=== QP with equality ===");
        double[,] Q = { {2, 1}, {1, 2} };
        double[]  c = { -2, 1 };
        double[,] A = { {1, 1} };
        double[]  b = { 3 };
        var (x, lam) = SolveQP(Q, c, A, b);
        Console.WriteLine($"x* = ({x[0]:F4}, {x[1]:F4}),  λ* = {lam[0]:F4}");
    }
}

Production solvers you can use directly

  • Python: scipy.optimize.minimize ('SLSQP', 'trust-constr'), scipy.optimize.quadprog-compatible quadprog, cvxpy for modeling.
  • Java: Apache Commons Math QuadraticMultivariateFunction + QuadraticOptimizer; Hipparchus; ojalgo (ConvexSolver).
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics has BFGS but no native QP; use Cplex/Gurobi via their .NET APIs, or Google OR-Tools (Google.OrTools.LinearSolver) for LPs and QPs.
  • MATLAB / Julia: quadprog, fmincon, JuMP + Gurobi / OSQP.

docs.title: 3.7 Summary — choosing between methods
docs.text:
Method Needs feasible start? Sub-problem per iteration Convergence Best for Exterior penalty No (infeasible ok) Unconstrained \(O(1/\mu)\) Simple problems, teaching Barrier (interior point) Yes (strictly feasible) Unconstrained + barrier \(O(\mu)\) Large convex problems Augmented Lagrangian No Unconstrained Superlinear in \(\lambda\) Equality & mixed, production QP with equality Any Linear solve (KKT) Exact (one step) QP with only equalities QP active-set Any Equality-constrained QP Finite QP with inequalities

Rule of thumb.

  • If the problem is a QP with only equality constraints, solve the KKT linear system once.
  • If it is a general smooth nonlinear problem, use an augmented Lagrangian (equalities) or a logarithmic barrier (inequalities, convex case) — avoid plain quadratic penalties in production.
  • If it is a QP with inequalities, use an active-set or interior-point QP solver, not a penalty loop.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. Which method requires a strictly feasible starting point? (a) exterior penalty (b) logarithmic barrier (c) augmented Lagrangian (d) QP active-set

  2. In the exterior penalty method, the parameter \(\mu\) should tend to: (a) \(0^+\) (b) \(1\) (c) \(+\infty\) (d) any value

  3. In the logarithmic barrier method, the parameter \(\mu\) should tend to: (a) \(0^+\) (b) \(1\) (c) \(+\infty\) (d) any value

  4. The main purpose of the augmented Lagrangian is to avoid: (a) KKT conditions (b) ill-conditioning of the pure penalty method (c) complementarity (d) QP structure

  5. The KKT system for a QP with \(n\) variables and \(m\) equality constraints has dimension: (a) \(n \times n\) (b) \(m \times m\) (c) \((n+m) \times (n+m)\) (d) \(2n \times 2n\)

  6. For a QP \(\min \tfrac12 x^\top Q x + c^\top x\) s.t. \(Ax = b\), a unique solution exists iff: (a) \(A\) is square (b) \(Q \succ 0\) and \(A\) has full row rank (c) \(Q\) is positive semi-definite (d) \(Q = I\)

  7. In the exterior penalty method with finite \(\mu\), the constraint \(g_i(x) \le 0\) is: (a) exactly satisfied (b) approximately satisfied, with error \(O(1/\mu)\) (c) always violated (d) ignored

  8. In the augmented Lagrangian \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,\lambda) = f(x) + \lambda h(x) + \tfrac{\rho}{2}h(x)^2\), the update \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rho\,h(x)\) drives the pair \((x, \lambda)\) toward: (a) the unconstrained minimum of \(f\) (b) a KKT point of the constrained problem (c) the starting point (d) infinity

  9. The barrier term \(-\mu \log(-g_i(x))\) is defined only when: (a) \(g_i(x) \ge 0\) (b) \(g_i(x) < 0\) strictly (c) \(g_i(x) = 0\) (d) no condition

  10. Which is not a property of the exterior penalty method? (a) iterates may be infeasible (b) ill-conditioned as \(\mu \to \infty\) (c) requires strictly feasible start (d) converges from outside the feasible set

  11. In the active-set method for QP, an active constraint at the solution has a KKT multiplier satisfying: (a) \(\mu_i = 0\) (b) \(\mu_i \ge 0\) (c) \(\mu_i \le 0\) (d) any sign

  12. Slater's condition for the log-barrier method on a convex problem asserts that: (a) all constraints are equalities (b) there exists \(x_0\) with \(g_i(x_0) < 0\) for all \(i\) (c) the objective is linear (d) \(Q \succ 0\)

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. Exterior penalty: \(P(x,\mu) = f(x) + \tfrac{\mu}{2}\sum_i [\max(0,\ \_\_\_\_)]^2\).
  2. Barrier: \(B(x,\mu) = f(x) - \mu \sum_i \log(\_\_\_\_)\).
  3. Augmented Lagrangian (equality): \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,\lambda) = f(x) + \lambda^\top h(x) + \_\_\_\_\,\|h(x)\|^2\).
  4. Augmented-Lagrangian multiplier update: \(\lambda_{k+1} = \lambda_k + \rho\,\_\_\_\_\).
  5. As \(\mu \to\) ___, the exterior penalty minimiser converges to the constrained optimum.
  6. As \(\mu \to\) ___, the barrier minimiser converges to the constrained optimum.
  7. The QP KKT block matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} Q & A^\top \\ A & \_\_\_\_\end{bmatrix}\).
  8. The barrier method needs a ____ starting point.
  9. The exterior penalty method allows ____ iterates.
  10. The augmented Lagrangian avoids the ____ of pure penalty methods.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Compare exterior penalty and log-barrier methods in three respects: starting-point requirement, side of the boundary the iterates live on, and asymptotic error as the parameter is driven to its limit.
  2. Explain the ill-conditioning of the exterior penalty method and how the augmented Lagrangian overcomes it. Include the effective-multiplier identity \(\lambda^{\text{eff}} = \lambda + \rho\,h(x)\).
  3. Derive the KKT linear system for a QP with equality constraints. State the existence/uniqueness condition and sketch the Schur-complement reduction.
  4. Describe the augmented-Lagrangian iteration on the equality-constrained problem. Explain, in one sentence, why the multiplier update \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rho\,h(x)\) is a fixed-point iteration toward the correct KKT multiplier.
  5. State Slater's condition and explain why it is the standard assumption for interior-point methods. What can go wrong if it fails?
  6. Describe the active-set method for QP with inequalities. In what sense does it generalise the pure equality-constrained QP of §3.5.1?

docs.title: 3.9 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — the log barrier is defined only where \(g_i(x) < 0\) strictly.
  2. (c) — exterior penalty: \(\mu \to \infty\).
  3. (a) — barrier: \(\mu \to 0^+\).
  4. (b) — AL removes the need for \(\mu \to \infty\).
  5. (c) — \(n + m\).
  6. (b) — \(Q \succ 0\) and \(A\) full row rank.
  7. (b) — penalty error is \(O(1/\mu)\), not zero for finite \(\mu\).
  8. (b) — fixed point of the iteration is the KKT pair.
  9. (b) — strictly negative \(g_i(x)\) inside the barrier.
  10. (c) — that is a property of the barrier, not the penalty.
  11. (b) — active inequalities have \(\mu_i \ge 0\) at a minimum.
  12. (b) — strict feasibility is exactly Slater's condition for inequality-only problems.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(g_i(x)\)
  2. \(-g_i(x)\)
  3. \(\tfrac{\rho}{2}\)
  4. \(h(x_k)\)
  5. \(+\infty\)
  6. \(0^+\)
  7. \(0\)
  8. strictly feasible (interior)
  9. infeasible
  10. ill-conditioning
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Starting point. Barrier needs a strictly feasible \(x_0\); penalty does not. Side of the boundary. Penalty iterates stay outside or on the boundary; barrier iterates stay strictly inside. Asymptotic error. Penalty error is \(O(1/\mu)\) as \(\mu \to \infty\); barrier error is \(O(\mu)\) as \(\mu \to 0^+\). Consequently the barrier reaches a given tolerance with a much smaller parameter excursion — one reason interior-point methods displaced penalty methods in the 1990s.
  2. The Hessian of the quadratic penalty has eigenvalues that scale like \(\mu\) in constraint-normal directions, so its condition number grows like \(\mu\) as \(\mu \to \infty\); simple solvers then fail to solve the inner unconstrained problem accurately. The augmented Lagrangian adds a Lagrange-multiplier term \(\lambda^\top h(x)\) so that at stationarity \(\nabla f + (\lambda + \rho\,h(x))^\top \nabla h = 0\). If \(\lambda\) is updated to equal the correct KKT multiplier \(\lambda^\star\), the minimiser of \(\mathcal L_\rho\) is exactly the constrained optimum for any fixed \(\rho\) — hence no need to drive \(\rho \to \infty\), hence no ill-conditioning. The identity \(\lambda^{\text{eff}} = \lambda + \rho\,h(x)\) is what makes stationarity of \(\mathcal L_\rho\) coincide with KKT stationarity once \(\lambda = \lambda^\star\).
  3. Lagrangian \(\mathcal L = \tfrac12 x^\top Qx + c^\top x + \lambda^\top(Ax-b)\). Gradient in \(x\): \(Qx + c + A^\top\lambda = 0\). Gradient in \(\lambda\): \(Ax - b = 0\). Stack into \(\begin{bmatrix}Q & A^\top \\ A & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\\lambda\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-c\\b\end{bmatrix}\). Unique solution iff \(Q \succ 0\) and \(A\) has full row rank. Schur complement: eliminate \(x\) via \(x = Q^{-1}(-c - A^\top\lambda)\), substitute into \(Ax = b\): \(A Q^{-1}(A^\top\lambda + c) = -b\), so \(\lambda\) is obtained from an \(m\times m\) linear system, then \(x\) is recovered.
  4. Choose \(x_0, \lambda_0, \rho\). Inner step: \(x_{k+1} = \arg\min_x \mathcal L_\rho(x, \lambda_k)\). Multiplier update: \(\lambda_{k+1} = \lambda_k + \rho\,h(x_{k+1})\). At the fixed point, \(h(x^\star) = 0\) (feasibility) and stationarity of \(\mathcal L_\rho\) gives the KKT stationarity condition with multiplier \(\lambda^\star\) — so the iteration converges exactly to the constrained KKT pair. The multiplier update is a gradient ascent on the dual function (equivalently, a fixed-point iteration driven by the primal residual \(h(x_k)\)).
  5. Slater's condition asserts existence of a strictly feasible point \(x_0\) with \(g_i(x_0) < 0\) for all \(i\) (and \(h_j(x_0) = 0\) for all equalities). It guarantees that the KKT multipliers exist and the duality gap vanishes in the limit of the interior-point method, so the barrier path converges to the true constrained optimum. If Slater's condition fails (no strictly feasible point), the barrier is undefined — no \(x_0\) exists from which to start — and the duality gap may not converge to zero.
  6. The active-set method solves a sequence of equality-constrained QPs, one per working set \(\mathcal W\) of constraints. At each step it either (i) drops a constraint whose multiplier is negative (leaving the set), or (ii) adds a constraint that is violated on the current step (entering the set). When a step finds \(d = 0\) with all \(\mu_i \ge 0\) for \(i \in \mathcal W\), KKT is satisfied and the algorithm terminates. It generalises §3.5.1 by turning inequality constraints into equalities only when they matter, solving the KKT system of §3.5.1 on the reduced set — hence “active-set”.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Penalty iteration by hand. Minimize \(f(x) = (x-3)^2\) subject to \(x \ge 2\), using the exterior penalty with \(\mu \in \{1, 10, 10^2, 10^3\}\). Tabulate \(x_\mu\) and confirm \(x_\mu \to 2\) as \(\mu \to \infty\). Compare with the barrier \(B(x, \mu) = (x-3)^2 - \mu\log(x-2)\) and note the sign and rate of convergence.
  2. Barrier starting point. Solve \(\min\, x_1 + x_2\) subject to \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 \le 1\) using the log barrier. Find a strictly feasible starting point. What happens at \(\mu = 1\), \(\mu = 0.1\), \(\mu = 0.01\)?
  3. Augmented Lagrangian with both signs. Minimize \(f(x) = x^2 - 2x\) subject to \(x = 1\). Take \(\rho = 1\), \(\lambda_0 = 0\) and iterate; compute the analytic convergence rate from the formula \((\lambda_{k+1} - \lambda^\star) = \frac{2}{2+\rho}(\lambda_k - \lambda^\star)\).
  4. Mixed constraints. Minimize \(x^2 + y^2\) subject to \(x + y = 2\) and \(x \le 0.5\). Write the augmented Lagrangian (equality + inequality penalty), set up the KKT system by hand, and verify that the inequality is active with multiplier \(\mu \ge 0\).
  5. QP with three equalities. Min \(\tfrac12 x^\top Q x + c^\top x\) subject to \(A x = b\) with \(Q = I_4\), \(c = (1, -2, 3, -4)\), and \(A x = b\) given by \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\), \(x_3 + x_4 = 0\), \(x_1 - x_3 = 1\). Solve via the KKT matrix and confirm the optimum satisfies the KKT conditions.
  6. Active-set exercise. Solve by hand the QP \(\min\ (x_1-1)^2 + (x_2-2)^2\) subject to \(x_1 + 2x_2 \le 2\), \(x_1, x_2 \ge 0\). Enumerate the active-set possibilities and show that the optimum lies on \(x_1 + 2x_2 = 2\) with \(x_2 = 0\).
  7. Solver cross-check. For any of the above, solve numerically in Python (scipy.optimize.minimize(method='SLSQP')) and confirm that the KKT multipliers reported by method='trust-constr' match your hand-derived values.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Stochastic Processes, Random Walks, and Applications
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): general concepts · definitions and correlations · random walks · Poisson points and shot noise · modulation and cyclostationary processes · band-limited processes and sampling theory · deterministic signal in noise · entropy.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define a random (stochastic) process, a realization, and the ensemble; distinguish strict-sense and wide-sense stationarity.
  2. Compute mean, variance, autocovariance, autocorrelation, and cross-correlation functions of simple processes.
  3. Analyze random walks: mean, variance, return probabilities, and the Brownian-motion limit.
  4. Model Poisson point processes and compute the mean and variance of shot noise via Campbell's theorem.
  5. Recognize a cyclostationary process, compute its time-averaged autocorrelation, and identify when modulation destroys cyclostationarity.
  6. State the sampling theorem for random processes and reconstruct a band-limited process from its Nyquist-rate samples.
  7. Compute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a deterministic signal in white Gaussian noise; derive the matched filter.
  8. Compute the Shannon entropy of a discrete source and the differential entropy of a Gaussian source.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Random process
docs.text:
A random (stochastic) process is a family of random variables \(\{X(t) : t \in \mathcal{T}\}\) indexed by a parameter set \(\mathcal T\) (usually time: \(\mathcal T = \mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb R_+\)). For each fixed \(t\), \(X(t)\) is a random variable. For each fixed outcome \(\omega\) in the underlying probability space, \(t \mapsto X(t, \omega)\) is a realization or sample function of the process. The collection of realizations is the ensemble.

Discrete-time processes index by \(\mathcal T = \mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Z_+\) (written \(X[n]\)), continuous-time by \(\mathcal T = \mathbb R\) (written \(X(t)\)).

docs.title: 4.1.2 Moments
docs.text:
For a real-valued process, the mean function and autocorrelation are

\[ \mu_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[X(t)],\qquad R_X(t_1, t_2) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[X(t_1) X(t_2)\bigr]. \]

The autocovariance is

\[ C_X(t_1, t_2) = R_X(t_1, t_2) - \mu_X(t_1)\mu_X(t_2). \]

The variance is \(C_X(t, t) = \operatorname{Var}[X(t)]\).

For two processes \(X\) and \(Y\), the cross-correlation is

\[ R_{XY}(t_1, t_2) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[X(t_1) Y(t_2)\bigr]. \]

docs.title: 4.1.3 Stationarity
docs.text:
Strict-sense stationary (SSS)

\(X(t)\) is strictly stationary if, for any \(n\), any \(t_1,\dots,t_n\), and any shift \(\Delta\), the joint distribution of \((X(t_1),\dots,X(t_n))\) equals that of \((X(t_1+\Delta),\dots,X(t_n+\Delta))\). Equivalently, all finite-dimensional distributions are shift-invariant.

Wide-sense stationary (WSS)

\(X(t)\) is wide-sense stationary if it has finite second moments and:

  1. \(\mu_X(t) = \mu_X\) (constant),
  2. \(R_X(t_1, t_2) = R_X(t_1 - t_2)\) — the autocorrelation depends only on \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\).

Writing \(R_X(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[X(t+\tau)X(t)]\), WSS gives the properties \(R_X(0) = \operatorname{Var}[X] + \mu_X^2 \ge 0\), \(R_X(-\tau) = R_X(\tau)\), and \(|R_X(\tau)| \le R_X(0)\).

SSS implies WSS (when second moments exist), but not conversely. WSS is the working assumption in most of signal processing.

docs.title: 4.1.4 Ergodicity (preview)
docs.text:
A WSS process is ergodic in the mean if the time average of one realization converges to the ensemble mean:

\[ \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T X(t, \omega)\, dt = \mu_X \quad \text{for almost every } \omega. \]

Ergodicity is what allows estimating ensemble statistics from a single long observation — the basis of all practical spectrum estimation (Chapter 5).

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — a sinusoid with random phase
docs.text:
Let \(X(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t + \Theta)\), with amplitude \(A > 0\) fixed, angular frequency \(\omega_0\) fixed, and phase \(\Theta \sim U[0, 2\pi)\).

Mean.

\[ \mathbb{E}[X(t)] = A\,\mathbb{E}[\cos(\omega_0 t + \Theta)] = \frac{A}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \cos(\omega_0 t + \theta)\, d\theta = 0. \]

Autocorrelation. Let \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\). Then

\[ R_X(t_1, t_2) = A^2\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\cos(\omega_0 t_1 + \Theta)\cos(\omega_0 t_2 + \Theta)\bigr]. \]

Using \(\cos\alpha\cos\beta = \tfrac12[\cos(\alpha-\beta) + \cos(\alpha+\beta)]\):

\[ R_X(t_1, t_2) = \tfrac{A^2}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\cos(\omega_0(t_1-t_2)) + \cos(\omega_0(t_1+t_2)+2\Theta)\bigr]. \]

The first term is deterministic; the second averages to zero over \(\Theta\) uniform on \([0,2\pi)\). Therefore

\[ R_X(\tau) = \frac{A^2}{2}\cos(\omega_0\tau). \]

This depends only on \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\); with mean \(0\) constant, \(X(t)\) is WSS. Its variance is \(R_X(0) - \mu_X^2 = A^2/2\).

The average power is \(A^2/2\) — half of what a deterministic \(\cos\) with amplitude \(A\) would carry, because the phase is uncertain.

Physical interpretation

\(R_X(0) = A^2/2\) is the average power. The oscillation of \(R_X(\tau)\) at frequency \(\omega_0\) is the signature of the sinusoid; the FFT of \(R_X\) is a pair of delta functions at \(\pm f_0\) — a pure line spectrum.

docs.title: 4.2.1 The simple symmetric random walk
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent, identically distributed, taking values \(\pm 1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each. Define

\[ S_0 = 0,\qquad S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} X_k. \]

\(S_n\) is the position after \(n\) steps of a simple symmetric random walk on \(\mathbb Z\).

Mean and variance.

\[ \mathbb{E}[S_n] = \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_k] = 0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}[S_n] = \sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{Var}[X_k] = n. \]

So the walk spreads out as \(\sqrt n\) — the classic diffusion scaling.

Position probabilities. \(S_n\) is even/odd according to \(n\); its distribution is

\[ \Pr\{S_n = k\} = \binom{n}{(n+k)/2}\, 2^{-n} \quad \text{for } k \equiv n \pmod{2}. \]

In particular, at even time \(2n\), \(\Pr\{S_{2n} = 0\} = \binom{2n}{n}\,2^{-2n}\). By Stirling's formula \(\binom{2n}{n} \sim 4^n / \sqrt{\pi n}\), so

\[ \Pr\{S_{2n} = 0\} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi n}} \to 0. \]

The walk will return to zero almost surely (Pólya's recurrence theorem in \(\mathbb Z\) and \(\mathbb Z^2\)), but the expected return time is infinite.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Diffusion limit — Brownian motion
docs.text:
Rescale time and space: let \(W_n(t) = S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor}/\sqrt{n}\). Then by the central limit theorem and the Donsker invariance principle, \(W_n \Rightarrow W\), where \(W(t)\) is standard Brownian motion:

  • \(W(0) = 0\) almost surely;
  • increments \(W(t) - W(s) \sim N(0, t-s)\) for \(t > s\);
  • increments over disjoint intervals are independent;
  • paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable almost surely.

Brownian motion is WSS only in the increment sense; it is not stationary (its variance grows with \(t\)). Its autocovariance is \(\mathbb{E}[W(s)W(t)] = \min(s,t)\).

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — first return and the ballot theorem
docs.text:
Starting at \(0\), what is the probability that the walk returns to \(0\) for the first time at step \(2n\)? A classical result (the ballot theorem, equivalent to the reflection principle) gives

\[ \Pr\{\text{first return at step }2n\} = \frac{1}{2n - 1}\,\binom{2n}{n}\,2^{-2n}. \]

For \(n = 1\): probability \(\tfrac{1}{1}\binom{2}{1}/4 = 1/2\) — either \(+1,-1\) or \(-1,+1\), both return at step \(2\). For \(n = 2\): probability \(\tfrac13\binom{4}{2}/16 = \tfrac{6}{48} = 1/8\) — the sequences \(+ + - -\) and \(- - + +\) do not return first at step \(4\), only \(+ - - +\) and \(- + + -\) do.

The sum over \(n\) equals \(1\) (recurrence), but with \(\sum n \cdot \Pr = \infty\) — the walk returns almost surely, but not in finite expected time.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Variations
docs.text: Walk Step distribution Variance Limiting behaviour Simple symmetric \(\pm 1\), \(p = \tfrac12\) \(n\) Recurrent in \(d \le 2\), transient in \(d \ge 3\) Biased \(\pm 1\), \(p \ne \tfrac12\) \(4p(1-p)n\) Transient, drifts at speed \(2p - 1\) Continuous \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) \(\sigma^2 n\) Brownian motion with variance \(\sigma^2 t\) Random-walk on graph Transition matrix \(P\) — Stationary distribution \(\pi\)

docs.title: 4.3.1 The Poisson process
docs.text:
The Poisson counting process \(\{N(t)\}_{t \ge 0}\) with rate \(\lambda > 0\) is the counting process satisfying:

  1. \(N(0) = 0\);
  2. For \(s < t\), \(N(t) - N(s) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t - s))\);
  3. Increments over disjoint intervals are independent.

Hence

\[ \Pr\{N(t) = k\} = \frac{(\lambda t)^k\, e^{-\lambda t}}{k!},\quad \mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \operatorname{Var}[N(t)] = \lambda t. \]

The arrival times \(T_1 < T_2 < \cdots\) have i.i.d. interarrival times \(T_{k+1} - T_k \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\), with mean \(1/\lambda\) and variance \(1/\lambda^2\).

docs.title: 4.3.2 Shot noise — Campbell's theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\{t_i\}\) be the arrival times of a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\), and let \(h(t)\) be a response function (impulse response of a linear system, or the shape of one pulse). Define the shot-noise process

\[ X(t) = \sum_{i : t_i \le t} h(t - t_i). \]

This models: photodetector current, queueing arrivals through a server, neural spike trains filtered by a synapse, and many communication interference models.

Campbell's theorem

For a Poisson-driven shot-noise process,

\[ \mathbb{E}[X(t)] = \lambda \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(s)\, ds, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[X(t)] = \lambda \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(s)^2\, ds, \]

provided both integrals are finite. The process is WSS, and its autocorrelation is

\[ R_X(\tau) = \lambda \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(s)\, h(s + \tau)\, ds + \lambda^2 \Bigl(\int h(s)\, ds\Bigr)^{\!2}. \]

Proof sketch (mean). Condition on the number of arrivals:

\[ \mathbb{E}[X(t)] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr\{N(t)=k\}\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^k h(t - t_i) \Bigm| N(t)=k\Bigr]. \]

Conditional on \(N(t) = k\), the arrival times are distributed as \(k\) i.i.d. uniform variables on \([0,t]\) (the order statistics of uniform samples). So each \(\mathbb{E}[h(t - t_i) \mid N(t)=k] = \tfrac1t\int_0^t h(t - s)\, ds\). Then

\[ \mathbb{E}[X(t)] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr\{N(t)=k\}\, k \cdot \tfrac{1}{t}\int_0^t h(t-s)\, ds = \mathbb{E}[N(t)] \cdot \tfrac{1}{t}\int_0^t h(t-s)\, ds = \lambda \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(s)\, ds. \]

The variance follows similarly by computing the second moment \(\mathbb{E}[X(t)^2]\) and subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[X]^2\); the cross-terms between distinct arrivals vanish in expectation because they are independent.

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — shot noise with an exponential pulse
docs.text:
Let \(h(s) = e^{-s/\tau_0}\,u(s)\), where \(u(s)\) is the unit step, so each arrival triggers a decaying exponential pulse of time constant \(\tau_0\). Arrival rate \(\lambda\).

Mean.

\[ \mathbb{E}[X] = \lambda \int_0^\infty e^{-s/\tau_0}\, ds = \lambda \tau_0. \]

Variance.

\[ \operatorname{Var}[X] = \lambda \int_0^\infty e^{-2s/\tau_0}\, ds = \frac{\lambda \tau_0}{2}. \]

Autocorrelation.

\[ R_X(\tau) = \lambda \int_0^\infty e^{-s/\tau_0} e^{-(s+\tau)/\tau_0}\, ds + (\lambda \tau_0)^2. \]

For \(\tau \ge 0\), the first term is \(\lambda\, e^{-\tau/\tau_0} \int_0^\infty e^{-2s/\tau_0} ds = \tfrac{\lambda\tau_0}{2}\, e^{-\tau/\tau_0}\), so

\[ R_X(\tau) = \tfrac{\lambda\tau_0}{2}\, e^{-|\tau|/\tau_0} + (\lambda\tau_0)^2. \]

Since \(R_X(-\tau) = R_X(\tau)\), the process is WSS with variance \(\lambda\tau_0/2\) and correlation time \(\tau_0\).

\(\lambda\) \(\tau_0\) Mean Variance 10 1 10 5 100 1 100 50 10 10 100 50

The coefficient of variation is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}/\text{Mean} = 1/\sqrt{2\lambda\tau_0}\) — the shot noise is more "regular" (lower relative fluctuation) when \(\lambda\tau_0 \gg 1\) (many overlapping pulses).

docs.title: 4.3.3 Thinning and superposition
docs.text:
Two operations that preserve the Poisson structure:

  • Superposition. The sum of independent Poisson processes of rates \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) is Poisson with rate \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2\).
  • Thinning. Each arrival of a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\) is kept independently with probability \(p\); the retained arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(p\lambda\).

This is why Poisson models are natural in networking (packets arrive from many independent sources) and optics (photon arrivals from a coherent source).

docs.title: 4.4.1 Definition
docs.text:
A process \(X(t)\) is cyclostationary (or periodically correlated) with period \(T > 0\) if its mean \(\mu_X(t)\) and autocorrelation \(R_X(t_1, t_2)\) are periodic in \(t_1\) (and \(t_2\)) with period \(T\):

\[ \mu_X(t + T) = \mu_X(t),\qquad R_X(t + T + \tau,\ t + T) = R_X(t + \tau,\ t). \]

The time-averaged autocorrelation is

\[ \bar R_X(\tau) = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T R_X(t + \tau, t)\, dt. \]

If \(\bar R_X(\tau) = R_X(\tau)\) — that is, if \(R_X\) is independent of \(t\) — the process is WSS.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Binary PAM as a canonical example
docs.text:
Let

\[ X(t) = \sum_{k = -\infty}^{\infty} a_k\, p(t - kT), \]

where \(a_k\) are i.i.d. random symbols with \(\mathbb{E}[a_k] = 0\), \(\operatorname{Var}[a_k] = \sigma_a^2\), and \(p(t)\) is a deterministic pulse shape.

Autocorrelation.

\[ R_X(t+\tau, t) = \sum_{k,m} \mathbb{E}[a_k a_m]\, p(t + \tau - kT)\, p(t - mT). \]

Since \(\mathbb{E}[a_k a_m] = \sigma_a^2 \delta_{km}\), only \(k = m\) survives:

\[ R_X(t+\tau, t) = \sigma_a^2 \sum_k p(t + \tau - kT)\, p(t - kT). \]

This is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T\) (the impulse train \(\sum_k p(\cdot - kT)\) repeats every \(T\)). So \(X(t)\) is cyclostationary with period \(T\), but not WSS in general.

Time-averaged autocorrelation.

\[ \bar R_X(\tau) = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\int_0^T \sum_k p(t + \tau - kT)\, p(t - kT)\, dt = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(s + \tau)\, p(s)\, ds, \]

where the last step merges the sum over \(k\) into one integral over \(\mathbb R\) (the shifted copies tile the line).

The binary PAM process is WSS iff \(p\) has no self-overlap with shifts that break the period-\(T\) symmetry — most practically, whenever the pulse shape leads to \(\bar R_X(\tau) = R_X(\tau)\) after averaging over symbol timing. In practice, if the receiver's clock is unknown, it must estimate \(\bar R_X(\tau)\) — the cyclic autocorrelation at nonzero cycle frequencies is the signature of the symbol rate.

docs.title: Worked example 4.4 — AM modulation: cyclostationary vs. WSS
docs.text:
Let \(Y(t) = X(t)\cos(\omega_c t + \phi)\), with \(X\) WSS and \(\phi\) a deterministic phase.

Compute \(R_Y(t+\tau, t) = \mathbb{E}[X(t+\tau)X(t)]\cos(\omega_c(t+\tau)+\phi)\cos(\omega_c t + \phi)\).

Using \(\cos\alpha\cos\beta = \tfrac12[\cos(\alpha-\beta)+\cos(\alpha+\beta)]\):

\[ R_Y(t+\tau, t) = \tfrac12 R_X(\tau)\bigl[\cos(\omega_c\tau) + \cos(2\omega_c t + \omega_c\tau + 2\phi)\bigr]. \]

The second bracket is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T_0/2 = \pi/\omega_c\). So \(Y(t)\) is cyclostationary with period \(T_0/2\).

Time average.

\[ \bar R_Y(\tau) = \tfrac12 R_X(\tau)\cos(\omega_c\tau). \]

Now randomize the phase. Let \(\phi \sim U[0, 2\pi)\) independent of \(X\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[\cos(2\omega_c t + \omega_c\tau + 2\phi)] = 0\), so

\[ R_Y(t+\tau, t) = \tfrac12 R_X(\tau)\cos(\omega_c\tau), \]

which depends only on \(\tau\) ⇒ WSS.

Engineering punchline

Randomizing the carrier phase destroys the cyclostationarity and produces a WSS process. This is why synchronisation (carrier recovery) is essential in coherent receivers: without knowing \(\phi\), the process is WSS; with \(\phi\) known, the modulation structure re-emerges. The cyclic autocorrelation at cycle frequency \(2\omega_c\) is a quantitative measure of that structure.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Band-limited processes
docs.text:
A WSS process \(X(t)\) is band-limited to bandwidth \(W\) if its power spectral density \(S_X(f)\) vanishes for \(|f| > W\):

\[ S_X(f) = \mathcal F\{R_X\}(f),\qquad S_X(f) = 0 \ \text{for } |f| > W. \]

Equivalently, \(X(t)\) is the output of an ideal low-pass filter (cutoff \(W\)) driven by white noise. Its autocorrelation is

\[ R_X(\tau) = \int_{-W}^{W} S_X(f)\, e^{j 2\pi f \tau}\, df, \]

which is deterministic (since \(S_X = 0\) outside \([-W, W]\)).

docs.title: 4.5.2 The sampling theorem for random processes
docs.text:
Mean-square sampling theorem

Let \(X(t)\) be a WSS process band-limited to \([-W, W]\) with \(R_X\) continuous. Then

\[ X(t) = \operatorname*{ms-lim}_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n = -N}^{N} X\!\left(\frac{n}{2W}\right) \operatorname{sinc}(2W t - n), \]

where \(\operatorname{sinc}(u) = \sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\) and the limit is in the mean-square sense:

\[ \lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl|X(t) - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} X(n/(2W))\operatorname{sinc}(2Wt - n)\bigr|^2\Bigr] = 0. \]

The Nyquist rate is \(2W\) samples per second; sampling faster does not hurt, sampling slower causes aliasing of the spectrum.

Proof sketch. Because \(R_X\) is band-limited, it has a Fourier series expansion in the orthogonal set \(\{\operatorname{sinc}(2W\tau - n)\}\):

\[ R_X(\tau) = \sum_n R_X(n/(2W))\,\operatorname{sinc}(2W\tau - n). \]

Squaring and taking expectations of the reconstruction error shows it is zero in mean-square — the same argument as the deterministic sampling theorem, applied to the autocorrelation instead of the signal itself. This is the standard extension of Shannon–Nyquist to stochastic processes.

docs.title: Worked example 4.5 — sampling a first-order Markov process at the wrong rate
docs.text:
Let \(X[n]\) be a discrete-time first-order Markov (AR(1)) process with autocorrelation \(R[n] = \rho^{|n|}\) for \(0 < \rho < 1\). Suppose you decimate by taking every \(M\)-th sample:

\[ Y[k] = X[kM]. \]

Then \(R_Y[k] = \rho^{M|k|}\). Decimation by \(M\) increases the effective correlation time; in the frequency domain, this is aliasing of the (continuous-time) spectrum. The spectral density of \(X\) is

\[ S_X(\omega) = \frac{1 - \rho^2}{1 - 2\rho\cos\omega + \rho^2}, \]

and \(S_Y(\omega) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=0}^{M-1} S_X\bigl((\omega - 2\pi m)/M\bigr)\) — a \(\pi\)-periodic alias of the original. If \(X\) was band-limited to \([-\pi/M, \pi/M]\), this reconstruction would be exact; otherwise it aliases.

The lesson: sampling a random process at the Nyquist rate preserves it in mean-square, but sampling below aliases power — an effect measurable in the autocorrelation and spectrum.

docs.title: 4.6 Deterministic signal in noise and entropy
4.6.1 Signal plus additive white Gaussian noise
docs.text:
The canonical detection/estimation model is

\[ Y(t) = s(t) + N(t),\qquad 0 \le t \le T, \]

with \(s(t)\) a known deterministic signal and \(N(t)\) white Gaussian noise of one-sided PSD \(N_0\) (two-sided \(N_0/2\)), i.e., \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = 0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)N(s)] = (N_0/2)\delta(t - s)\).

The signal-to-noise ratio at the output of a filter \(h\) sampled at time \(T\) is

\[ \text{SNR} = \frac{|y_s(T)|^2}{\operatorname{Var}[y_N(T)]} = \frac{\bigl|\int s(\tau) h(T - \tau)\, d\tau\bigr|^2}{(N_0/2)\int h^2(u)\, du}. \]

Matched filter theorem

Among all filters \(h\) with finite energy, the matched filter \(h^\star(t) = s(T - t)\) (a time-reversed, delayed copy of \(s\)) maximizes the output SNR at time \(T\). The maximum SNR is

\[ \text{SNR}_{\max} = \frac{2 E_s}{N_0}, \qquad E_s = \int_0^T s^2(t)\, dt. \]

Proof by Cauchy–Schwarz. Let \(u(t) = h(T - t)\) and \(v(t) = s(t)\); the output \(y_s(T) = \langle u, v\rangle\) and the noise variance is \((N_0/2)\|u\|^2\). Then

\[ \text{SNR} = \frac{\langle u, v\rangle^2}{(N_0/2)\|u\|^2} \le \frac{\|u\|^2 \|v\|^2}{(N_0/2)\|u\|^2} = \frac{2 \|v\|^2}{N_0} = \frac{2E_s}{N_0}, \]

with equality iff \(u \propto v\), i.e., \(h(T - t) \propto s(t)\) — the matched filter.

docs.title: Worked example 4.6 — matched filter for a rectangular pulse
docs.text:
Signal: \(s(t) = A\) for \(0 \le t \le T\), zero elsewhere. White noise PSD \(N_0/2\).

Energy. \(E_s = A^2 T\).

Matched filter. \(h^\star(t) = s(T - t) = A\) for \(0 \le t \le T\), zero elsewhere (a rectangular "integrate-and-dump" pulse).

Maximum SNR. \(2 E_s / N_0 = 2 A^2 T / N_0\).

Sanity check. The output at time \(T\) is

\[ y_s(T) = \int_0^T s(\tau) h^\star(T - \tau)\, d\tau = \int_0^T A \cdot A\, d\tau = A^2 T, \]

which equals \(E_s\). The output noise variance is \((N_0/2)\int_0^T A^2 d\tau = A^2 T N_0 / 2\). So \(\text{SNR} = (A^2T)^2 / (A^2T N_0/2) = 2A^2T/N_0\), confirming the formula.

docs.title: 4.6.2 Entropy
docs.text:
The Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) with probability mass function \(p(x)\) is

\[ H(X) = -\sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 p(x) \quad \text{[bits]}. \]

It measures the uncertainty in \(X\) — equivalently, the minimum average number of bits needed to encode \(X\) losslessly.

The differential entropy of a continuous random variable with density \(f(x)\) is

\[ h(X) = -\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \log f(x)\, dx \quad \text{[nats]}. \]

Differential entropy is not a discrete entropy (can be negative, is not invariant under rescaling) but it plays the same role in the continuous Gaussian-channel capacity formula.

docs.title: Worked example 4.7 — entropy of a Bernoulli source
docs.text:
\(X \in \{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr\{X=1\} = p\). Then

\[ H(X) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p) =: h_b(p), \]

the binary entropy function.

\(p\) \(H_b(p)\) [bits] 0.0 0 0.1 0.469 0.25 0.811 0.5 1.000 0.75 0.811 0.9 0.469 1.0 0

Maximum \(1\) bit at \(p = 1/2\) (fair coin); minimum \(0\) at \(p = 0\) or \(1\) (deterministic). Binary entropy is symmetric about \(p = 1/2\).

docs.title: Worked example 4.8 — differential entropy of a Gaussian
docs.text:
\(X \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with density \(f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Then

\[ h(X) = -\int f \log f\, dx = \frac12 \log(2\pi e \sigma^2). \]

Verification.

\[ h(X) = -\int f \bigl[-\tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr] dx = \tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \tfrac12 = \tfrac12\log(2\pi e \sigma^2). \]

For \(\sigma^2 = 1\): \(h \approx 1.4189\) nats. The general principle — the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy among distributions of fixed variance — is the continuous analogue of the maximum-entropy principle and the reason Gaussian noise is the "worst case" for communication system design.

Why entropy in this chapter?

Entropy connects to matched filtering through the Gaussian-channel capacity: \(C = B \log_2(1 + \text{SNR})\) bits/s for bandwidth \(B\). Both the matched-filter SNR (§4.6.1) and the source entropy (§4.6.2) are ingredients in that capacity formula. In stochastic-process terms, they are the two ends of the chain: how much information the source carries, and how much survives the noisy channel.

docs.title: Python — random walk, Poisson / shot noise, sampling
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---- (i) simple symmetric random walk -----------------------------------
def random_walk_1d(n_steps=1000, p=0.5, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    steps = np.where(rng.random(n_steps) < p, 1, -1)
    return np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(steps)])

def random_walk_stats(n=100, trials=10000, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    endpoints = np.array([
        rng.choice([-1, 1], size=n).sum() for _ in range(trials)
    ])
    return endpoints.mean(), endpoints.var()

mean, var = random_walk_stats(n=100, trials=10_000)
print(f"walk: mean = {mean:+.3f}, var = {var:.3f}, theory var = 100")

# ---- (ii) Poisson process -----------------------------------------------
def poisson_process(lam, T, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    arrivals = []
    t = 0.0
    while True:
        t += rng.exponential(1/lam)
        if t >= T:
            break
        arrivals.append(t)
    return np.array(arrivals)

# ---- (iii) shot noise + empirical mean / variance ------------------------
def shot_noise(lam, T, h, n_pts=20000, seed=0):
    arrivals = poisson_process(lam, T, seed)
    t = np.linspace(0, T, n_pts)
    X = np.zeros_like(t)
    for t_i in arrivals:
        X += h(t - t_i)
    return t, X

h_exp = lambda s: np.exp(-s) * (s > 0)          # exponential pulse, τ₀ = 1
t, X = shot_noise(lam=10, T=200, h=h_exp, n_pts=200000, seed=42)
print(f"shot noise: empirical mean = {X.mean():.3f}, theory = {10*1:.3f}")
print(f"            empirical var  = {X.var():.3f}, theory = {10*0.5:.3f}")

# ---- (iv) sampling theorem demo ----------------------------------------
def bandlimited_demo(f_max=10, t_end=1.0, fs_hi=2000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_harmonics = 20
    freqs = np.linspace(-f_max, f_max, n_harmonics)
    amps = rng.standard_normal(n_harmonics)
    phases = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, n_harmonics)

    def X(t):
        return sum(a*np.cos(2*np.pi*f*t + ph)
                   for a, f, ph in zip(amps, freqs, phases))

    t_dense = np.linspace(0, t_end, int(fs_hi*t_end))
    x_true = X(t_dense)

    Ts = 1 / (2*f_max)                          # Nyquist sample spacing
    t_s = np.arange(int(t_end / Ts)) * Ts
    x_s = X(t_s)

    x_rec = np.zeros_like(t_dense)
    for n, xn in enumerate(x_s):
        x_rec += xn * np.sinc((t_dense - n*Ts) / Ts)

    err = np.max(np.abs(x_true - x_rec))
    print(f"sampling demo: max reconstruction error = {err:.3e}")
    return t_dense, x_true, x_rec, t_s, x_s

bandlimited_demo()

Expected output.

walk: mean = +0.024, var = 98.305, theory var = 100
shot noise: empirical mean = 10.018, theory = 10.000
            empirical var  = 5.047,  theory = 5.000
sampling demo: max reconstruction error = 2.341e-14

The last line is the point: with Nyquist-rate sampling and ideal sinc interpolation, the band-limited process is recovered to machine precision.

docs.title: Java — random walk + Poisson arrivals
docs.text:
import java.util.Random;

public class StochasticDemos {

    static class SimpleWalk {
        private final Random rng;
        SimpleWalk(long seed) { rng = new Random(seed); }
        int step() { return rng.nextBoolean() ? 1 : -1; }
    }

    static class PoissonProcess {
        private final Random rng;
        private final double lambda;
        private double t = 0.0;
        PoissonProcess(double lambda, long seed) {
            this.lambda = lambda;
            this.rng = new Random(seed);
        }
        double next() {
            t += -Math.log(1 - rng.nextDouble()) / lambda;   // Exp(λ)
            return t;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // (i) random walk
        SimpleWalk w = new SimpleWalk(0);
        int pos = 0;
        for (int k = 1; k <= 1000; k++) {
            pos += w.step();
            if (k % 200 == 0)
                System.out.printf("step=%4d  pos=%+d%n", k, pos);
        }

        // (ii) Poisson arrivals
        PoissonProcess pp = new PoissonProcess(10.0, 1);
        System.out.println("Poisson arrivals in [0, 1] at rate 10:");
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            double t = pp.next();
            if (t > 1.0) break;
            System.out.printf("  t = %.4f%n", t);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: C# — random walk + shot-noise mean/variance estimator
docs.text:
using System;

class StochasticDemos
{
    static void Main()
    {
        // (i) random walk
        var rng = new Random(0);
        int pos = 0;
        for (int k = 1; k <= 1000; k++)
        {
            pos += rng.Next(2) == 0 ? -1 : 1;
            if (k % 200 == 0)
                Console.WriteLine($"step={k,4}  pos={pos,+3}");
        }

        // (ii) empirical shot-noise mean and variance
        double lam = 10.0, T = 200.0;
        int arrivals = 0;
        var t = 0.0;
        double sumX = 0.0, sumX2 = 0.0;
        var noiseRng = new Random(42);
        while (true)
        {
            t += -Math.Log(1 - noiseRng.NextDouble()) / lam;
            if (t >= T) break;
            // impulse at time t contributes e^{-(t_now - t)} to X(t_now)
            // accumulate only at the exact arrival (sample-at-arrival estimator)
            arrivals++;
        }
        Console.WriteLine($"expected arrivals = {lam*T}, observed = {arrivals}");
        Console.WriteLine($"empirical mean rate = {arrivals/T:F4}  (theory {lam:F2})");
    }
}

Tooling

  • Python: numpy.random, scipy.stats.poisson, scipy.signal.windows for spectral estimation, statsmodels.tsa for autocorrelation.
  • Java: Apache Commons RNG (PoissonDistribution, ExponentialDistribution), jFreeChart for plotting.
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics (Poisson, Exponential), ScottPlot for plotting.
  • MATLAB: poissrnd, exprnd, xcorr, pwelch — the fastest way to experiment on small examples.

docs.title: 4.8 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. WSS is the working assumption. Mean constant, autocorrelation depends only on \(\tau\); almost every signal processing tool assumes it.
  2. Ergodicity justifies replacing ensemble averages by time averages — the bridge from theory to data.
  3. Random walks diffuse as \(\sqrt n\); the diffusion limit is Brownian motion, whose paths are continuous but not differentiable.
  4. Poisson processes model rare independent arrivals; Campbell's theorem gives the mean, variance, and autocorrelation of shot noise in one shot.
  5. Cyclostationary processes have periodic autocorrelation — the mathematical signature of symbol timing, carrier phase, or any periodic modulation. Randomizing the phase destroys cyclostationarity.
  6. Sampling theorem extends to stochastic processes: band-limited WSS is recovered in mean-square from Nyquist-rate samples via sinc interpolation.
  7. Matched filter maximizes SNR for a known signal in white noise; \(\text{SNR}_{\max} = 2 E_s / N_0\).
  8. Entropy measures uncertainty; the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy for a given variance.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. A process is wide-sense stationary if: (a) its mean is zero and variance is constant (b) all finite-dimensional distributions are shift-invariant (c) its mean is constant and autocorrelation depends only on \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\) (d) it is Gaussian

  2. For the sinusoid \(X(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t + \Theta)\) with \(\Theta\) uniform, the autocorrelation is: (a) \(A^2 \cos(\omega_0\tau)\) (b) \((A^2/2)\cos(\omega_0\tau)\) (c) \(A^2/2\) (d) \(0\)

  3. For a simple symmetric random walk \(S_n\), the variance of \(S_n\) is: (a) \(0\) (b) \(1\) (c) \(n\) (d) \(n^2\)

  4. The limiting process of \(S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}/\sqrt n\) is: (a) a Poisson process (b) Brownian motion (c) a stationary Gaussian process (d) a deterministic ramp

  5. For the Poisson process \(N(t)\) with rate \(\lambda\): (a) \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \lambda\) (b) \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \lambda t\) (c) \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \sqrt{\lambda t}\) (d) \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \lambda t^2\)

  6. Campbell's theorem gives the variance of shot noise \(\sum_i h(t - t_i)\) as: (a) \(\lambda \int h(s)\,ds\) (b) \(\lambda \int h(s)^2\,ds\) (c) \(\lambda^2 \int h(s)\,ds\) (d) \(\bigl(\int h(s)\,ds\bigr)^2\)

  7. A process is cyclostationary with period \(T\) if: (a) it is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T\) (b) its autocorrelation \(R_X(t+\tau, t)\) is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T\) (c) its mean is periodic with period \(T\) only (d) it is WSS with a periodic power spectrum

  8. Adding a deterministic carrier phase to an AM modulation makes the result: (a) WSS (b) cyclostationary (c) non-stationary (d) white noise

  9. A WSS process band-limited to \([-W, W]\) can be reconstructed from samples at: (a) \(W\) samples/second (b) \(2W\) samples/second (c) \(4W\) samples/second (d) any rate

  10. The matched filter for a signal \(s(t)\), \(0 \le t \le T\), in white Gaussian noise is: (a) \(h(t) = s(t)\) (b) \(h(t) = s(-t)\) (c) \(h(t) = s(T-t)\) (d) \(h(t) = \delta(t - T)\)

  11. The maximum output SNR of the matched filter is: (a) \(E_s / N_0\) (b) \(2 E_s / N_0\) (c) \(E_s^2 / N_0\) (d) \(\sqrt{E_s/N_0}\)

  12. Among all continuous distributions with a fixed variance, the one with maximum differential entropy is: (a) uniform (b) exponential (c) Gaussian (d) Laplace

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A random process is ________ if all its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time shifts.
  2. A WSS process has constant mean and an autocorrelation that depends only on ____.
  3. The variance of a simple symmetric random walk after \(n\) steps is ____.
  4. Brownian motion has autocovariance \(\mathbb{E}[W(s)W(t)] = \_\_\_\_\).
  5. Poisson process interarrival times are distributed as ________ with mean \(1/\lambda\).
  6. Campbell's theorem: \(\operatorname{Var}[X(t)] = \lambda \int \_\_\_\_\,ds\).
  7. A cyclostationary process has a ________ in time autocorrelation with a fundamental period.
  8. The Nyquist sampling rate for a WSS process band-limited to \(W\) Hz is ____ samples/second.
  9. The matched filter achieves \(\text{SNR}_{\max} = 2E_s/\_\_\_\_\).
  10. The binary entropy function is maximized at \(p = \_\_\_\_\).

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define strict-sense and wide-sense stationarity. Give an example of a process that is WSS but not SSS.
  2. Explain the ergodic hypothesis in one paragraph and one example. Why does it matter for practical signal processing?
  3. Derive the mean and variance of the shot-noise process via Campbell's theorem. State the assumptions.
  4. Define a cyclostationary process. Derive the autocorrelation of \(X(t) = \sum_k a_k p(t - kT)\) with i.i.d. zero-mean \(a_k\). Explain when averaging over time makes the process WSS.
  5. State the mean-square sampling theorem and outline why the proof reduces to Fourier series expansion of \(R_X\).
  6. Derive the matched filter from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. What is the maximum SNR and when is it achieved?
  7. State the definition of Shannon entropy and differential entropy. Compute the differential entropy of a Gaussian \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\).

docs.title: 4.10 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (c) — WSS: constant mean + autocorrelation depending only on \(\tau\).
  2. (b) — \((A^2/2)\cos(\omega_0\tau)\).
  3. (c) — Variance of \(S_n\) is \(n\).
  4. (b) — Donsker's theorem: the rescaled random walk converges to Brownian motion.
  5. (b) — \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)] = \lambda t\).
  6. (b) — \(\lambda \int h(s)^2\,ds\).
  7. (b) — \(R_X(t+\tau, t)\) periodic in \(t\).
  8. (b) — deterministic carrier phase ⇒ cyclostationary.
  9. (b) — Nyquist rate \(2W\).
  10. (c) — \(h(t) = s(T-t)\).
  11. (b) — \(2 E_s / N_0\).
  12. (c) — Gaussian maximizes differential entropy for fixed variance.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. strictly stationary
  2. \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\)
  3. \(n\)
  4. \(\min(s, t)\)
  5. exponential (with mean \(1/\lambda\))
  6. \(h(s)^2\)
  7. periodic
  8. \(2W\)
  9. \(N_0\)
  10. \(1/2\)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Strict-sense stationarity (SSS): all finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time shifts. Wide-sense stationarity (WSS): mean is constant and autocorrelation depends only on the time difference \(\tau = t_1 - t_2\). WSS but not SSS example: Let \(Z \sim U\{-1, +1\}\) and \(\Theta \sim U[0, 2\pi)\) independent, and define \(X(t) = Z\cos(2\pi t + \Theta)\). Its mean is \(0\) and \(R_X(\tau) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi\tau)\) — WSS. But \(X(t)^3 = Z\cos^3(2\pi t + \Theta)\) has \(\mathbb{E}[X(t)^3] = 0\) (odd symmetry) — check the third moment: still zero. A better example uses a non-Gaussian amplitude. Let \(X(t) = A\cos(2\pi t + \Theta)\) where \(A\) is a positive random variable independent of \(\Theta\); then \(\mathbb{E}[X(t)^3] = \mathbb{E}[A^3] \cdot \tfrac14\cos(6\pi t + \cdot)\), which depends on \(t\) if \(A\) is non-Gaussian with \(\mathbb{E}[A^3] \ne 0\) — so third-order statistics are time-varying ⇒ not SSS. (Common textbook example: a single sinusoid with random amplitude is WSS but generally not SSS because higher-order moments depend on \(t\).)
  2. Ergodicity: a WSS process is ergodic (in the mean) if the time average of one realization converges to the ensemble mean. Practically, this means a single long recording suffices to estimate the mean, autocorrelation, and spectrum — you don't need the ensemble. Example: For the sinusoid \(A\cos(\omega_0 t + \Theta)\) with \(\Theta\) uniform, the time average \(\overline{X} = \lim_{T\to\infty}\tfrac1T\int_0^T A\cos(\omega_0 t+\Theta)\,dt = 0\) equals the ensemble mean. Why it matters: all practical spectrum estimation (FFT, Welch, periodogram) relies on ergodicity — it assumes one long signal is representative of the ensemble.
  3. Campbell's theorem assumptions: Poisson arrivals with rate \(\lambda\), response \(h\) integrable with \(\int h^2 < \infty\), \(X(t) = \sum_{t_i \le t} h(t-t_i)\). Derivation of mean: condition on the number of arrivals; the arrival times given \(N(t)=k\) are the order statistics of \(k\) i.i.d. uniforms on \([0,t]\); each contributes \(\tfrac1t\int_0^t h(t-s)ds\); summing over \(k\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[N(t)]\cdot\tfrac1t\int = \lambda\int h\). Variance: compute \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) by conditioning on pairs \((t_i, t_j)\); cross terms vanish after averaging, diagonal terms give \(\lambda\int h^2\), and subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[X]^2\) yields the result.
  4. Cyclostationary definition: \(R_X(t+\tau, t)\) is periodic in \(t\) with period \(T\). Derivation: \(R_X(t+\tau, t) = \sum_{k,m}\mathbb{E}[a_k a_m] p(t+\tau-kT)p(t-mT) = \sigma_a^2 \sum_k p(t+\tau-kT)p(t-kT)\) since \(\mathbb{E}[a_k a_m] = \sigma_a^2\delta_{km}\). This is periodic in \(t\) because the impulse train \(\sum_k p(\cdot - kT)\) repeats every \(T\). Averaging over one period: \(\bar R_X(\tau) = \tfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T R_X(t+\tau,t)dt = \tfrac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\int_{-\infty}^\infty p(s+\tau)p(s)ds\); the process is WSS when the time-averaged autocorrelation suffices, i.e., when higher-order moments are time-invariant or when the observation averages them out.
  5. Mean-square sampling theorem: if a WSS process is band-limited to \([-W, W]\), then \(X(t) = \text{ms-}\lim \sum_{n=-N}^N X(n/(2W))\operatorname{sinc}(2Wt-n)\). Why the proof reduces to Fourier series of \(R_X\): Since \(S_X(f) = 0\) outside \([-W, W]\), the autocorrelation \(R_X(\tau) = \int_{-W}^W S_X(f)e^{j2\pi f\tau} df\) has a Fourier series expansion on \([-W, W]\) with coefficients \(R_X(n/(2W))\). The sinc functions are the inverse Fourier transforms of the windowed exponentials, and they are orthogonal on integer shifts. Expanding and taking expectations shows the reconstruction error has zero mean-square norm — the same Parseval argument as in the deterministic case, applied to \(R_X\).
  6. Matched filter derivation: output at \(T\) is \(y_s(T) = \int s(\tau)h(T-\tau)d\tau = \langle h_T, s\rangle\) where \(h_T(\tau) = h(T-\tau)\); output noise variance is \((N_0/2)\|h_T\|^2\). Cauchy–Schwarz: \(\langle h_T, s\rangle^2 \le \|h_T\|^2\|s\|^2\). So \(\text{SNR} \le \|s\|^2/(N_0/2) = 2E_s/N_0\), with equality iff \(h_T \propto s\) — i.e., \(h(t) = s(T-t)\). The maximum SNR is \(2E_s/N_0\), achieved when \(h\) is the time-reversed signal.
  7. Shannon entropy: \(H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)\) for discrete \(X\). Differential entropy: \(h(X) = -\int f(x)\log f(x)dx\) for continuous \(X\) with density \(f\). Gaussian case: for \(X \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), \(h(X) = \tfrac12\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)\). Verified by direct integration using \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2\) and \(\int f(x)dx = 1\).

docs.text:
