docs.text:
• Gross, Shortle, Thompson & Harris, Fundamentals of Queueing Theory, 5th ed., Wiley, 2018 — the standard textbook.
  • Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory, Wiley, 1975 — the classical reference, still worth reading.
  • Wolff, Stochastic Modeling and the Theory of Queues, Prentice-Hall, 1989 — rigorous treatment including Little's formula and Burke's theorem.
  • Harchol-Balter, Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems, Cambridge University Press, 2013 — modern treatment with computer-science applications.
  • Bertsekas & Gallager, Data Networks, 2nd ed. — Chapters 3 and 5 for queueing in communication networks.
  • Medhi, Stochastic Models in Queueing Theory, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2003.
  • Jackson, J. R., "Networks of Waiting Lines", Operations Research 5(4), 1957 — the original Jackson theorem.
  • Burke, P. J., "The Output of a Queueing System", Operations Research 4(6), 1956 — Burke's theorem.
  • Pollaczek–Khinchine formula — see Gross et al. §5, or any standard reference.
  • Python simpy, queueing_tool; Java SSJ; C# SimSharp; MATLAB queueing toolbox; R queueing package.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Little's formula applications. A hospital ward has an average of \(18\) patients, each staying \(4\) days on average. What is the average arrival rate? If management introduces a policy that reduces average stay to \(3\) days at the same rate, what is the new average census?
  2. M/M/1 by hand. For \(\lambda = 8\) pkt/s, \(\mu = 10\) pkt/s, compute \(L, L_q, W, W_q\), \(\pi_0\), \(\Pr\{N \ge 5\}\), and \(\Pr\{W > 0.5\ \text{s}\}\). Verify Little's formula for both \(L\) and \(L_q\).
  3. Unstable queue. For \(\lambda = 12\), \(\mu = 10\) in an M/M/1 queue, show that the expected queue length diverges. Simulate for \(T = 10^4\) time units and comment on the empirical trend.
  4. Erlang C sensitivity. For \(\lambda = 50\) calls/min, \(\mu = 20\) calls/min, find the smallest \(s\) such that the wait probability is below \(10\%\). Compute \(W_q\) for that \(s\), then for \(s + 1\). Comment on the marginal cost of the extra server.
  5. M/M/1/K buffer. For \(\lambda = 5\), \(\mu = 10\), and \(K = 1, 2, 5, 10\), compute the blocking probability and effective arrival rate. Plot blocking probability vs. \(K\).
  6. PK formula comparison. For \(\lambda = 6\), mean service time \(= 0.1\), compare \(L_q\) for exponential, deterministic, and Erlang-2 (\(k=2\)) service. Verify that \(L_q^{M/D/1} < L_q^{M/E_2/1} < L_q^{M/M/1}\).
  7. Jackson network. Two queues in series: queue 1 with \(\lambda_1 = 4\), \(\mu_1 = 10\); queue 2 with \(\mu_2 = 8\) and no external arrivals. Write the traffic equations, compute \(\lambda_2\), verify stability, and compute the network mean \(L_{\text{net}}\) and mean end-to-end time.
  8. Simulation project. Simulate an M/M/1 with \(\lambda = 7\), \(\mu = 10\) for \(T = 10^6\). Report the empirical \(L, L_q, W, W_q\) with \(95\%\) confidence intervals from \(20\) batches. Compare with the analytical values. Then change the service distribution to deterministic (\(1/\mu = 0.1\)) keeping \(\lambda\) fixed, and compare — is the empirical M/D/1 queue really about half as crowded as the M/M/1?
  9. Real-data analysis. Take a publicly available packet trace (e.g. pcap files from the WIDE backbone) or a synthetic interarrival dataset; fit both an exponential and a log-normal to the interarrival times; run a discrete-event simulation with each, and compare predicted vs. observed queue-length distributions. Where does the exponential assumption break down?

docs.title: Chapter 1: Optimization - Preliminary
docs.text: Weeks: 1 - 3 | Contact Hours: 6 Lectures, 9 Tutorials

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:

  1. Formulate engineering problems as mathematical optimization models.
  2. Distinguish between local and global minima, and understand Pareto-optimality.
  3. Compute and interpret the Gradient and Hessian matrices for linear and quadratic functions.
  4. Apply First-Order and Second-Order Necessary/Sufficient conditions for unconstrained optimization.
  5. Formulate and solve constrained optimization problems using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions.
  6. Implement line search algorithms and understand the Adjoint Variable method for gradient computation.

docs.title: 1.1 Basics of Optimization
docs.text:
An optimization problem seeks to find the best element from a set of available alternatives. Mathematically, it is formulated as:

\[\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{x}} \quad & f(\mathbf{x}) \\ \text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \end{aligned}\]

where \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the decision variable vector, \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is the objective function, and \(\mathcal{X}\) is the feasible set.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Characterization of a Minimum
docs.text:
• Local Minimum: A point \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is a local minimum if there exists an \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(f(\mathbf{x}^*) \le f(\mathbf{x})\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\) in the \(\epsilon\)-neighborhood of \(\mathbf{x}^*\) (i.e., \(\Vert{}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^*\Vert{} \le \epsilon\)).
  • Global Minimum: A point \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is a global minimum if \(f(\mathbf{x}^*) \le f(\mathbf{x})\) for all feasible \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}\).

Engineering Insight: In communication engineering (e.g., beamforming or resource allocation), we often deal with non-convex problems where algorithms only guarantee finding a local minimum. Convexity is the key to ensuring a local minimum is also a global minimum.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Pareto-Optimality in Multi-Objective Optimization
docs.text:
When multiple conflicting objectives exist (e.g., maximizing data rate while minimizing power consumption), we define a vector objective \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = [f_1(\mathbf{x}), f_2(\mathbf{x}), \dots, f_k(\mathbf{x})]^T\).

A solution \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is Pareto-optimal (or non-dominated) if there is no other feasible \(\mathbf{x}\) that improves one objective without worsening at least one other objective. The set of all Pareto-optimal solutions forms the Pareto Front.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Calculus Tools: Gradient and Hessian
docs.text:
To find minima, we rely on differential calculus to measure the slope and curvature of the objective function.

  • Gradient (Slope): The vector of first partial derivatives. $\(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{bmatrix}\)$ It points in the direction of the steepest ascent.

  • Hessian (Curvature): The square matrix of second partial derivatives. $\(\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n \partial x_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2} \end{bmatrix}\)$ It describes the local curvature of the function.

docs.title: 1.1.4 Properties of Linear and Quadratic Functions
docs.text:
Understanding these two classes of functions is critical, as many optimization algorithms approximate complex functions using them.

  1. Linear Functions: \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + b\)
  2. Gradient: \( abla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}\)
  3. Hessian: \( abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}\) (Zero curvature; no local minima).
  4. Quadratic Functions: \(f(\mathbf{x}) = rac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{c}^T \mathbf{x} + d\) (where \(\mathbf{Q}\) is symmetric).
  5. Gradient: \( abla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{c}\)
  6. Hessian: \( abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{Q}\) (Constant curvature).
  7. Note: If \(\mathbf{Q}\) is Positive Definite (\(\mathbf{Q} \succ 0\)), the function is strictly convex and has a unique global minimum.

docs.title: 1.2 Optimality Conditions
docs.text: Optimality conditions are mathematical equations/inequalities that a point must satisfy to be a candidate for a minimum.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Unconstrained Optimization
docs.text: For \(\min f(\mathbf{x})\) with no constraints: * First-Order Necessary Condition (FONC): If \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is a local minimum, then \( abla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}\). (These are called stationary points). * Second-Order Necessary Condition (SONC): If \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is a local minimum, then \( abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^*) \succeq 0\) (Positive Semi-Definite). * Second-Order Sufficient Condition (SOSC): If \( abla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}\) and \( abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^*) \succ 0\) (Positive Definite), then \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is a strict local minimum.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Constrained Optimization
docs.text: When constraints are present, the gradient of the objective function does not have to be zero; it only needs to be zero in the directions that remain feasible.

docs.title: Linear Equality Constraints
docs.text: \(\min f(\mathbf{x})\) subject to \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\). We introduce the Lagrangian: $\(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{\lambda}^T (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})\)$ The necessary conditions are \(\nabla_\mathbf{x} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: Nonlinearly Constrained Optimization (KKT Conditions)
docs.text:
For \(\min f(\mathbf{x})\) subject to \(g_i(\mathbf{x}) \le 0\) and \(h_j(\mathbf{x}) = 0\). The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions are the necessary conditions for a local minimum:

  1. Stationarity: $\( abla f(\mathbf{x}^*) + \sum \mu_i abla g_i(\mathbf{x}^*) + \sum \lambda_j abla h_j(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}\)$
  2. Primal Feasibility: $\(g_i(\mathbf{x}^*) \le 0, \quad h_j(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0\)$
  3. Dual Feasibility: $\(\mu_i \ge 0\)$
  4. Complementary Slackness: $\(\mu_i g_i(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0\)$

docs.title: 1.3 Linear Search Subproblem & Derivatives
docs.text: In iterative optimization (like Gradient Descent or Newton's method), we update our estimate as: $\(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \alpha_k \mathbf{d}_k\)$ where \(\mathbf{d}_k\) is the search direction and \(\alpha_k\) is the step size. Finding \(\alpha_k\) is the Linear Search problem: \(\min_{\alpha > 0} \phi(\alpha) = f(\mathbf{x}_k + \alpha \mathbf{d}_k)\).

docs.title: 1.3.1 Bracketing and Sectioning Phase
docs.text:
1. Bracketing: Find three points \(a < b < c\) such that \(\phi(b) < \phi(a)\) and \(\phi(b) < \phi(c)\). The minimum must lie between \(a\) and \(c\).
  2. Sectioning (e.g., Golden Section Search): Iteratively narrow the bracket by evaluating the function at specific interior points based on the golden ratio, discarding the section that cannot contain the minimum.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Derivatives of the Objective Function
docs.text:
Algorithms require gradients. How do we get them?

1. Numerically Derived Gradient (Finite Differences): If the analytical derivative is too complex, we approximate it. * Forward difference: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{f(\mathbf{x} + h\mathbf{e}_i) - f(\mathbf{x})}{h}\) * Central difference (more accurate): \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{f(\mathbf{x} + h\mathbf{e}_i) - f(\mathbf{x} - h\mathbf{e}_i)}{2h}\)

2. Analytically Derived Gradient & The Adjoint Variable Approach: In communication systems (e.g., inverse scattering, channel estimation), the objective function often depends on a state variable \(\mathbf{u}\) (like an electromagnetic field), which is governed by a physical constraint (like Maxwell's equations) \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{m}) = \mathbf{0}\), where \(\mathbf{m}\) are the design parameters.

  • Direct differentiation requires solving a linear system for every single parameter in \(\mathbf{m}\). If \(\mathbf{m}\) has 10,000 variables, this is computationally impossible.
  • The Adjoint Variable Approach: By introducing an adjoint state variable \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) (the Lagrange multiplier for the physical constraint), we can compute the exact analytical gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{m}\) by solving only one adjoint equation, regardless of the number of parameters. This reduces the computational complexity from \(O(N_{params})\) to \(O(1)\).

docs.title: 📝 Worked Example: Constrained Optimization
docs.text:
Problem: Minimize the power \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) subject to the linear constraint \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\).

Solution using Lagrange Multipliers: 1. Form the Lagrangian: \(\mathcal{L}(x_1, x_2, \lambda) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - \lambda(x_1 + x_2 - 1)\) 2. Apply Stationarity (take derivatives and set to 0): * \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_1} = 2x_1 - \lambda = 0 \implies x_1 = \lambda / 2\) * \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_2} = 2x_2 - \lambda = 0 \implies x_2 = \lambda / 2\) * \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = -(x_1 + x_2 - 1) = 0 \implies x_1 + x_2 = 1\) 3. Substitute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) into the constraint: \((\lambda / 2) + (\lambda / 2) = 1 \implies \lambda = 1\) 4. Calculate optimal \(\mathbf{x}^*\): \(x_1^* = 0.5, \quad x_2^* = 0.5\)

Check Hessian: \(\nabla^2 f = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \succ 0\). The solution is a strict global minimum.

docs.title: 💻 Computational Implementation (Python)
docs.text:
Here is how we implement gradient checking and constrained optimization using Python's scipy.optimize.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# 1. Define the Objective Function (Quadratic)
def objective(x):
    return x[0]**2 + x[1]**2

# 2. Define the Analytical Gradient
def gradient(x):
    return np.array([2*x[0], 2*x[1]])

# 3. Numerical Gradient Check (Central Difference)
def numerical_gradient(f, x, h=1e-5):
    grad = np.zeros_like(x)
    for i in range(len(x)):
        x_plus = x.copy(); x_plus[i] += h
        x_minus = x.copy(); x_minus[i] -= h
        grad[i] = (f(x_plus) - f(x_minus)) / (2*h)
    return grad

# Test Gradient Check
x_test = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
print("Analytical Grad:", gradient(x_test))
print("Numerical Grad: ", numerical_gradient(objective, x_test))

# 4. Solve the Constrained Problem
# Constraint: x1 + x2 = 1  =>  x1 + x2 - 1 = 0
cons = ({'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda x: x[0] + x[1] - 1})

# Initial guess
x0 = np.array([0.0, 0.0])

# Run Optimization (SLSQP handles equality constraints well)
result = minimize(objective, x0, method='SLSQP', jac=gradient, constraints=cons)

print("\nOptimization Result:")
print("Optimal x:", result.x)
print("Minimum f(x):", result.fun)

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 1 — Optimization Preliminaries
docs.text:
Back to Chapter 1

Key steps and final answers. See the corresponding worked examples in the chapter for full derivations.

docs.title: 1.1 Unconstrained minimum of a cubic
docs.text:
\(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1\) on \([0,4]\).

  • \(f'(x) = 3(x-1)(x-3)\) → stationary points \(x = 1, 3\).
  • \(f''(x) = 6(x-2)\): \(f''(1) = -6\) (local max, \(f=5\)); \(f''(3) = 6\) (local min, \(f=1\)).
  • Boundary values: \(f(0) = 1\), \(f(4) = 5\).

Global min: \(x=0\) and \(x=3\), \(f^\star = 1\). Global max: \(x=1\) and \(x=4\), \(f=5\).

Golden-section on \([0,4]\) finds \(x \approx 3\) (the interior min); the other global min at \(x=0\) is a boundary point that golden-section cannot reach.

docs.title: 1.2 Pareto front of two objectives
docs.text:
\(\min (x^2+y^2,\ (x-1)^2+y^2)\) over \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

For any fixed \(x\), \(y=0\) Pareto-dominates any \(y \ne 0\) (both objectives strictly smaller). Along \(y=0\):

\[ f_1 = x^2,\quad f_2 = (x-1)^2. \]

For \(x<0\): moving to \(x=0\) reduces both. For \(x>1\): moving to \(x=1\) reduces both. So Pareto set \(= \{(x,0): 0 \le x \le 1\}\), Pareto front \(= \{(x^2, (x-1)^2): 0 \le x \le 1\}\) — a segment from \((0,1)\) to \((1,0)\).

Three Pareto-optimal points: \((0,0) \to (0,1)\); \((0.5,0) \to (0.25, 0.25)\); \((1,0) \to (1,0)\).

docs.title: 1.3 Lagrange multiplier with equality constraint
docs.text:
\(\min x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\) s.t. \(x_1+2x_2+3x_3=6\).

Lagrangian \(\mathcal L = \sum x_i^2 + \lambda(x_1+2x_2+3x_3-6)\). From \(\partial/\partial x_i = 0\):

\[ x_1 = -\tfrac{\lambda}{2},\quad x_2 = -\lambda,\quad x_3 = -\tfrac{3\lambda}{2}. \]

Constraint: \(-\tfrac{\lambda}{2} - 2\lambda - \tfrac{9\lambda}{2} = -7\lambda = 6 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\tfrac{6}{7}\).

\(x^\star = \bigl(\tfrac{3}{7}, \tfrac{6}{7}, \tfrac{9}{7}\bigr)\), \(f^\star = \tfrac{135}{49} \approx 2.755\), \(\lambda^\star = -\tfrac{6}{7}\).

Envelope theorem check: \(df^\star/db = \lambda = -6/7\) — raising \(b\) by \(\epsilon\) reduces \(f^\star\) by \(\epsilon \cdot 6/7\).

docs.title: 1.5 Golden-section search
docs.text:
\(\phi(\alpha) = \sin(3\alpha) + \alpha^2/4\) on \([0,2]\), tolerance \(10^{-4}\).

Numerically, the global minimum is \(\alpha^\star \approx 0.14\), \(\phi^\star \approx 0.42\). But golden-section is a local method — depending on the bracket, it can converge to the local minimum near \(\alpha \approx 1.5\), which is deeper in some runs. This is a cautionary example: a global-scope claim for golden-section is wrong; verify against scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar(method='bounded') and, if needed, multi-start.

docs.title: 1.6 Adjoint for \(N=4\)
docs.text:
\(x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k\), \(x_0 = 2\), \(J = x_4^2 + \sum_{k=0}^3 u_k^2\).

Direct. \(x_4 = 2 + \sum u_k\); \(\partial J/\partial u_k = 2x_4 + 2u_k = 0\) ⇒ \(u_k = -x_4\) for all \(k\). Then \(x_4 = 2 - 4x_4\) ⇒ \(x_4 = 2/5\).

\(u^\star = (-0.4, -0.4, -0.4, -0.4)\), \(J^\star = 0.8\).

Adjoint check. \(\lambda_4 = 2x_4\); \(\lambda_k = \lambda_{k+1}\) (costates constant); \(\partial J/\partial u_k = 2u_k + \lambda_{k+1}\). At optimum \(u_k = -\lambda/2 = -x_4\) — identical to direct. ✓

docs.title: 1.7 Gradient check
docs.text:
\(f = \sin(x_1x_2) + x_3^4 - x_1 e^{x_2 x_3}\).

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = x_2\cos(x_1x_2) - e^{x_2 x_3},\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = x_1\cos(x_1x_2) - x_1 x_3 e^{x_2 x_3},\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_3} = 4x_3^3 - x_1 x_2 e^{x_2 x_3}. \]

At \((0.5, -1, 0.3)\): \(\nabla f \approx (-1.511,\ -0.328,\ -0.262)\).

Central differences with \(h=10^{-6}\) match to 6 digits. jax.grad matches to machine precision.

docs.text: Back to Chapter 2

docs.title: 2.1 Nelder–Mead by hand
docs.text:
\(f(x,y) = (x-2)^2+(y-3)^2\) from simplex \(\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}\).

Iteration 1. \(f\)-values \(13, 10, 8\) → best \((0,1)\), worst \((0,0)\). Centroid of the other two: \((0.5, 0.5)\). Reflection: \((1, 1)\), \(f=5 < f(v_{\text{best}})=8\) → expand to \((1.5, 1.5)\), \(f=2.5 < 5\) → accept expansion. New simplex: \(\{(1,0), (0,1), (1.5, 1.5)\}\).

Iteration 2. Values \(10, 8, 2.5\) → best \((1.5, 1.5)\), worst \((1, 0)\). Centroid \((0.75, 1.25)\). Reflection: \((0.5, 2.5)\), \(f=2.5 < 2.5\)? No — \(\ge\) the best, so contract: \(c = (0.5, 2.5) \to\) midpoint \((1, 1.75)\), \(f=2.5625\). Compare to \(f(v_{\text{worst}})=10\): accept contract.

Nelder–Mead converges very slowly here — many iterations are needed to get close to \((2,3)\).

docs.title: 2.2 Newton with line search on Rosenbrock
docs.text:
\(f = (1-x)^2 + 100(y-x^2)^2\), start \((-1, 1)\).

  • Plain Newton diverges (indefinite Hessian near the valley).
  • Damped Newton (Armijo, \(c_1 = 10^{-4}\)) reaches \(f < 10^{-6}\) in ~30 iterations.
  • Gradient descent (Armijo) reaches \(f < 10^{-6}\) in ~14,800 iterations.

Takeaway: the line search is essential for robustness; once close to the solution, Newton's quadratic convergence dominates.

docs.title: 2.3 BFGS update
docs.text:
\(f = x_1^2 + 2x_2^2\), \(x_0 = (1,1)\), \(H_0 = I\), exact line search.

From the worked example: \(s_0 = \left(-\tfrac{5}{9}, -\tfrac{10}{9}\right)\), \(y_0 = \left(-\tfrac{10}{9}, -\tfrac{40}{9}\right)\), \(y_0^\top s_0 = \tfrac{450}{81}\).

\[ H_1 = \frac{1}{45}\begin{bmatrix} 46 & 22 \\ 22 & 169\end{bmatrix}. \]

Checks.

  • Secant: \(H_1 y_0 = s_0\) ✓
  • Positive-definite: eigenvalues of \(H_1\) are both positive ⇒ \(H_1 \succ 0\) ✓

docs.title: 2.4 Quasi-Newton failure when \(y_k^\top s_k \le 0\)
docs.text:
\(f(x) = x^3\), \(x_0 = 1\), \(d_0 = -f'(x_0) = -3\), \(\alpha_0 = 1\).

\(x_1 = -2\); \(s_0 = -3\); \(y_0 = f'(-2) - f'(1) = 12 - 3 = 9\); \(y_0^\top s_0 = -27 < 0\).

The BFGS denominator \(y_0^\top s_0 < 0\) → the update loses positive-definiteness (and can even break down). A Wolfe line search guarantees \(y_k^\top s_k > 0\) on convex \(f\); for non-convex \(f\), skip the update when \(y_k^\top s_k \le 0\).

docs.title: 2.5 Gauss–Newton on exponential fit
docs.text:
\(y = a e^{bx}\), data \((0,1), (1,3), (2,8)\), start \((1,1)\).

After 3 iterations: \((a^\star, b^\star) \approx (1.084, 1.000)\), cost \(\approx 0.004\).

Why so fast. The residuals at the solution are small (the exponential fits the data almost exactly), so the dropped residual-curvature term \(\sum r_i \nabla^2 r_i\) is negligible — GN behaves like Newton and converges quadratically.

docs.title: 2.6 Rank-deficient Jacobian
docs.text:
\(f(\theta) = (a-b)^2 + (a-b-1)^2\) (two residuals, both proportional to \(a-b\)). The Jacobian \(J\) has rank 1 at every point, so \(J^\top J\) is singular → pure Gauss–Newton fails at the first step (\(a=b=0\)).

Levenberg–Marquardt adds \(\lambda I\): $$ (J^\top J + \lambda I)\,\Delta = -J^\top r $$ is nonsingular for any \(\lambda > 0\). LM converges to any point on the line \(a-b = 0.5\) — the non-uniqueness reflects the flat direction of the objective.

docs.title: 2.7 Rastrigin global optimisation
docs.text:
\(f(x) = 20 + \sum_{i}[x_i^2 - 10\cos(2\pi x_i)]\) (2-D), global min \(0\) at origin, many local minima.

  • Nelder–Mead, BFGS, Newton: from three different starts, each converges to the nearest local minimum (usually not the global).
  • scipy.optimize.basinhopping with minimize_scalar as the local method: finds the global minimum in >95% of runs on 2-D Rastrigin.

Takeaway: for multi-modal objectives, local methods fail regardless of how sophisticated they are. Use a global-scope method (basin-hopping, differential evolution, simulated annealing) or multi-start.

docs.text: Back to Chapter 3

docs.title: 3.3 Augmented Lagrangian
docs.text:
\(\min x^2-2x\) s.t. \(x = 1\).

\(\mathcal L_\rho(x,\lambda) = x^2-2x + \lambda(x-1) + \tfrac{\rho}{2}(x-1)^2\).

Inner minimisation. \(\partial/\partial x = 2x-2+\lambda+\rho(x-1) = 0\) ⇒ \(x = (2-\lambda+\rho)/(2+\rho)\).

Update. \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rho(x-1)\).

The convergence rate is \(\frac{2}{2+\rho}\) per iteration: for \(\rho=1\) the rate is \(2/3\).

docs.title: 3.5 QP with three equalities
docs.text:
\(Q = I_4\), \(c = (1,-2,3,-4)\), constraints \(x_1+x_2=1\), \(x_3+x_4=0\), \(x_1-x_3=1\).

KKT system is \(7 \times 7\). Solving:

\(x^\star = (0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5)\), \(\lambda^\star = (-1.5, 0.5, -1)\).

Check: \(\nabla f + A^\top\lambda = (1,-2,3,-4) + A^\top\lambda = 0\) with these multipliers ✓.

docs.title: 3.7 Solver cross-check
docs.text: scipy.optimize.minimize(..., method='SLSQP') gives the same \(x^\star\). method='trust-constr' returns the multipliers in the result object (.v for inequality, .multipliers in newer SciPy), which match the hand-computed values in 3.4, 3.5, and 3.6.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 4 — Stochastic Processes
docs.text: Back to Chapter 4

docs.title: 4.1 WSS check
docs.text:
• \(X_1(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t + \Theta)\), \(\Theta\) uniform: mean \(0\), \(R_X(\tau) = (A^2/2)\cos(\omega_0\tau)\) → WSS.
  • \(X_2(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t) + B\), \(A,B,\Theta\) independent: \(\mathbb E[X_2] = \mathbb E[B]\), \(R_{X_2}\) depends only on \(\tau\) → WSS.
  • \(X_3(t) = W(t)\cos(\omega_0 t)\), \(W\) zero-mean WSS: \(R_{X_3}(t+\tau,t) = R_W(\tau)\cos(\omega_0(t+\tau))\cos(\omega_0 t)\) — depends on \(t\) → not WSS, but cyclostationary with period \(T_0/2 = \pi/\omega_0\).

docs.title: 4.2 Random-walk moments
docs.text:
\(S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k\), \(X_k \in \{\pm 1\}\), \(\Pr\{X_k=+1\}=p\).

\(\mathbb E[S_n] = n(2p-1)\); \(\operatorname{Var}[S_n] = 4p(1-p)n\).

For \(p \ne 1/2\): \(S_n/n \to 2p-1\) a.s. (SLLN). So \(|S_n| \to \infty\) a.s. — the walk drifts to \(\pm\infty\); it is transient.

docs.title: 4.3 Poisson superposition
docs.text:
PGFs: \(G_{N_1}(z) = e^{\lambda_1 t(z-1)}\), \(G_{N_2}(z) = e^{\lambda_2 t(z-1)}\).

For \(N = N_1+N_2\) independent: \(G_N = G_{N_1}G_{N_2} = e^{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t(z-1)}\) — the PGF of Poisson(\((\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t\)). ✓

docs.title: 4.4 Shot noise with rectangular pulse
docs.text:
\(h(s) = 1\) for \(0 \le s \le T_p\), \(0\) otherwise.

Mean. \(\mathbb E[X] = \lambda\int_0^{T_p} ds = \lambda T_p\). Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}[X] = \lambda\int_0^{T_p} ds = \lambda T_p\). Autocorrelation. \(R_X(\tau) = \lambda(T_p - |\tau|)^+ + (\lambda T_p)^2\) — a triangular term plus a constant. Correlation time: \(T_p\).

docs.title: 4.5 Cyclostationary PAM
docs.text:
\(p(t) = \sqrt{2/T}\cos(2\pi t/T)\cdot\mathbf 1_{|t|\le T/2}\).

\(\bar R_X(\tau) = \dfrac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\int p(s+\tau)\,p(s)\,ds\) — a raised-cosine-shaped autocorrelation. Its Fourier transform is the raised-cosine spectrum with bandwidth \(W = 1/T\); this is the pulse shape that satisfies the Nyquist zero-ISI criterion and is standard in digital communications.

docs.title: 4.6 Sampling of a band-limited Gaussian process
docs.text:
\(W = 10\) Hz, sampled at \(20\) Hz (Nyquist): sinc reconstruction error \(\sim 10^{-14}\) — machine precision.

Sampled at \(15\) Hz (below Nyquist): spectrum above \(7.5\) Hz folds into lower frequencies — aliasing. Reconstruction error depends on the power above \(7.5\) Hz; for a typical smooth spectrum, 5–15% of total power is aliased.

docs.title: 4.7 Matched filter for a triangular pulse
docs.text:
\(s(t) = 1-|t|/T\) on \([-T, T]\). Energy \(E_s = 2T/3\).

Matched filter \(h(t) = s(T-t)\); maximum SNR \(= 2E_s/N_0 = 4T/(3N_0)\).

Comparison with a rectangular pulse of the same energy: the matched-filter SNR depends only on \(E_s\), so the two are identical — shape does not affect the maximum achievable SNR. Shape affects robustness to timing errors and spectral containment, not the peak SNR.

docs.title: 4.8 Entropy chain
docs.text:
(a) Discrete: Fair coin \(H = 1\) bit; biased \(p=0.1\) → \(H = -0.1\log_2(0.1) - 0.9\log_2(0.9) \approx 0.469\) bits; degenerate (p=0 or 1) → \(H = 0\).

(b) Differential: \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) → \(h = \tfrac12\log(2\pi e) \approx 1.419\) nats. \(\mathcal N(0,4)\) → \(h = \tfrac12\log(8\pi e) \approx 2.305\) nats. Uniform on \([-1,1]\) (variance \(= 1/3\)) → \(h = \log 2 \approx 0.693\) nats.

Gaussian maximizes differential entropy for a given variance — the uniform's entropy at variance \(1/3\) is smaller than the Gaussian's entropy at variance \(1/3\) (which would be \(\approx 0.919\) nats).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 5 — Spectral Representation
docs.text: Back to Chapter 5

docs.title: 5.1 Wiener–Khinchin for a Bernoulli sequence
docs.text:
\(X[n]\) = Bernoulli(1/2) on \(\{\pm 1\}\) ⇒ \(R_X[k] = \delta[k]\).

\[ S_X(\omega) = \sum_{k}\delta[k]e^{-j\omega k} = 1. \]

Check: \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}1\,d\omega = 1 = R_X[0]\) ✓. White sequence — flat spectrum.

docs.title: 5.2 Karhunen–Loève of AR(1)
docs.text:
Covariance \(K(s,t) = \rho^{|s-t|}\) on \([0,T]\). Sturm–Liouville eigen-problem with \(\tan\) boundary conditions:

\[ \tan(\mu T) = \frac{2\mu\rho}{\mu^2 - \rho^2},\qquad \lambda_k = \frac{2\rho}{1-\rho^2+\mu_k^2}. \]

For large \(T\): \(\lambda_k \propto 1/(1 + k^2\pi^2/T^2)\) — polynomial decay, slower than Brownian (\(1/k^2\)) at leading order but with \(\rho\)-dependent coefficients. Numerical check against \(100\times 100\) Toeplitz discretisation matches the low-order eigenvalues to 3 digits.

docs.title: 5.3 Spectral factorization
docs.text:
\(S_X(z) = \dfrac{(1+0.5z^{-1})(1+0.5z)}{(1-0.8z^{-1})(1-0.8z)}\).

Causal, monic, minimum-phase factor:

\[ L(z) = \frac{1+0.5z^{-1}}{1-0.8z^{-1}},\qquad \sigma_E^2 = 1. \]

The innovations \(E[n]\) are the output of the whitening filter \(L^{-1}(z) = (1-0.8z^{-1})/(1+0.5z^{-1})\) applied to \(X\) — an ARMA process driven by white noise.

docs.title: 5.4 Periodogram statistics
docs.text:
White Gaussian, \(N=1024\), \(\sigma^2=2\).

  • Empirical mean of \(\hat S_X\) across frequency bins \(\approx 2 = S_X\).
  • Empirical std across frequency bins \(\approx 2 = S_X\) — the periodogram is inconsistent (std \(\approx\) mean).
  • \(\hat S_X(\omega_k)/S_X\) ≈ exponential with mean 1.
  • Welch with \(K=4\) segments: mean unchanged, std reduced by \(\sqrt 4 = 2\).

docs.title: 5.5 LMMSE with two observations
docs.text:
\(X \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\); \(Y_1 = X+N_1\), \(Y_2 = 0.5X+N_2\); \(N_i \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\) i.i.d.

\[ \Sigma_{YY} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0.5\\0.5 & 1.25\end{bmatrix},\quad \Sigma_{XY} = (1,\ 0.5),\quad \det(\Sigma_{YY}) = 2.5 - 0.25 = 2.25. \] \[ \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2.25}\begin{bmatrix}1.25 & -0.5\\-0.5 & 2\end{bmatrix},\qquad \Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2.25}(1.0,\ 0.5). \]

\(\hat X = \dfrac{Y_1 + 0.5\,Y_2}{2.25}\).

MSE. \(= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2.25}(1\cdot 1 + 0.5\cdot 0.5) = 1 - \tfrac{1.25}{2.25} = \tfrac{4}{9} \approx 0.444\).

Using \(Y_1\) alone: \(\hat X = Y_1/2\), MSE \(= 1/2\). Combining reduces MSE by ~11% — because \(Y_2\) is a noisier linear scaling of the same signal, its incremental information is small.

docs.title: 5.6 Wiener filter for AR(1) signal + white noise
docs.text:
\(S\) AR(1) with \(a=0.7\), \(\sigma_W^2=1\); \(N\) white with \(\sigma_N^2 = 0.5\).

\(S_{SS}(\omega) = 1/|1-0.7e^{-j\omega}|^2\); \(S_{YY} = S_{SS} + 0.5\).

Non-causal Wiener. \(H(\omega) = S_{SS}/S_{YY}\) — at DC, \(H \to 1/(1+0.5\cdot 0.09) \approx 0.957\); at high frequency, \(H \to 0\). MSE reduction is typically 30–40% vs. \(\hat S = Y\).

Causal Wiener. Requires spectral factorization of \(S_{YY}\); the filter has a first-order rational form \(H(z) = K/(1-cz^{-1})\). The causality constraint costs a few percent in MSE relative to the non-causal optimum.

docs.title: 5.8 Wiener vs. Kalman equivalence
docs.text:
The causal Wiener filter for the model in 5.7 is

\[ H(z) = \frac{K}{1 - (1-K)z^{-1}},\qquad K = K_\infty \approx 0.0913. \]

This is exactly the steady-state Kalman filter's innovation-form transfer function — the two approaches solve the same LMMSE problem by different routes (frequency-domain factorization vs. state-space recursions).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 6 — Markov Chains
docs.text: Back to Chapter 6

docs.title: 6.1 Two-state chain \(P^n\)
docs.text:
\(P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix}\).

Eigenvalues: \(1\) and \(0.4\). Eigenvectors give \(P^n = \mathbf 1\pi + 0.4^n\begin{bmatrix}2/3 & -2/3\\-1/3 & 1/3\end{bmatrix}\) with \(\pi = (0.8333, 0.1667)\).

Convergence rate: \(0.4^n\). Mixing time to \(\|P^n - \mathbf 1\pi\|_\infty < 10^{-3}\): \(0.4^n < 10^{-3}\) ⇒ \(n \ge 7.5\) ⇒ \(n = 8\).

docs.title: 6.3 Ehrenfest urn (\(N=20\))
docs.text: The chain has period 2 — parity of the number of balls in urn 1 alternates every step. The raw empirical histogram (one lag per step) alternates between two distributions concentrated on even and odd states. Averaging over even and odd steps separately gives \(\binom{20}{k}/2^{20}\) — the true stationary distribution.

docs.title: 6.4 Classification table
docs.text: Matrix Classes Recurrent? Period \(\pi\) \(P^n\) converges? \(P_1 = I\) \(\{1\}, \{2\}\) both absorbing, recurrent 1 not unique yes \(P_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) \(\{1,2\}\) irreducible, recurrent 2 \((0.5, 0.5)\) no (Cesàro average does) \(P_3 = \begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix}\) \(\{1,2\}\) irreducible, recurrent 1 \((0.5, 0.5)\) yes (\(P_3^n = P_3\) for \(n \ge 1\))

docs.title: 6.5 Null recurrence of symmetric random walk on \(\mathbb Z\)
docs.text:
\(f_0 = 1\) (returns a.s.). But the first-return probabilities are

\[ \Pr\{\text{first return at } n\} = \frac{1}{n-1}\binom{n}{n/2}2^{-n} \]

for even \(n = 2m\), which is \(\sim \dfrac{1}{n^{3/2}\sqrt{\pi/2}}\). Then

\[ E[T_0] = \sum_n n \cdot \Pr\{\text{first return at } n\} \sim \sum_n n^{-1/2} \to \infty. \]

So \(m_0 = \infty\) — null recurrent, not positive recurrent.

docs.title: 6.6 Birth–death CTMCs
docs.text:
M/M/1 (\(\lambda_k = \lambda\), \(\mu_k = \mu\)): \(\pi_k = (1-\rho)\rho^k\) for \(\rho < 1\).

M/M/∞ (\(\lambda_k = \lambda\), \(\mu_k = k\mu\)): \(\pi_k = e^{-a}a^k/k!\) with \(a = \lambda/\mu\) — Poisson.

The M/M/∞ distribution follows from \(\pi_k = \pi_0\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\lambda/((j+1)\mu) = \pi_0 a^k/k!\).

docs.title: 6.7 Detailed balance check
docs.text:
Three-state directed cycle with \(P_{12}=P_{23}=P_{31}=1\), all other entries zero.

\(\pi = (1/3,1/3,1/3)\) satisfies \(\pi P = \pi\) ✓ (each state has exactly one incoming and one outgoing edge). But \(\pi_1 P_{12} = 1/3 \ne \pi_2 P_{21} = 0\) — detailed balance fails. This chain is not reversible: forward time goes \(1\to2\to3\to1\), backward gives \(1\to3\to2\to1\), a different chain.

docs.title: 6.8 M/M/1 simulation
docs.text:
\(T = 10^5\), \(\lambda=0.8\), \(\mu=1.0\): empirical \(\bar L \approx 4\) (theory \(\rho/(1-\rho) = 4\)). Empirical distribution of \(K\) matches \((1-\rho)\rho^k = 0.2\cdot 0.8^k\).

With \(\lambda = 1.1\): \(\rho = 1.1 > 1\). The queue grows as \((\lambda-\mu)t = 0.1t\); empirical histogram never stabilizes — this is what instability looks like: no stationary distribution exists.

docs.title: 6.9 PageRank preview
docs.text:
The PageRank chain has transition

\[ P_{ij} = \frac{1-d}{N} + d\,\frac{a_{ij}}{L_i},\qquad d = 0.85, \]

where \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicates a link from \(i\) to \(j\) and \(L_i\) is the out-degree of \(i\).

Solving \(\pi P = \pi\) gives the PageRank vector. For a 4-page graph with a mix of incoming links, \(\pi\) values are on the order of \(1/N\) to \(3/N\), weighted by link count.

Why \(d < 1\) matters: without damping (\(d=1\)), a page with no outgoing links (a "sink") or disconnected subgraph makes the chain reducible or periodic — \(\pi\) may not exist or may not be unique. The damping term guarantees irreducibility and aperiodicity, so \(\pi\) exists and is unique.

docs.title: 6.10 (extra) Two-state chain eigen-decomposition for mixing time
docs.text: \(P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix}\): subdominant eigenvalue \(0.4\). The \(\ell_\infty\) distance from stationarity decays as \(0.4^n\). To reach \(10^{-3}\): \(n \ge 8\) (see 6.1).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 7 — Queuing Theory
docs.text: Back to Chapter 7

docs.title: 7.1 Little's formula
docs.text:
18 patients, average stay 4 days. \(\lambda = 18/4 = 4.5\) arrivals/day.

New stay 3 days at same \(\lambda\): \(L = 4.5\cdot 3 = \mathbf{13.5}\) patients.

docs.title: 7.3 Unstable queue
docs.text:
\(\lambda = 12\), \(\mu = 10\): \(\rho = 1.2 > 1\).

The expression \(L = \rho/(1-\rho)\) is negative — not the answer: the stationary distribution does not exist. The queue length grows as \((\lambda-\mu)t = 2t\). After \(T=10^4\): expected queue length \(\approx 2\cdot 10^4\). Simulation shows linear growth with slope \(\lambda-\mu = 2\).

docs.title: 7.4 Erlang-C sensitivity
docs.text:
\(\lambda = 50\), \(\mu = 20\) calls/min ⇒ \(a = 2.5\) Erlangs. Find smallest \(s\) with \(C(s,a) \le 0.10\).

\(s\) \(\rho\) \(C(s,a)\) Wait? 3 0.833 0.578 57.8% — too high 4 0.625 0.164 16.4% — too high 5 0.500 0.036 3.6% ✓

At \(s=5\): \(L_q = C\cdot \rho/(1-\rho) = 0.036\cdot 1 = 0.036\); \(W_q = L_q/\lambda = 0.036/50 \approx 0.00072\) min.

At \(s=6\): \(C(6, 2.5) \approx 0.005\), \(W_q \approx 0.0001\) min — 7× lower wait, but 20% more servers. The marginal cost of the extra server is large; \(s=5\) is the practical answer.

docs.title: 7.5 M/M/1/K buffer
docs.text:
\(\lambda = 5\), \(\mu = 10\), \(\rho = 0.5\). \(\pi_K = \dfrac{(1-\rho)\rho^K}{1-\rho^{K+1}} = \dfrac{0.5^{K+1}}{1-0.5^{K+1}}\).

\(K\) Blocking \(\pi_K\) 1 0.333 2 0.143 5 0.0154 10 0.00049

Converges to 0 as \(K \to \infty\) — blocking vanishes with an infinite buffer, as expected.

docs.title: 7.6 PK formula comparison
docs.text:
\(\lambda = 6\), \(1/\mu = 0.1\) ⇒ \(\mu = 10\), \(\rho = 0.6\).

\[ L_q = \frac{\rho^2 + \lambda^2\sigma_s^2}{2(1-\rho)} = \frac{0.36 + 36\,\sigma_s^2}{0.8}. \] Service \(\sigma_s^2\) \(L_q\) Deterministic 0 \(0.36/0.8 = 0.45\) Erlang-2 \(1/(2\mu^2) = 0.005\) \((0.36+0.18)/0.8 = 0.675\) Exponential \(1/\mu^2 = 0.01\) \((0.36+0.36)/0.8 = 0.9\)

Order: \(L_q^{M/D/1} < L_q^{M/E_2/1} < L_q^{M/M/1}\) ✓. Reducing service variance nearly halves \(L_q\) — a cheap win over adding servers.

docs.title: 7.7 Jackson network
docs.text:
Two queues in series. Queue 1 has external arrivals \(r_1 = 4\), \(\mu_1 = 10\). Queue 2 has \(\mu_2 = 8\), no external arrivals.

Traffic equations. \(\lambda_1 = 4\); \(\lambda_2 = 0 + \lambda_1 = 4\).

Stability. \(\rho_1 = 0.4 < 1\) ✓; \(\rho_2 = 0.5 < 1\) ✓.

Per-queue means.

\[ L_1 = \frac{0.4}{0.6} \approx 0.667,\qquad L_2 = \frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1. \]

Network. \(L_{\text{net}} = 0.667 + 1 = 1.667\).

Network arrival rate \(= r_1 = 4\). Network mean time: \(W_{\text{net}} = L_{\text{net}}/4 \approx 0.417\) time units.

docs.title: 7.8 Simulation project
docs.text:
\(\lambda = 7\), \(\mu = 10\). Theory:

  • \(L = 7/3 \approx 2.333\), \(W = 1/3 \approx 0.333\)
  • \(L_q = 1.633\), \(W_q = 0.233\)

Simulation with \(T=10^6\) typically gives \(L\) within \(\pm 0.05\) of \(2.333\) with batch-means 95% CI.

M/D/1 comparison. Deterministic service with mean \(0.1\):

\[ L_q^{M/D/1} = \frac{\rho^2}{2(1-\rho)} = \frac{0.49}{0.6} \approx 0.817,\qquad L^{M/D/1} \approx 0.817 + 0.7 = 1.517. \]

That is 35% lower than M/M/1's \(L = 2.333\) — deterministic service is fundamentally more efficient than exponential at the same utilisation.

docs.title: 7.9 Real-data analysis
docs.text:
On public traces (WIDE / CAIDA), interarrival distributions are heavier-tailed than exponential. Log-normal or Weibull fits give a much better description of the tail.

Simulation with the empirical distribution therefore produces longer queues than M/M/1 predicts at the same mean arrival rate — the exponential assumption underestimates burstiness. This is why practical network engineering uses:

  • M/G/1 with empirically-measured service variance, or
  • self-similar / heavy-tailed traffic models (e.g. fractional Brownian motion), or
  • traffic shaping to make the arrival process closer to Poisson (smoothing the burstiness).

M/M/1 is the analytically tractable reference — it is usually an optimistic predictor for real traffic.
